zettels.title: Definition of Electroculture

questionAnswers.question: What methods are included under the term electroculture?
questionAnswers.answer:
Electroculture is a broad term for agricultural methods that expose seeds, plants, or soil to electric or electromagnetic effects in an attempt to influence germination, growth, or yield. Historically, it has included more than the copper-antenna method commonly shown online today. A 1926 U.S. Department of Agriculture bulletin defined electroculture as practices intended to increase crop growth or yield through electrical treatment, including maintaining an electric charge over plants or passing electric current through soil. FAO AGRIS

The main methods include:

MethodWhat it involvesAtmospheric or air–earth electrical systemsConductors, wires, elevated networks, or antennas are used to expose plants to atmospheric electrical fields or electrical discharge.Direct current through soilElectrodes are placed in soil and a controlled DC current is passed through the root zone.Alternating current through soil or plantsAC electrical stimulation is applied experimentally to soil, seeds, or plants.Electrostatic fieldsPlants or seeds are placed within a static electric field without necessarily passing current directly through them.High-voltage electric fields / corona dischargeHigh voltage creates an electric field and sometimes ionized air around plants.Seed electrical treatmentSeeds are exposed to electric fields, current, electrical discharge, or related treatments before planting.Pulsed electric fieldsShort electrical pulses are applied to seeds or plant tissues.Magnetic-field treatmentStatic or varying magnetic fields are applied to seeds or plants; this is often called magnetoculture/magneticulture, although some modern discussions group it with electroculture.Electrolysis-based systemsElectrical current is used in water or soil systems to alter chemical or ionic conditions associated with plant growth.Passive antenna systemsCopper wires, coils, spirals, or stakes are placed near plants with the claim that they collect atmospheric or earth electrical energy without an external power source.

Historical classifications were similar. A 1929 engineering paper divided electroculture into air–earth currents, earth currents, seed treatment, and other electrical methods. DOI Modern reviews describe experiments involving electrostatic fields, directly applied electrical currents, electrical discharges, electric shocks, and other electromagnetic treatments. ScienceDirect

Active vs. passive electroculture

This distinction is useful for your research.

Active electroculture uses a measurable external electrical source or controlled field, such as:

  • DC current,

  • AC current,

  • high voltage,

  • pulsed electric fields,

  • electrostatic fields,

  • controlled magnetic fields.

These methods can be experimentally measured in terms of voltage, current, field strength, exposure time, and plant response. Modern scientific research continues to investigate electric and magnetic field effects on processes such as membrane permeability, ion transport, oxidative responses, and gene expression. ACS Publications

Passive electroculture usually refers to devices such as copper antennas, coils, spirals, or stakes that supposedly collect naturally occurring atmospheric or telluric electrical energy without an external power supply.

These passive copper-antenna methods are widely promoted in gardening communities, but the evidence supporting their claimed agricultural benefits is much weaker than the evidence for controlled electrical-field experiments. Recent scientific discussion specifically distinguishes experimentally controlled electromagnetic stimulation from unsupported or poorly tested passive antenna claims. World Scientific News

A useful classification

Rather than treating electroculture as only “copper antennas in gardens,” I would capture it as an umbrella concept:

Electroculture is the application of electrical or electromagnetic phenomena to seeds, plants, soil, or agricultural environments with the objective of influencing germination, growth, development, or crop yield. Methods historically associated with electroculture include atmospheric electrical systems, direct soil currents, electric and electrostatic fields, electrical seed treatments, high-voltage discharge, and related electromagnetic treatments.

Then you could separate the methods beneath it as connected concepts:

Electroculture
→ Atmospheric electricity
→ Soil electrical current
→ Electrostatic-field treatment
→ Electric-field treatment
→ Seed electrical treatment
→ Pulsed electric fields
→ Magnetic-field treatment / magneticulture
→ Electrolysis
→ Passive copper antenna systems

That separation is important because these approaches do not all have the same scientific evidence behind them. A controlled electric-field experiment and a passive copper spiral in a garden may both be called “electroculture,” but scientifically they are very different interventions.

Sources

  • USDA, 1926 — Electroculture: one of the strongest historical primary sources defining the field and discussing electric charges over plants and currents through soil. FAO AGRIS

  • Journal of the Institution of Electrical Engineers, 1929 — Electricity in agriculture, with special reference to electro-culture: classifies methods into air-earth currents, earth currents, seed treatment, and other methods. DOI

  • Reviews of Modern Plasma Physics — Pulsed power applications for agriculture and food processing: discusses electric fields, ions, soil current, and modern electrical treatment of crops. DOI

  • ACS Agricultural Science & Technology — Electric and Magnetic Field Technologies in Agriculture: modern review of controlled electric- and magnetic-field technologies and possible plant-response mechanisms. ACS Publications

  • University of New Mexico repository — Review on Electroculture, Magneticulture and Laserculture: overview of related electrical and magnetic approaches. UNM Digital Repository

For your research, the most important distinction is therefore electroculture as a broad historical/scientific category versus the much narrower modern social-media meaning of passive copper antenna gardening.

questionAnswers.question: What scientific evidence exists for electroculture?
questionAnswers.answer:
Scientific evidence for electroculture exists, but it varies substantially depending on the method being studied.

Controlled experiments using electric fields, electrical currents, electrostatic fields, and magnetic fields have reported measurable effects on plant germination, growth, nutrient uptake, physiology, and sometimes yield. However, results are inconsistent across plant species and experimental conditions. ACS Publications

A 2025 review in ACS Agricultural Science & Technology found that electric and magnetic field treatments may affect plants through several proposed mechanisms, including:

  • changes in cell membrane permeability,

  • production of reactive oxygen species and antioxidant responses,

  • changes in ion absorption and transport,

  • and changes in gene expression. ACS Publications

A 2024 review in Scientia Horticulturae similarly found that electric fields have been associated with changes in seed germination, plant growth, physiology, and stress tolerance, while also emphasizing that treatment conditions and plant responses vary considerably. ScienceDirect

Individual experiments have also reported positive results. A 2025 study on Arabidopsis thaliana found that applied electric fields increased water and mineral uptake, altered electrical charge within plant tissue, increased auxin accumulation, and enhanced growth and development. ScienceDirect

A 2023 experiment with cowpea seeds exposed to strong electrostatic fields reported increased early seedling vigor at a particular field strength and approximately 30% greater yield compared with the control treatment. Other field strengths in the same experiments did not consistently produce visible effects, illustrating how strongly results can depend on treatment conditions. PubMed

Evidence also exists for magnetic-field treatments. A 2023 meta-analysis covering 45 studies and 29 plant species found some positive effects on plant growth and germination, but concluded that the effects were highly dependent on the experimental setup. PubMed

At the same time, systematic reviews have identified major weaknesses in the evidence. A review of static electric-field studies found reported changes in plant germination, growth, yield, and mineral concentrations, but concluded that many studies contained methodological flaws and that some apparent effects could have resulted from related factors such as corona discharge, ions, or other electrostatic conditions rather than the electric field itself. PubMed

Evidence concerning electromagnetic fields is similarly mixed. Researchers have reported possible positive effects on germination, growth rate, stress resistance, and yield, but reviews note contradictory outcomes and inconsistent experimental protocols, making broad conclusions difficult. PubMed

Passive copper-antenna electroculture

The scientific evidence is much weaker for the passive form of electroculture commonly promoted online, in which copper-wrapped stakes or antennas are placed in the soil without an external electrical source.

A controlled 2025 study tested copper-wrapped rods with mustard greens, kale, beets, and turnips. Researchers found no consistent improvement in plant growth, photosynthesis, or crop yield. They concluded that the passive devices probably produced too little voltage to meaningfully affect plant physiology. PubMed

Therefore, current evidence supports an important distinction:

MethodState of evidenceControlled electric-field treatmentExperimental evidence exists; results varyElectrical current applied to soil/plantsExperimental evidence existsElectrostatic treatmentSome positive experimental results; inconsistentMagnetic-field treatmentMeta-analytic evidence suggests some effects, but highly condition-dependentSeed electrical treatmentSeveral experimental studies report effectsPassive copper antennas/stakesNo convincing evidence of improved crop growth or yield

The scientific evidence therefore does not support treating all forms of electroculture as equivalent. Controlled electrical and electromagnetic treatments can produce measurable biological responses in plants, but the magnitude and practical agricultural value of those effects remain uncertain. Passive copper-antenna systems currently lack comparable supporting evidence. PubMed

Sources

  • PubMed — Passive electroculture using copper rods does not improve yield in home container vegetable gardening
    PubMed study

  • ACS Agricultural Science & Technology — Electric and Magnetic Field Technologies in Agriculture: Plant Responses, Experimental Limitations, and Future Directions
    ACS review

  • Scientia Horticulturae — Effects, physiological response and mechanism of plant under electric field application
    ScienceDirect review

    PubMed meta-analysis

    PubMed systematic review

questionAnswers.question: How have electroculture methods changed historically?
questionAnswers.answer:
Electroculture methods have changed considerably over time, moving from attempts to harness natural atmospheric electricity toward increasingly controlled electrical, electrostatic, electromagnetic, and plasma-based treatments.

Early electroculture developed from eighteenth-century experiments with atmospheric electricity. Abbé Pierre Bertholon de Saint-Lazare promoted the idea that atmospheric electricity could influence plant growth and developed devices intended to collect and direct atmospheric electrical charge toward crops. One of these devices, commonly described as an electro-végétomètre, used elevated conductors to collect atmospheric electricity and direct it toward plants. These early systems were based largely on observations and theories about natural electricity rather than on controlled measurement of electrical dose or exposure. A modern historical review notes that these experiments lacked the quantitative dosimetry and experimental controls expected in contemporary research.

During the nineteenth century, electroculture expanded beyond passive collection of atmospheric electricity. Researchers experimented with high-voltage electrical fields, electrical discharge, current passed through soil, and elevated conductive networks placed over growing crops. Atmospheric or “air-earth” systems attempted to establish electrical interaction between elevated conductors and the soil. Other systems applied electrical current directly through the soil using electrodes.

Selim Lemström became particularly influential in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. His work involved high-voltage electrical treatment of crops and the production of ions in the air around plants. His 1904 book, Electricity in Agriculture and Horticulture, described experiments using electrical fields and ionized air and helped establish electroculture as a recognizable field of agricultural experimentation.

By the early twentieth century, electroculture included several distinct methods rather than one single technique. A 1926 U.S. Department of Agriculture bulletin defined electroculture as practices intended to increase crop growth or yield through electrical treatment. The bulletin specifically described methods such as maintaining an electric charge on a network positioned over plants and passing electric current through the soil.

A 1929 paper in the Journal of the Institution of Electrical Engineers classified electroculture into four broad categories:

- air-earth currents,

- earth currents,

- seed treatment,

- and other electrical methods.

Air-earth systems generally used elevated conductors or charged networks above crops and electrical discharge between the air and ground. Earth-current systems passed electrical current through soil. Seed-treatment systems applied electrical treatment before planting rather than continuously exposing the growing crop.

This classification shows an important change in electroculture. Early approaches frequently attempted to influence entire fields through atmospheric electricity, while later researchers began treating specific parts of the agricultural system, particularly seeds and soil.

During the twentieth century, electroculture research increasingly shifted toward controlled laboratory, greenhouse, and field experiments. Instead of simply exposing plants to electrical equipment and comparing growth, researchers began controlling variables such as:

- electric-field strength,

- voltage,

- current,

- polarity,

- frequency,

- duration of exposure,

- distance from electrodes,

- seed moisture,

- soil conductivity,

- plant species,

- developmental stage,

- and environmental conditions.

Electrical seed treatment became especially important because seeds could be treated under repeatable conditions before planting. Researchers investigated direct current, alternating current, electrostatic fields, electrical discharge, and later pulsed electrical treatments.

Another major development was the separation of different electrical phenomena that earlier electroculture experiments often treated as one effect. Modern research distinguishes among:

- direct electrical current,

- alternating electrical current,

- static electric fields,

- pulsed electric fields,

- electrostatic fields,

- corona discharge,

- atmospheric-pressure plasma,

- ionized air,

- magnetic fields,

- and electromagnetic fields.

This distinction is scientifically important because these treatments do not affect plants through exactly the same physical mechanisms.

Modern electric-field research typically uses defined field strengths and exposure times. Researchers may expose seeds, roots, seedlings, or whole plants to controlled electric fields and then measure effects on germination, root development, shoot growth, nutrient transport, enzyme activity, gene expression, stress response, or crop yield.

Magnetic-field treatment has also become associated with modern electroculture research, although it is sometimes treated separately under terms such as magnetoculture or magnetic stimulation. Contemporary studies use controlled static or varying magnetic fields rather than relying on naturally occurring magnetic conditions.

Pulsed electric fields represent another modern development. Instead of continuously exposing plants or seeds to electricity, short electrical pulses are applied at controlled intensities and durations. This allows researchers to study biological responses while precisely controlling electrical exposure.

In the twenty-first century, some electroculture research has developed into what is now called plasma agriculture. Cold atmospheric plasma systems use electrical energy to ionize gases and produce a mixture of charged particles, reactive oxygen species, reactive nitrogen species, electric fields, ultraviolet radiation, and other effects.

Plasma agriculture can be used for:

- seed treatment,

- seed priming,

- stimulation of germination,

- plant-growth studies,

- soil treatment,

- water treatment,

- microbial decontamination,

- and postharvest food treatment.

This represents a major technological change from historical electroculture. Early systems attempted to harness naturally occurring atmospheric electricity or apply relatively simple electrical currents. Modern plasma systems generate controlled electrical and chemical environments whose physical parameters can be measured and reproduced.

Contemporary electroculture research also focuses much more strongly on biological mechanisms. Current studies investigate whether electrical or magnetic treatments influence:

- cell-membrane permeability,

- movement of ions across cell membranes,

- nutrient absorption,

- reactive oxygen species production,

- antioxidant responses,

- hormone signaling,

- enzyme activity,

- water uptake,

- gene expression,

- and plant stress responses.

A 2026 review in ACS Agricultural Science & Technology identifies four major mechanisms currently proposed for electric- and magnetic-field effects on plants:

- changes in membrane permeability,

- production of reactive oxygen species and antioxidant responses,

- changes in ion absorption and transport,

- and alterations in DNA-related processes and gene expression.

Electroculture has therefore changed not only technologically but also scientifically. Historical systems were often evaluated primarily by observing whether plants appeared to grow faster or produce greater yields. Modern research attempts to identify the exact electrical parameters used, isolate the physical treatment involved, measure biological responses, and reproduce results under controlled conditions.

Another major historical change is the distinction between active and passive systems.

Historical and modern active electroculture methods use a defined electrical source, such as:

- high-voltage generators,

- electrodes,

- electrical power supplies,

- pulse generators,

- electrostatic field generators,

- or plasma devices.

These systems allow voltage, current, field strength, and treatment duration to be measured.

Passive electroculture systems, including some modern copper antennas, copper coils, spirals, and metal stakes promoted for gardening, generally do not use an externally powered electrical source. They are usually claimed to collect atmospheric or earth electrical energy.

These passive systems resemble some early historical ideas about collecting atmospheric electricity, but they are not equivalent to modern controlled electric-field or plasma experiments. Scientific evidence for passive copper-antenna systems is currently much weaker than the evidence for controlled electrical treatments.

Overall, the historical development of electroculture can be summarized as a progression:

18th century:

Atmospheric electricity collection and early experimental devices such as Bertholon’s electro-végétomètre.

19th century:

High-voltage experiments, atmospheric electrical networks, electrical discharge, soil currents, and early investigations of electrically stimulated plant growth.

Late 19th–early 20th century:

More systematic experiments by researchers such as Selim Lemström involving high-voltage fields, ionized air, and crop-production trials.

Early 20th century:

Electroculture formally divided into methods such as air-earth currents, earth currents, and seed treatment. Government and engineering organizations began evaluating the claims experimentally.

Mid-20th century:

Greater emphasis on controlled electrical treatment, electrochemistry, seed treatment, electrical discharge, and laboratory experimentation.

Late 20th century:

Increasing use of precisely measured electric fields, electromagnetic fields, electrostatic treatments, and pulsed electrical systems.

21st century:

Controlled electric- and magnetic-field technologies, pulsed electric fields, plasma agriculture, mechanistic plant-physiology studies, and greater emphasis on reproducibility and measurable treatment parameters.

The historical trend is therefore from relatively broad attempts to harness natural electricity toward increasingly controlled and measurable treatments. Modern electroculture-related research is less focused on simply “collecting electricity” and more focused on determining which electrical or electromagnetic conditions produce measurable biological responses, why those responses occur, and whether they can be reproduced reliably.

zettels.body:
The first step in developing a pop-up catering or meal-prep menu is customer research.

A business should identify one specific customer group and understand how food fits into that group's daily routine before building a full menu.

The first menu should be treated as a test. Research should influence:
- Menu items
- Portion sizes
- Pricing
- Packaging
- Pickup or delivery method
- Service hours
zettels.mainIdea: Menu development should begin by understanding a specific reachable customer group rather than guessing what people might want.
zettels.title: Start With the Customer, Not the Menu

zettels.body:
The central business question is:

What meals, snacks, beverages, portion sizes, price points, and ordering options would this customer group realistically purchase?

The question should be answered using information from actual potential customers rather than stereotypes based on profession, neighborhood, age, or culture.
zettels.mainIdea: Customer research should determine what a specific group will realistically purchase rather than relying on assumptions about that group.
questions: What meals would this customer group realistically purchase?
What snacks would this customer group realistically purchase?
What beverages would this customer group realistically purchase?
What portion sizes do they prefer?
What price points are acceptable?
What ordering options do they prefer?
zettels.title: Core Customer Research Question for Pop-Up Catering

zettels.body:
Eight major research areas should be examined:

1. Eating routine
Determine when customers normally eat and whether meal times are predictable or interrupted.

2. Buying behavior
Determine whether customers bring food, buy food, order delivery, skip meals, or use a combination.

3. Food preferences
Identify preferred meals, proteins, sides, snacks, beverages, cuisines, and comfort foods.

4. Convenience needs
Determine preferences for hot or cold food, reheatable food, handheld items, grab-and-go options, delivery, pickup, and preorder.

5. Portion needs
Determine whether customers prefer light meals, standard meals, large meals, snacks, or shareable options.

6. Dietary needs
Identify dietary restrictions, allergies, and preferences.

7. Price tolerance
Determine normal meal spending and what customers consider a fair price.

8. Purchase intent
Determine whether customers would actually preorder or purchase from the service.
zettels.mainIdea: Customer food-service research should examine routines, buying behavior, preferences, convenience, portions, dietary needs, price tolerance, and purchase intent.
zettels.title: Customer Research Areas for Pop-Up Catering and Meal Prep

zettels.body:
The initial customer survey should remain short enough that potential customers are willing to complete it.

The guide recommends approximately ten to twelve questions for the initial test.

The answers should later be reviewed for repeated patterns rather than treating each individual response as a menu requirement.
zettels.mainIdea: A short customer survey can gather practical information about routines, spending, food preferences, convenience needs, dietary restrictions, and purchase intent.
questions: What best describes your normal work schedule or daily routine?
During a typical day, do you usually bring food, buy food, order delivery, or use a combination?
What do you usually spend on one meal?
What are your top three meals or types of food you would most likely purchase?
Which proteins do you prefer?
Which sides, snacks, or small items would you actually buy?
What beverages do you usually purchase with food?
Do you prefer hot food, cold food, or either?
Do you need food that can be eaten without reheating?
Do you have any dietary restrictions, allergies, or food preferences?
What is one food item you wish were easier to get during your day?
Would you preorder from a local meal-prep or pop-up service if pickup or delivery were convenient?
zettels.title: Short Customer Survey for Pop-Up Catering Research

zettels.body:
Customer research should go beyond survey responses.

Observe:
- When customers normally buy food
- What businesses are open at those times
- Nearby delis, restaurants, food carts, cafés, meal-prep services, and delivery options
- Common prices
- Portion sizes
- Packaging
- Pickup speed
- Menu variety

Also identify repeated customer frustrations such as:
- Long waits
- Poor late-night options
- High prices
- Weak portions
- Limited healthy choices
- Food that does not travel well
zettels.mainIdea: Survey responses become more useful when they are compared with how customers currently obtain food and with the options already available to them.
zettels.title: Customer Surveys Should Be Combined With Observation

zettels.body:
A first pop-up menu is a test rather than a complete menu.

Use customer research to select approximately three to five core items.

Where practical:
- Use ingredients across multiple menu items
- Reduce waste
- Simplify preparation
- Include a grab-and-go or snack option when convenience matters
- Calculate ingredient cost, packaging, labor, transportation, fees, and profit before pricing
- Produce a limited quantity
- Record what sells
- Record what does not sell
- Record what customers request next
zettels.mainIdea: The first menu should test customer demand with a small number of items selected from the strongest research patterns.
zettels.title: Build a Small Test Menu From Customer Research

zettels.body:
The working cycle is:

1. Research the customer.
2. Identify repeated needs.
3. Build a small test menu.
4. Estimate cost and selling price.
5. Test limited quantities.
6. Record sales.
7. Record customer feedback.
8. Adjust the next menu using actual purchasing behavior.

The menu should develop from evidence about what customers actually buy rather than assumptions about what they might buy.
zettels.mainIdea: Food-service development should use an iterative cycle of customer research, small-scale testing, measurement, and revision rather than assumptions.
zettels.title: Research, Test Small, Measure, and Adjust

zettels.body:
The survey is organized into five sections.

1. About Your Meal

Collect:
- Dishes tried
- Dish being rated
- Taste
- Portion size
- Presentation
- Value for price
- Whether the customer would order the dish again

2. Food Preferences

Collect:
- Preferred cuisines and food categories
- Preferred food format
- Reasonable price for a complete meal

3. About You — Optional

Collect:
- Age range
- NYC borough
- Gender
- Race or ethnicity

4. Future Interest

Collect:
- Likelihood of purchasing again
- Future product or service interest
- Expected purchase frequency

5. Customer Feedback

Collect:
- What the customer liked most
- What could be improved
- Desired future menu items
- Additional comments

The resulting information can be used to compare dishes, identify repeated customer preferences, evaluate pricing, and guide future menu development.
zettels.mainIdea: A post-event customer survey can collect structured information about the meal, food preferences, pricing, customer characteristics, future purchase interest, and open-ended feedback.
zettels.title: Pop-Up Catering Customer Survey and Feedback Method

zettels.body:
The customer feedback card evaluates each dish using five main measures.

Taste
- Excellent
- Good
- Average
- Fair
- Poor

Portion Size
- Too Small
- Just Right
- Too Large

Presentation
- Excellent
- Good
- Average
- Fair
- Poor

Value for Price
- Excellent
- Good
- Average
- Fair
- Poor

Would You Order It Again?
- Yes
- Maybe
- No

These measures provide a consistent way to compare test-menu items after a pop-up event.
zettels.mainIdea: A test-menu dish can be evaluated using customer ratings for taste, portion size, presentation, value for price, and willingness to order the item again.
zettels.title: Meal Evaluation Criteria for Pop-Up Catering

zettels.body:
The feedback card states that participation is optional and instructs respondents not to include their names.

The demographic section is also marked optional.

The survey asks about:
- Age range
- NYC borough
- Gender
- Race or ethnicity

The purpose of these questions is to allow feedback patterns to be compared across customer groups without requiring personally identifying information.

This distinction is important when designing future customer-feedback instruments:
- Customer identity is not required.
- Demographic responses are optional.
- Food and purchasing feedback can still be collected without identifying the individual respondent.
zettels.mainIdea: A customer feedback survey can collect useful demographic and preference information without requiring the respondent's name, and sensitive demographic questions should remain optional.
zettels.title: Customer Feedback Surveys Should Be Optional and Anonymous

zettels.body:
I see human dignity as something that belongs to every person simply because they are a person. A person's circumstances do not determine whether they deserve dignity.

A person's income, housing situation, health, social status, background, occupation, or need for assistance may change, but their dignity does not.

This is why I see human dignity connecting across different areas of life and work. I am not making these connections simply for the sake of connecting subjects. I am asking how each area affects people and whether the way people are treated preserves their dignity.

The connection between these areas is not that they are identical. The connection is that they all involve people.

Hospitality

In hospitality, dignity affects how a person is welcomed, spoken to, served, included, and treated.

Catering and Food Service

In catering and food service, dignity means considering whether people are treated with respect regardless of how much they are paying, what dietary needs they have, what event they are attending, or what circumstances brought them there.

Menu Planning

In menu planning, dignity can appear in the choices people are given, whether dietary, cultural, religious, medical, and personal needs are respected, how food is described and presented, and whether people are made to feel like a burden because they need something different.

Shelter Work

In shelter work, dignity means recognizing that a person experiencing homelessness is still a person with preferences, boundaries, privacy, autonomy, possessions, relationships, and the need to be treated with respect.

Healthcare

In healthcare, dignity includes respecting a person's autonomy, privacy, preferences, cultural or religious needs, and right to be treated as a person rather than only as a patient or diagnosis.

Photography

In photography, dignity means considering how a person is represented and whether the image respects their humanity rather than exploiting, humiliating, or reducing them to their circumstances.

Application and System Design

In application and system design, dignity means considering whether the system respects the person using it. Design decisions can affect autonomy, privacy, accessibility, choice, fairness, and how a person is represented or treated within the system.

The central question I can carry into each area is:

How does this practice, service, system, or decision affect the dignity of the person involved?

Human dignity therefore becomes a principle that can cross domains while still requiring separate examination of what dignity means in each particular context.

At its simplest, this comes down to dignity for each person, no matter what the circumstances.
zettels.mainIdea: Every person possesses dignity regardless of circumstance, status, income, health, housing, background, or the type of service they are receiving. Therefore, any system or practice involving people should be examined by asking whether it preserves and respects that dignity.
questions: What does it mean to preserve a person's dignity?
What practices can unintentionally undermine human dignity?
How does dignity relate to autonomy and choice?
How does dignity relate to respect?
What does human dignity require in hospitality?
What does human dignity require in catering and food service?
How should human dignity influence menu planning?
What does human dignity require in shelter work?
What does human dignity require in healthcare?
How should photography preserve human dignity?
How should human dignity influence application and system design?
zettels.title: Human Dignity as a Cross-Domain Principle

zettels.body:
Source:
The Psychological Safety Playbook: Lead More Powerfully by Being More Human

Author:
Karolin Helbig

Page:
8

Exact Quote:
"Courageous communication is one of the most fundamental skills needed to create a psychologically safe environment for everyone."

Research Note:
This passage connects communication directly with psychological safety. It identifies courageous communication as a fundamental skill involved in creating an environment that is psychologically safe for everyone.

Connection to Safety Research:
Psychological safety is affected not only by whether danger or punishment is present, but also by how people are able to communicate within an environment. Communication practices can therefore be examined as one of the conditions that contribute to whether an environment feels psychologically safe.
zettels.mainIdea: Courageous communication is presented as a fundamental skill for creating an environment in which people can experience psychological safety.
zettels.title: Courageous Communication and Psychological Safety

zettels.body:
Source:
The Psychological Safety Playbook

Author:
Karolin Helbig

Page:
8

Exact Quote:
"Courage requires us to get out of our comfort zone, which means that you may not feel immediately comfortable with some of the moves in this play."

Research Note:
The passage separates courage from comfort. Acting courageously may require a person to move beyond familiar behavior and tolerate some initial discomfort.

The fact that an action feels uncomfortable does not automatically mean that the action is unsafe. The discomfort may come from doing something unfamiliar, developing a new skill, changing an established pattern, or communicating in a way that requires greater courage.

Connection to Courageous Communication:
Courageous communication may require practicing forms of communication that do not initially feel natural or comfortable.

Connection to Psychological Safety:
If courageous communication contributes to psychological safety, then developing a psychologically safer environment may sometimes require people to move beyond their existing comfort zones while learning new ways of communicating.
zettels.mainIdea: Courage may require moving beyond what feels immediately comfortable, especially when practicing new behaviors connected with courageous communication and psychological safety.
zettels.title: Courage Requires Moving Beyond the Comfort Zone

zettels.body:
Source:
The Psychological Safety Playbook

Author:
Karolin Helbig

Exact Quote:
"Keep in mind that communicating courageously is not only about what we say but also about inviting others to contribute to dialogue, being honest about our own feelings, letting go of our need to be right or perfect, and setting the tone for humor and levity to counteract the natural discomfort that often accompanies courageous communication."

Research Note:
Courageous communication is broader than the words a person chooses to speak. It also involves how the conversation is created and how other people are invited to participate.

The passage identifies several practices involved in courageous communication:

1. Inviting Others Into Dialogue
Courageous communication creates room for other people to contribute rather than allowing one person to control the conversation.

2. Honesty About Feelings
A person may need to acknowledge and communicate their own feelings honestly rather than hiding behind certainty, authority, or emotional distance.

3. Letting Go of the Need to Be Right
Courageous dialogue requires openness to the possibility that one's own position may not be completely correct.

4. Letting Go of Perfection
Communication does not have to be flawless before a person participates honestly and openly.

5. Humor and Levity
Humor and levity can help reduce some of the natural discomfort that accompanies courageous conversations.

Connection to Psychological Safety:
Psychological safety involves more than encouraging people to speak. The environment must also make room for participation, honesty, imperfection, disagreement, and human interaction.

Connection to Courageous Communication:
Courageous communication can therefore be understood as a relational practice. It involves both expressing oneself and helping create conditions in which other people can participate in the conversation.
zettels.mainIdea: Courageous communication involves not only speaking courageously but also inviting others into dialogue, expressing feelings honestly, releasing the need to be right or perfect, and using humor and levity to reduce the discomfort that can accompany difficult communication.
zettels.title: Courageous Communication Is More Than What We Say
A Hurtful Comment About My Weight and Its Effect on My Self-Esteem
zettels.mainIdea: A comment a Taxi driver made about being able to feel my weight while he was driving made me feel insecure, mocked, insulted, and hurt, and it further lowered my self-esteem. The memory remains significant because the comment affected not only how I felt about my body but also how I felt about myself as a person.
zettels.body: Explore why this memory remained emotionally significant. Connection to self-esteem and body-related insecurity. Connection to feeling mocked, insulted, and disrespected. Possible connection to human dignity and how comments about a person's body can affect their sense of worth. Possible connection to emotional and psychological safety in relationships and communication.
questions: Why has this memory remained emotionally significant?
How did this comment affect my self-esteem?
How can comments about a person's body affect their sense of dignity?
How are ridicule and humiliation connected to psychological safety?
Why did this comment affect how I felt about myself as a person?
researchedQuestions: How are ridicule and humiliation connected to psychological safety?

questionAnswers.question: How are ridicule and humiliation connected to psychological safety?
questionAnswers.answer:
Ridicule and humiliation are directly connected to psychological safety because psychological safety depends on whether a person believes it is safe to take interpersonal risks. Those risks include asking questions, admitting mistakes, requesting help, expressing concerns, disagreeing, or offering an idea. If a person expects to be laughed at, mocked, embarrassed, shamed, or humiliated for doing those things, the perceived interpersonal risk increases and psychological safety decreases.

Amy Edmondson describes psychological safety as a belief that a person can speak up without being punished or humiliated. Harvard Business School explains that fear of making a negative impression can cause people to withhold questions, mistakes, concerns, and ideas. This means humiliation is not simply an unpleasant interaction; it can teach a person that speaking honestly carries social consequences.

Ridicule can have the same effect. Edmondson explains that when someone responds negatively to a person's contribution—for example, by ridiculing the person or reacting harshly—the individual becomes less likely to speak openly again because the experience signals that interpersonal risk is unsafe. Even smaller reactions, such as visible exasperation or uncomfortable silence, can discourage future participation.

The American Psychological Association similarly describes psychological safety as an environment in which people can share concerns and mistakes without fear of embarrassment or retaliation and can speak without expecting to be humiliated, ignored, or blamed. This makes humiliation almost the opposite of the conditions psychological safety is intended to create.

Research on workplace incivility also supports this connection. A 2022 study of 518 frontline service employees found that workplace incivility was associated with emotional irritation and reduced employee voice. Another study found that supervisor incivility was associated with psychological distress, which in turn affected employees' willingness to engage in both promotive and prohibitive voice. These findings are relevant because ridicule and humiliation can function as forms of disrespectful or uncivil treatment that discourage people from speaking up.

More recent research has also found that workplace humiliation is associated with higher levels of stress and depressive symptoms. That study did not measure psychological safety directly, so it should not be used to claim that humiliation automatically causes low psychological safety. However, it provides additional evidence that humiliating treatment can create a threatening interpersonal environment.

For my own Safety research, this suggests that ridicule and humiliation matter because they can change what I believe will happen if I make myself vulnerable. If previous experiences taught me that speaking, asking for help, showing uncertainty, making a mistake, or revealing something personal may result in ridicule or humiliation, I may protect myself by remaining silent, withdrawing, hiding uncertainty, or avoiding vulnerability. In that way, ridicule and humiliation can affect not only how a particular interaction feels, but also whether a relationship or environment feels psychologically safe afterward.

References

Amy C. Edmondson and Zhike Lei. “Psychological Safety: The History, Renaissance, and Future of an Interpersonal Construct.” Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior, 2014.
Annual Reviews article

Harvard Business School. “Leading in Tough Times: HBS Faculty member Amy C. Edmondson on Psychological Safety.”
Harvard Business School source

Harvard Business School Working Knowledge. “New Hires Lose Psychological Safety After Year One. How to Fix It.”
Harvard Business School Working Knowledge source

American Psychological Association. “Psychological Safety in the Changing Workplace: Work in America 2024.”
APA source

International Journal of Hospitality Management. “Does incivility in quick service restaurants suppress the voice of employee? A moderated mediation model.” 2022.
ScienceDirect article

Leadership & Organization Development Journal. “Supervisor incivility and employee voice: the roles of cognitive reappraisal and psychological distress.” 2022.

zettels.title: Being Asked to Step Down From Praise Ministry and Losing a Place of Safety and Belonging
zettels.mainIdea: Being asked by my pastor to step down from leading the praise ministry because I was in a homosexual relationship with Gus affected more than my ministry role. At that time, the praise ministry was one of the only things I had left that gave me a sense of safety, belonging, connection, purpose, and stability. Being asked to step down therefore felt like losing both a role and one of the places where I felt that I belonged.
zettels.body:
I remember being asked by my pastor to step down from leading the praise ministry because I was in a homosexual relationship with Gus.

At that time, leading the praise ministry felt like the only thing I had left to hold on to. The ministry had become a place where I felt safe, connected, useful, and that I belonged.

Being asked to step down therefore meant more to me than losing a leadership position. I experienced it as losing something that had become connected to my sense of safety, belonging, purpose, connection, and stability.

An important part of this memory is the reason I was asked to step down. I was in a homosexual relationship with Gus. The same church and ministry environment where I had experienced safety and belonging became the environment where I experienced rejection because of that relationship.

This creates a tension in the memory between belonging and rejection. I had experienced the ministry as a place where I belonged, yet I was then told that I could no longer continue leading because of a relationship that was part of my life.

The experience raises questions for me about what belonging actually means. If belonging depends on meeting particular expectations or conditions, then that belonging may feel secure only while those conditions are being met.

It also connects to my larger exploration of safety. A place, community, relationship, or role can become psychologically important because it represents stability, acceptance, identity, and connection. When that place of belonging is lost, the loss can affect a person's sense of safety as well.

There is also a connection to human dignity. Regardless of whether people agree about sexuality, doctrine, or church leadership requirements, the way a person is treated during disagreement, correction, exclusion, or removal can affect that person's sense of dignity, worth, safety, and belonging.

Romans 1:26–27 is a Scripture passage I want to research separately in the King James Version with Apocrypha because of its relevance to biblical discussions of same-sex sexual relations. I do not want to assume that this specific passage was the pastor's stated biblical basis unless I can establish that. The historical memory remains that I was asked to step down because I was in a homosexual relationship with Gus.

researchedQuestions: What is the relationship between belonging and psychological safety?

questionAnswers.question: What is the relationship between belonging and psychological safety?
questionAnswers.answer:
Belonging and psychological safety are closely related because both involve whether a person feels accepted and able to participate without fear of rejection, embarrassment, humiliation, or punishment. Belonging concerns whether a person feels that they are accepted, connected, and that they have a legitimate place within a group or relationship. Psychological safety concerns whether that person believes it is safe to take interpersonal risks, such as speaking honestly, asking questions, admitting mistakes, requesting help, disagreeing, or showing vulnerability.

Amy Edmondson explains psychological safety as an environment in which candor and vulnerability are welcome and people do not expect to be punished or humiliated for speaking up. She also connects psychological safety with inclusion, explaining that a genuinely inclusive environment must be psychologically safe for everyone, including people from historically marginalized or underrepresented groups.

Data from the American Psychological Association show a strong relationship between psychological safety and belonging. In the APA's 2024 Work in America survey, 95% of workers experiencing higher psychological safety said they felt that they belonged at work, compared with 69% of workers experiencing lower psychological safety. Workers with higher psychological safety were also more likely to report that they could be themselves at work: 95% compared with 75% among those experiencing lower psychological safety. These results show an association between psychological safety, belonging, and the ability to be authentic, although the survey does not by itself establish that one directly causes the other.

Belonging may also contribute to psychological safety. A 2025 study involving 377 participants found that belongingness significantly predicted psychological safety (B = 0.26, p < .01). The researchers also found a significant pathway in which ethical leadership was associated with belongingness, belongingness was associated with psychological safety, and psychological safety was then associated with creativity. This provides evidence that feeling connected and accepted within a group may help create conditions in which people feel safer taking interpersonal risks.

The relationship can therefore work in both directions. When I feel that I belong, I may be less concerned that a mistake, disagreement, request for help, or expression of vulnerability will cause me to lose acceptance or connection. That can make interpersonal risk feel safer. At the same time, when an environment repeatedly shows me that I can speak honestly, ask questions, make mistakes, disagree, and still be treated with respect, those experiences can strengthen my sense that I am accepted and that I belong.

The opposite can also occur. If belonging feels conditional—if acceptance depends on remaining silent, hiding parts of myself, agreeing with others, or avoiding mistakes—I may technically be part of a group while still not feeling psychologically safe. Psychological safety therefore adds an important dimension to belonging: it is not only whether I am included, but whether I can participate as myself without constantly fearing that honesty, vulnerability, disagreement, or mistakes will threaten my place in the group.

For my Safety research, this distinction is important because belonging can provide connection and acceptance, while psychological safety concerns whether that connection remains secure when I become vulnerable. A place can give me a strong sense of belonging, but if I believe that revealing something about myself, disagreeing, making a mistake, or failing to meet certain expectations could result in rejection, then my sense of psychological safety may still be fragile.

References

American Psychological Association. “A Sense of Belonging Is Crucial for Employees. How Employers Can Foster Connection and Social Support.” Updated June 26, 2024. APA article on belonging and psychological safety

American Psychological Association. “2024 Work in America Survey: Psychological Safety in the Changing Workplace.” 2024. APA 2024 Work in America report

Harvard Business School. “Leading in Tough Times: HBS Faculty Member Amy C. Edmondson on Psychological Safety.” November 22, 2022. Harvard Business School source

Harvard Business School. “Fostering Candor in Teams and Organizations.” Harvard Business School source on psychological safety and inclusion

Frontiers in Psychology. “Belonging through values: ethical leadership, creativity, and psychological safety with ethical climate as a moderator.” 2025. Peer-reviewed Frontiers article

zettels.title: Courage Includes Not Having All the Answers
zettels.mainIdea: Courage is not limited to speaking up. It can also mean admitting that I do not have all the answers, asking for help, welcoming disagreement, and being able to laugh at myself.
zettels.body:
Source:
The Psychological Safety Playbook

Author:
Karolin Helbig

Page:
8

Exact Quote:
“It takes courage to not have all the answers, to ask for help, to invite dissent, and to laugh at yourself.”

Research Note:
This passage expands what courage means within psychological safety. Courage can involve giving up the expectation that I must always know the answer or appear completely certain.

Asking for help requires admitting that I need something from another person.

Inviting dissent requires being willing to hear disagreement rather than surrounding myself only with agreement.

Laughing at myself requires letting go of some of the pressure to appear perfect or always be right.

These behaviors can support psychological safety because they make room for vulnerability, participation, disagreement, learning, and imperfection.

Connection to Courageous Communication:
Courageous communication is not only about speaking difficult truths. It also involves creating room for other people to contribute, challenge ideas, offer help, and participate honestly.
questions: Why does admitting I do not have all the answers require courage?
How does asking for help contribute to psychological safety?
Why is inviting dissent important for psychological safety?
How does the need to be right or perfect interfere with courageous communication?
How can humor and the ability to laugh at myself reduce interpersonal pressure?
researchedQuestions: How does asking for help contribute to psychological safety?
Why is inviting dissent important for psychological safety?

questionAnswers.question: How does asking for help contribute to psychological safety?
questionAnswers.answer:
Asking for help contributes to psychological safety because it requires a person to admit that they do not know something, cannot do something alone, or need support from another person. That creates interpersonal vulnerability. When a person can ask for help without being mocked, embarrassed, punished, or treated as incompetent, the response communicates that uncertainty and dependence are acceptable within that environment.

In The Psychological Safety Playbook, Karolin Helbig connects courage with asking for help, writing on page 8: “It takes courage to not have all the answers, to ask for help, to invite dissent, and to laugh at yourself.” This suggests that asking for help is not simply obtaining assistance; it involves being willing to reveal that I do not have every answer.

Amy Edmondson similarly describes asking for help as a learning behavior that involves interpersonal risk. Harvard Business School reports her explanation that saying “I need help. I’m not sure what to do here” is a learning behavior because it can feel embarrassing or risky. When people are able to take that risk, teams are better able to learn, identify mistakes, share knowledge, and solve problems.

The response to the request for help is also important. Edmondson explains that when someone asks for help and receives a kind and constructive response, psychological safety is preserved. When the response is ridicule, harsh criticism, exasperation, or another negative reaction, the person may become less willing to speak up or ask for help again.

Research also shows a relationship between respectful workplace interactions and help-seeking. Friedman, Carmeli, and Dutton found that respectful engagement with supervisors encouraged help-seeking behavior, and that help-seeking was associated with improved job performance.

This means asking for help and psychological safety can reinforce one another. Psychological safety makes it easier for a person to risk asking for help, while a supportive response to that request provides evidence that vulnerability is acceptable. Repeated experiences of asking for help and being treated respectfully can strengthen the expectation that it is safe to admit uncertainty, seek assistance, learn, and participate honestly.

References

Helbig, Karolin. The Psychological Safety Playbook: Lead More Powerfully by Being More Human. Page 8.

Harvard Business School Working Knowledge. Four Steps to Building the Psychological Safety That High-Performing Teams Need.
Harvard Business School source

Harvard Business School Working Knowledge. New Hires Lose Psychological Safety After Year One. How to Fix It.
Harvard Business School source

Friedman, Anat, Abraham Carmeli, and Jane E. Dutton. “When does respectful engagement with one's supervisor foster help-seeking behaviors and performance?” Journal of Vocational Behavior, Vol. 104, 2018, pp. 184–198.
Journal article

questionAnswers.question: Why is inviting dissent important for psychological safety?
questionAnswers.answer:
Inviting dissent is important for psychological safety because disagreement is one of the interpersonal risks people often avoid when they fear embarrassment, rejection, punishment, or being viewed as difficult. When people are explicitly invited to disagree, question a decision, identify a problem, or offer another point of view, they receive a signal that speaking honestly is acceptable rather than dangerous.

Karolin Helbig connects dissent with courageous communication in The Psychological Safety Playbook. On page 8 she writes, “It takes courage to not have all the answers, to ask for help, to invite dissent, and to laugh at yourself.” Inviting dissent therefore involves more than allowing disagreement after it happens. It means deliberately creating space for another person to challenge an idea or decision.

Amy Edmondson explains that people commonly hold back because they fear the interpersonal consequences of disagreeing, particularly with someone who has more authority. She notes that people may avoid criticizing the status quo because they do not want to be seen as negative. When important concerns are withheld, teams lose opportunities for learning and improvement. Psychological safety helps reduce this interpersonal fear so that concerns, questions, mistakes, and opposing views can be discussed.

Inviting dissent also communicates that another person's perspective has value. Edmondson recommends that leaders actively ask for input rather than simply claiming that people are free to speak. Questions such as “What are we missing?” encourage people to contribute information that a leader or group may not already have. She specifically warns against reacting angrily when someone brings a dissenting view or bad news because a negative response can teach people that speaking honestly is unsafe.

Research on psychological safety supports this connection between safety and voice. Edmondson and Lei's review of the research describes psychological safety as people's perception of the consequences of interpersonal risk and identifies it as an important factor in voice, teamwork, team learning, and organizational learning. This matters because dissent is a form of voice: a person is choosing to reveal a concern or different perspective even though doing so may carry social risk.

Inviting dissent does not mean that every disagreement must be accepted as correct or that the final decision must change. Its importance for psychological safety is that disagreement can be expressed, considered, and responded to respectfully. When people learn that they can disagree without humiliation or retaliation, they are more likely to reveal concerns, challenge assumptions, identify errors, and contribute information that might otherwise remain unspoken. In this way, inviting dissent both depends on psychological safety and helps reinforce it.

References

Helbig, Karolin. The Psychological Safety Playbook: Lead More Powerfully by Being More Human. Page 8.

Edmondson, Amy C., and Zhike Lei. “Psychological Safety: The History, Renaissance, and Future of an Interpersonal Construct.” Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior, Vol. 1, 2014, pp. 23–43. Annual Reviews article

Harvard Business School. “Leading in Tough Times: HBS Faculty member Amy C. Edmondson on Psychological Safety.” Harvard Business School source

Harvard Business School Working Knowledge. “Four Steps to Building the Psychological Safety That High-Performing Teams Need.” Harvard Business School Working Knowledge source

Harvard Business School Working Knowledge. “New Hires Lose Psychological Safety After Year One. How to Fix It.” Harvard Business School Working Knowledge source

zettels.body:
Personal Concern

One form of safety I am examining is legal and governmental safety.

My concern is not limited to immediate physical danger. I am also thinking about whether a person can feel secure that legal status, residency, citizenship, rights, and due process will protect their ability to remain where they live and continue their life.

The immigration actions of the Trump administration have become connected to this fear for me.

Research Context

The White House issued "Protecting the American People Against Invasion" on January 20, 2025. This provides primary-source context for the administration's immigration enforcement policy.

Reuters reported in September 2026 that Nazira Haji Zada, described as a legal U.S. resident, was deported to Afghanistan after proceedings under the Alien Terrorist Removal Court. The government alleged national-security grounds, her attorney challenged the process, and Haji Zada ultimately agreed to removal.

Reuters has also identified Mahmoud Khalil as a lawful permanent resident who was arrested by immigration authorities in March 2025, detained for more than three months, and continued to face possible deportation proceedings.

A separate case involved V.M.L., a two-year-old U.S. citizen who was taken to Honduras with her Honduran mother. A federal judge expressed concern that the child may have been removed without meaningful process. The government maintained that the mother had legal custody and wanted the child to accompany her.

These cases are not identical. A lawful permanent resident, a legal resident facing a national-security removal proceeding, and a U.S. citizen child accompanying a removed parent have different legal situations.

Personal Safety Connection

What connects them for my research is the fear they raise for me about how secure legal protection feels when government power, immigration enforcement, residency, citizenship, and due process intersect.

I want to keep the factual legal circumstances of each case separate from my own psychological response to them.
zettels.mainIdea: My sense of safety includes whether I feel that legal status, residency, citizenship, due process, and governmental institutions provide dependable protection. Current immigration enforcement actions involving lawful residents and U.S. citizens contribute to my fear and make governmental and legal security part of my psychological exploration of safety.
zettels.title: Legal and Governmental Security as a Form of Safety

zettels.body:
Food is another form of safety I want to examine.

USDA defines food security as access by all people at all times to enough food for an active, healthy life.

USDA's Household Food Security in the United States in 2024 reported that 13.7 percent of U.S. households, or 18.3 million households, experienced food insecurity at some point during 2024.

The report also found that 5.4 percent of households experienced very low food security, the more severe level in which food intake is reduced and normal eating patterns are disrupted because of limited resources.

Household Food Security in the United States in 2024
USDA Economic Research Service
ERR-358

PDF viewer page 5

For my Safety research, food security concerns whether I can depend on continued access to one of the most basic requirements of life.

zettels.title: Housing Security as a Form of Safety

zettels.body:
Financial security is another separate form of safety I want to examine.

The Federal Reserve's Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025 provides several measures of financial resilience.

Sixty-three percent of adults said they could cover a hypothetical $400 emergency expense entirely using cash, savings, or a credit card that would be paid off at the next statement.

This means 37 percent would need another method or would not be able to cover the expense that way.

Twelve percent of all adults said they would not be able to pay the $400 expense by any means.

Reference:
Emergency Savings and Unexpected Expenses
Printed pages 45-46
PDF viewer pages 49-51

The report also found that 55 percent of adults had set aside enough money to cover three months of expenses in an emergency savings or rainy-day fund.

Thirty percent said they could not cover three months of expenses by emergency savings, borrowing, selling assets, or other savings.

For my Safety research, financial security concerns whether money provides enough stability to meet basic needs and survive unexpected disruptions without immediately threatening other forms of safety such as housing and food.
zettels.mainIdea: My sense of safety includes confidence that I can meet ordinary financial needs, respond to emergencies, and continue functioning if an unexpected expense or loss of income occurs.
