I need to examine what applies to my idea, what does not apply, and how my concept would differ by focusing on local communities, food deserts, physical grocery access, community-grown crops, culinary education, and culturally relevant food.

entities.name: Farmer Lee Jones
entities.description: Farmer Lee Jones is a farmer, agricultural advocate, and co-owner of The Chef’s Garden near Huron, Ohio. His work connects sustainable agriculture, soil health, specialty crop production, chefs, and culinary education.
entities.roleUse:
A person I met while attending culinary school and someone whose work may be relevant to my ideas about local farm partnerships, food access, community growing, culinary education, and a grocery store centered on imperfect, surplus, and locally grown food.

This record identifies a possible person to contact or learn from later. It does not mean that a partnership has been discussed or established.

entities.name: The Chef’s Garden
entities.description: Family farm near Huron, Ohio, known for growing specialty vegetables, herbs, greens, and microgreens for chefs. Its work emphasizes flavor, crop quality, soil health, sustainable agricultural practices, and collaboration between farmers and culinary professionals.
entities.roleUse:
A specific farm to consider when researching possible local farm partnerships for my community food-system and grocery-store ideas.

Because I met Farmer Lee Jones while attending culinary school, The Chef’s Garden is not an abstract example to me. It is a real Ohio farm whose agricultural and culinary work I have encountered and may want to study further or approach later.

Possible areas to explore include:

local crop sourcing
specialty and culturally useful crops
imperfect or surplus produce
chef-farmer collaboration
community food access
culinary education
soil-centered agriculture

This record does not state that The Chef’s Garden has agreed to participate in the project.

entities.name: Doctor Henry Feldman
entities.description:
Doctor Henry Feldman is a geneticist, biotechnology researcher, and manipulator whose pursuit of control begins with early experiments in subliminal influence. Raised with wealth but lacking genuine attention and guidance, he develops an obsession with power and control. After medical school, an organization recruits him because of his ability to influence and manipulate others.

Feldman publicly presents himself as a renowned scientist while secretly conducting experiments beyond ethical and legal limits. His work includes genetic manipulation, behavioral control, programmed compliance, and the use of ancient technology.
entities.roleUse:
Feldman is a central antagonist whose actions connect Kido’s testing, manipulation, reprogramming, the ancient device, The Order, the Russian Federation, Colonel Reed Hawkes, and the effort to turn Kido into a controllable instrument.

His need for control places him in direct opposition to Kido. Feldman’s role must be tracked carefully because his influence extends across several chapters, organizations, experiments, and covert relationships.

entities.name: The Order
entities.description:
The Order is a covert organization that operates as an unseen force shaping nations, economies, political power, scientific research, and human development. It provides protection and resources to Doctor Henry Feldman in exchange for research and results that serve the private goals of its members.

The organization is not united by one moral purpose. Its members support Feldman for different reasons, including profit, political dominance, enhanced soldiers, technological advancement, control, and the reshaping of humanity.
entities.roleUse:
The Order supports and protects Feldman’s illegal genetic, behavioral, and technological experiments. It gives him access to funding, test subjects, political influence, materials, and secrecy.

Its members include people from corporate, political, military, mercenary, and technological backgrounds. Their alliance is transactional, and each member expects Feldman’s work to advance a separate agenda.

The Order connects Feldman’s private experiments to broader political and institutional power.

entities.name: Kido Thompson
entities.description:
Kido Thompson is a Bajan man in his thirties. He is Black, with black hair and brown eyes. He is loving, kind, loyal, shy, and a good listener, but he struggles with anger when he believes he or someone else is being treated unjustly.

Kido’s interests include photography, computers, poetry, music, fencing, soccer, chess, and reading. His childhood and adolescence were shaped by family mistreatment, bullying, sexual abuse, placement in St. John’s Home for Boys, and leaving home during high school. Music teacher George Hinkson became the supportive father figure Kido had lacked.

Despite his trauma, Kido remains caring and empathetic. His past affects his ability to trust, his response to injustice, and his struggle to control the power that awakens after the Mirrian attack.
entities.roleUse:
Kido is the central character of Emperor’s Earth. After surviving the Mirrian attack, he develops extraordinary abilities and becomes a leader among the remaining survivors.

His power places him between two possible paths: becoming a protector and builder of a better future or becoming SHIVA, the destroyer of worlds. His story follows his struggle with trauma, anger, leadership, manipulation, responsibility, forgiveness, and the ethical use of power.

Kido becomes the focus of Doctor Feldman’s experiments and behavioral programming, the Russian Federation’s strategic interest, Colonel Reed Hawkes’s capture attempts, and the political concerns of the Mirrians. His relationships with Ricky Chapman, Ken Nakamura, Mira Devereaux, Xavier, and Ja-Jorel help anchor him when his identity and control are threatened.

entities.name: Colonel Reed Hawkes
entities.description:
Colonel Reed Hawkes is a former member of the United Terran Navy SEAL Division who later operates independently as a mercenary and security contractor.

His experience includes high-risk retrieval, perimeter operations, secure transportation, containment, and off-the-books assignments. He is discreet, tactically precise, emotionally controlled, and willing to work under different aliases. His loyalties are conditional and primarily tied to payment rather than politics or long-term allegiance.

Reed previously crossed paths with Mira Devereaux during her work as a war correspondent. Her records describe him as a one-time contact who guided her through a siege perimeter before becoming difficult to trace. Doctor Feldman later finds Reed through Mira’s archived reports and hires him to capture Kido.
entities.roleUse:
Reed enters the story when Doctor Feldman needs someone capable of locating, containing, and capturing Kido after Feldman’s programming begins to fail.

Feldman provides Reed with containment technology, including a neural dampener, and uses him in multiple attempts to trap Kido. Reed’s operations connect him to Warehouse 9B, Prospect Park, Coney Island, the safehouse, transit-disruption technology, and Feldman’s wider effort to regain control.

Reed initially treats Kido as a high-value target and a paid assignment. His later confrontation and confession reveal information about Feldman’s involvement and Reed’s own role in the capture attempts.

entities.name: Petrichor
entities.description: The distinctive earthy smell associated with rain falling on dry soil, clay, rock, pavement, or other porous surfaces, particularly after warm or dry weather.
entities.roleUse: Central subject of the poem and primary concept of the Zettel. Connects the creative note to definitions, scientific studies, sensory vocabulary, and future poems about rain.

entities.name: Geosmin
entities.description: An organic compound with an intense earthy or musty odor. Geosmin is associated with soil microorganisms and contributes to the smell of wet earth.
entities.roleUse: Supplies scientific context for the earthy component of petrichor. It should remain distinct from petrichor, which describes the broader sensory phenomenon.

entities.name: Rain Aerosol
entities.description: Microscopic airborne droplets or particles generated when raindrops strike porous surfaces such as soil. These aerosols can carry material and odors from the ground into the surrounding air.
entities.roleUse: xplains how the scent connected with petrichor travels from the ground into the air and reaches the speaker.

entities.name: I. J. Bear
entities.description: Australian researcher from the CSIRO Division of Mineral Chemistry who co-authored the 1964 paper “Nature of Argillaceous Odour.”
entities.roleUse: Historical researcher associated with the scientific investigation and naming of petrichor.

entities.name: R. G. Thomas
entities.description: ustralian researcher from the CSIRO Division of Mineral Chemistry who co-authored the 1964 paper “Nature of Argillaceous Odour.”
entities.roleUse: Historical researcher associated with the scientific investigation and naming of petrichor.

entities.name: Soil
entities.description: he upper layer of earth containing minerals, organic matter, water, air, and microorganisms. Dry soil can hold plant-derived substances and microbial compounds that become airborne when rain strikes it.
entities.roleUse: Primary physical surface in the poem. Provides the ground, texture, dryness, color change, and earthy scent associated with the arrival of rain.

entities.name: Raindrop
entities.description: A drop of atmospheric water that falls to the ground. Its impact on porous soil can trap and release tiny air bubbles and aerosols.
entities.roleUse: Provides the poem’s first visible and physical action. The raindrop connects the dry surface to the release of scent.

entities.name: Clay
entities.description: A fine-grained natural material that can retain substances associated with the characteristic odor released after dry conditions and rainfall.
entities.roleUse: Provides historical and material context for the phrase “argillaceous odour.” It can also supply grounded images of mineral earth becoming wet.

entities.name: Handedness
entities.description: Natural hand dominance, discussed as part of neurological organization rather than simply a behavioral preference.
entities.roleUse: Central concept connecting left-handedness, motor function, forced switching, development, and expression.

entities.name: Forced Hand Switching
entities.description: The practice of preventing a person, especially a child, from using their naturally dominant hand and requiring use of the opposite hand.
entities.roleUse: Central experience being examined for its possible physical, psychological, developmental, and expressive effects.

entities.name: Left-Handedness Stigma
entities.description: Cultural or social beliefs that portray left-handedness as wrong, undesirable, dangerous, or associated with evil.
entities.roleUse: Provides cultural context for punishment, correction, shame, labeling, and suppression of natural handedness.

entities.name: Adaptive Expression
entities.description: The idea that suppression or redirection of natural behavior may lead a person to develop alternative ways of observing, processing, and expressing experience.
entities.roleUse: Connects childhood adaptation with later sensory, emotional, observational, and creative expression.

entities.name: Sensory Processing
entities.description: Processing experience through visual, spatial, physical, auditory, emotional, and environmental information.
entities.roleUse: Used in the document to explain the proposed relationship between neurological adaptation and sensory-centered expression.

entities.name: André Darlington
entities.description: Author and drinks writer. Co-author of The New Cocktail Hour: The Essential Guide to Handcrafted Drinks.
entities.roleUse: Author; source creator

entities.name: Tenaya Darlington
entities.description: Author and food and drinks writer. Co-author of The New Cocktail Hour: The Essential Guide to Handcrafted Drinks.
entities.roleUse: Author; source creator

entities.name: Marie-Antoine Carême
entities.description: French chef and culinary authority who helped systematize and codify classical French cuisine. Carême is associated with the development of grande cuisine and with organizing culinary preparations, including sauces, into defined systems that influenced later professional cooking.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary figure; development and codification of classical French cuisine.

entities.name: Georges Auguste Escoffier
entities.description: French chef who modernized and systematized professional cookery, building on the foundations of classical French cuisine. Escoffier simplified and reorganized earlier culinary practices and is particularly associated with the organization of the professional kitchen and the modernization of classical cuisine.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary figure; modernization and organization of professional cookery and classical French cuisine.

entities.name: Cultural Stigma
entities.description: Description: Negative cultural meanings, judgments, beliefs, or social expectations attached to a trait, behavior, identity, or difference. Cultural stigma may continue to influence self-perception, social behavior, relationships, and feelings of belonging even after the original practice or pressure that reinforced it has ended.
entities.roleUse: Used to examine how socially learned judgments can remain psychologically or socially significant after direct correction, punishment, or suppression stops.

entities.name: Guillaume Tirel
entities.description: Medieval French cook, usually known as Taillevent, born around 1310. He is associated with Le Viandier and with refining earlier cooking practices by reducing reliance on heavy spices and emphasizing the natural flavors of foods.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary figure; development of sauces, soups, and refined medieval French cooking.

entities.name: Le Viandier
entities.description: Important late-medieval cookbook associated with Guillaume Tirel, known as Taillevent. Written before the invention of the printing press, handwritten copies remained in use for more than a century. It was printed in 1490 and is described in the source as possibly the first cookbook ever printed.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary text; reference for medieval French cooking, sauces, soups, and the development of written culinary practice.

entities.name: François-Pierre de La Varenne
entities.description: French cook and author, 1615–1678, associated with Le Cuisinier François. His work helped present recipes and cooking techniques in a more orderly and systematic form than earlier unsystematic collections.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary figure; organization and systematization of seventeenth-century French cooking practices.

entities.name: Le Cuisinier François
entities.description: Cookbook by François-Pierre de La Varenne, published in 1651. It summarized cooking practices used in aristocratic households and was among the early works to organize recipes and cooking techniques systematically. It remained an important reference for cooks for more than 150 years.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary text; reference for seventeenth-century French cooking and the development of systematic recipe and technique presentation.

entities.name: Slow Food
entities.description: International food movement concerned with preserving local food traditions, encouraging greater awareness of where food comes from and how it tastes, and supporting sustainable and ecologically responsible agriculture. Over time, the movement expanded its focus to include issues such as race, poverty, hunger, environmental concerns, climate change, and stewardship of the land.
entities.roleUse: Used to study food culture, sustainability, local food traditions, agricultural practices, food awareness, environmental responsibility, and social issues connected to food systems.

entities.name: Fernand Point
entities.description: French chef, 1897–1955, who simplified and lightened classical cuisine at his restaurant La Pyramide in Vienne, France. Point emphasized perfection, careful development of dishes, and meals of exceptional quality. His approach strongly influenced the generation of chefs who later developed nouvelle cuisine.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary figure; transition from classical cuisine toward lighter twentieth-century French cooking and influence on nouvelle cuisine.

entities.name: La Pyramide
entities.description: Restaurant in Vienne, France, associated with chef Fernand Point. It became an important center of twentieth-century French cooking and the training ground for chefs who later became influential figures in nouvelle cuisine.
entities.roleUse: Historical restaurant; site of Fernand Point's culinary work and training of influential twentieth-century chefs.

entities.name: Paul Bocuse
entities.description: French chef and former apprentice of Fernand Point who became one of the prominent chefs associated with nouvelle cuisine during the twentieth century.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary figure; development and promotion of nouvelle cuisine.

entities.name: Jean Troisgros
entities.description: French chef and former apprentice of Fernand Point who became one of the influential chefs associated with nouvelle cuisine.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary figure; development of nouvelle cuisine and lighter approaches to classical French cooking.

entities.name: Pierre Troisgros
entities.description: French chef and former apprentice of Fernand Point who became one of the influential chefs associated with nouvelle cuisine.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary figure; development of nouvelle cuisine and lighter approaches to classical French cooking.

entities.name: Alain Chapel
entities.description: French chef and former apprentice of Fernand Point who later became an important figure in twentieth-century French cooking and nouvelle cuisine.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary figure; development of nouvelle cuisine.

entities.name: Nouvelle Cuisine
entities.description: Twentieth-century French culinary movement associated with chefs who reacted against heavy and overly complicated classical cuisine. It emphasized simpler and more natural flavors, lighter sauces and seasonings, shorter cooking times, reduced reliance on flour-thickened sauces, and artistic plating performed by the chef in the kitchen. Although the movement later became associated with excessive and elaborate presentations, many of its strongest ideas became incorporated into modern classical cooking.
entities.roleUse: Used to study the evolution of modern French cuisine, reactions to classical cuisine, lighter cooking methods, natural flavors, and chef-driven plating.

entities.name: Alice Waters
entities.description: American restaurateur and chef associated with the opening of Chez Panisse in Berkeley, California, in 1971. Her culinary philosophy emphasizes that good food depends on high-quality ingredients and favors seasonal, locally grown, organically raised products prepared simply.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary figure; development of ingredient-focused, seasonal, local, and sustainable approaches to modern North American cooking.

entities.name: Chez Panisse
entities.description: Restaurant opened by Alice Waters in Berkeley, California, in 1971. Its emphasis on high-quality seasonal and locally produced ingredients became influential in the development of modern North American cooking and the broader local-food movement.
entities.roleUse: Historical restaurant; example of ingredient-focused, seasonal, local, and sustainable restaurant cooking.

entities.name: Larry Forgione
entities.description: American chef who promoted local ingredients and regional American cuisine through his New York City restaurant An American Place, following the growing emphasis on ingredient quality established by chefs such as Alice Waters.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary figure; development of local and regional ingredient-focused American cuisine.

entities.name: An American Place
entities.description: New York City restaurant associated with chef Larry Forgione and the promotion of local ingredients and regional American cuisine.
entities.roleUse: Historical restaurant; example of the growth of local-ingredient and regional American cooking.

entities.name: Sustainable Agriculture
entities.description: Agricultural approach intended to produce healthful food while supporting economically viable farms and farming communities, providing fair working conditions, preserving soil, water, and air, treating animals humanely, and maintaining farmland productivity over the long term.
entities.roleUse: Used to examine the relationship between food production, environmental stewardship, farm economics, labor practices, animal welfare, and culinary sourcing.

entities.name: Organic Food
entities.description: Food produced according to standards that restrict or exclude specified artificial chemicals, drugs, and other prohibited agricultural inputs, allowing qualifying products to carry an organic designation.
entities.roleUse: Used to study agricultural production methods, ingredient sourcing, food labeling, sustainability, and consumer food choices.

entities.name: Biodynamic Agriculture
entities.description: Agricultural system that emphasizes natural soil nutrients such as compost and manure, avoids pesticides, herbicides, and other artificial chemicals, and treats soil, crops, and animals as parts of a single interconnected system. Biodynamic agriculture also incorporates cosmic forces and spiritual concepts into planting and harvesting practices.
entities.roleUse: Used to examine holistic agricultural systems, sustainability, soil management, natural agricultural inputs, farming philosophy, and alternatives to conventional agriculture.

entities.name: Heirloom Varieties
entities.description: Older varieties of fruits and vegetables that existed before industrial agriculture increasingly favored hybrids bred for higher productivity, mechanized harvesting, durability, and long-distance shipping. Heirloom varieties are often valued for flavor, texture, genetic diversity, and their connection to agricultural traditions.
entities.roleUse: Used to examine ingredient quality, agricultural biodiversity, flavor, sustainability, and the effects of industrial agriculture on food varieties.

entities.name: Farm-to-Table
entities.description: Food movement emphasizing the use of locally produced foods sourced from nearby farms, fisheries, ranches, and other producers. Farm-to-table restaurants often identify producers, emphasize ingredient provenance, and develop closer relationships between chefs, consumers, and local food producers.
entities.roleUse: Used to study local sourcing, ingredient provenance, restaurant purchasing, food-system transparency, freshness, sustainability, and relationships between chefs and producers.

entities.name: Indigenous Cuisine
entities.description: Cuisine based on foods and foodways of Indigenous peoples that existed within a region before European colonization. In the North American context described by the source, it emphasizes native wild and cultivated foods while excluding crops and livestock introduced by later European and other settlers.
entities.roleUse: Used to study Indigenous foodways, regional food systems, native ingredients, precolonial cuisine, cultural food history, and relationships between cuisine and place.

entities.name: Genetically Modified Organisms
entities.description: Plants or animals whose genes have been artificially altered to produce desired characteristics, such as increased productivity, disease resistance, or herbicide resistance. Their use is debated in relation to crop yields, land use, food safety, long-term health effects, and agricultural sustainability.
entities.roleUse: Used to examine genetic modification in agriculture, food production, food safety, sustainability, crop productivity, and debates surrounding modern agricultural technology.

entities.description: Agricultural approach that emphasizes natural soil nutrients, including compost and manure, while restricting or avoiding pesticides, herbicides, and other artificial chemicals. In the source, organic agriculture serves as a point of comparison for biodynamic agriculture.
entities.name: Organic Agriculture
entities.roleUse: Used to examine agricultural production methods, natural soil management, chemical avoidance, sustainability, ingredient sourcing, and relationships between organic and biodynamic farming systems.

entities.description: Precision cooking technique that uses controlled temperatures and cooking times to produce consistent results and can create new textures and flavors in familiar foods.
entities.name: Sous Vide
entities.roleUse: Used to examine precision cooking, temperature control, modern culinary technology, texture development, and controlled food preparation.

entities.description: Computer-controlled process that builds three-dimensional objects by depositing material layer upon layer. In culinary applications, 3D printers may use food powders, pastes, or gels to create garnishes, components, or potentially entire meals.
entities.name: 3D Printing
entities.roleUse: Used to examine digital fabrication in food preparation, automated food production, culinary design, food presentation, and emerging kitchen technologies.

entities.description: Manufacturing process in which a three-dimensional object is constructed by adding successive layers of material according to instructions controlled by a computer program. 3D printing is a form of additive manufacturing.
entities.name: Additive Manufacturing
entities.roleUse: Used to examine the underlying production principle of 3D printing and its application to culinary technology and food fabrication.

entities.description: Spanish chef associated with El Bulli who pioneered experimental approaches to cooking involving gels, foams, powders, infusions, extracts, and other unconventional methods of presenting flavors, textures, and aromas.
entities.name: Ferran Adrià
entities.roleUse: Historical and contemporary culinary figure; experimentation with modern cooking techniques, food transformation, texture, flavor, aroma, and molecular gastronomy.

entities.description: Acclaimed Spanish restaurant associated with chef Ferran Adrià and known for pioneering experimental approaches to flavor, texture, aroma, presentation, and modern culinary techniques.
entities.name: El Bulli
entities.roleUse: Historical restaurant; site of experimentation and development associated with molecular gastronomy and modernist culinary techniques.

entities.description: Approach to food and cooking that explores how scientific principles and modern techniques can produce new forms of flavor, texture, aroma, and presentation. Techniques may involve gels, foams, powders, infusions, extracts, natural gums, gelatin, pectin, and other ingredients used in unconventional ways.
entities.name: Molecular Gastronomy
entities.roleUse: Used to examine relationships between science, technology, ingredients, culinary technique, sensory experience, and innovative food presentation.

entities.description: French chemist associated with research into the scientific principles of cooking and credited in the source with coining the term molecular gastronomy.
entities.name: Hervé This
entities.roleUse: Scientific and culinary research figure; development and study of molecular gastronomy and the application of chemistry to food and cooking.

entities.description: Modern approach to cooking associated with the application of science, technology, unconventional ingredients, and experimental techniques to transform flavors, textures, aromas, and food presentation. The term was popularized by Nathan Myhrvold through his books of the same name.
entities.name: Modernist Cuisine
entities.roleUse: Used to examine technologically and scientifically informed culinary experimentation and the adaptation of modern techniques into professional cooking.

entities.description: Author and food researcher associated with popularizing the term modernist cuisine through the multivolume book collection Modernist Cuisine.
entities.name: Nathan Myhrvold
entities.roleUse: Culinary research and publishing figure; popularization and documentation of modernist cuisine and science-based cooking.

aliases: Modernist Cuisine: The Art and Science of Cooking
entities.description: Multivolume culinary work associated with Nathan Myhrvold that helped popularize the term modernist cuisine and documents scientific, technological, and experimental approaches to food and cooking.
entities.name: Modernist Cuisine

entities.description: English chef associated with the use and development of molecular gastronomy and modernist culinary techniques.
entities.name: Heston Blumenthal

entities.name: Water Activity

entities.roleUse: Used when analyzing microbial growth, preservation, fermentation, curing, dehydration, salt concentration, sugar concentration, and shelf stability.

entities.name: pH

entities.name: I Built the Dungeon That Killed Me
entities.description: A poetry concept centered on a speaker who gradually constructs the very dungeon that ultimately confines or destroys them. The construction occurs over time through accumulated choices, habits, actions, or repeated acts whose consequences may not be understood while they are happening. The dungeon should remain concrete in the poem: doors, locks, walls, keys, mortar, rooms, foundations, and individual stones. Its meaning should emerge through the progression of the poem rather than being defined in advance. The central unresolved question is: If I built it, why can't I leave it? Possible thematic meanings include self-sabotage, grief, addiction, ambition, isolation, guilt, identity,
entities.roleUse: Use as the central conceptual entity for developing a poem based on self-created confinement and its consequences. The poem may move through: foundation → construction → recognition → entrapment → consequence Preserve the sense of gradual accumulation: stone follows stone, choice follows choice. Allow emotion to emerge through that accumulation rather than through direct explanation. Do not determine what the dungeon ultimately represents before drafting. Its meaning should be discovered through the poem itself, and the central question may remain unanswered.

entities.name: Ricky Chapman
entities.description:
Age: 32

Ethnicity: Black

Gender: Male

Appearance: He has black hair, brown eyes, and a muscular build. He has tattoos on his arms and chest, and often wears casual clothes, such as T-shirts and jeans.

Personality: Impulsive, rebellious, hot-headed, loyal to those he cares about, and struggles with addiction and substance abuse.

Background: Grew up in a rough neighborhood and had a troubled childhood, often getting into fights and trouble with the law. Despite his tough exterior, he has a soft spot for those he cares about and is fiercely loyal to his friends. He fell into a life of drug use and crime, which caused him to be in and out of prison. His girlfriend cheated on him with his best friend while he was in prison, leading him to choose Kido as his new partner and support system.

Interests/Hobbies: He enjoys drawing and sketching, has a talent for graffiti art, listens to music, and plays video games.

Goals/Motivations: To turn his life around, stay out of trouble, support his children, make amends for past mistakes, help Kido, and be a good partner to him.

Challenges/Obstacles: Struggling with addiction and avoiding trouble with the law, while dealing with his past mistakes and their consequences.

Relationship with Other Characters: He is Kido’s partner, cares deeply for him, and wants to support him in any way he can. He has a tense relationship with Doctor Feldman, whom he distrusts and believes is manipulating Kido.

Background: Mira was born and raised in France to a family of journalists. She inherited her passion for uncovering the truth from her parents and followed in their footsteps. Mira moved to the United States to work for a prominent news outlet before the Mirrain attack. She lost everything in the following chaos and was forced to adapt to survive. She received military training to protect herself and those she cared about. Despite her training, Mira retains her journalistic curiosity and often puts herself in dangerous situations to uncover the truth.

typeData.definition:
The term is most commonly associated with military and government operations. For example, a psychological operation might try to:

  • reduce an opponent’s morale,

  • encourage surrender or cooperation,

  • influence civilian behavior,

  • counter misinformation or propaganda,

  • shape perceptions of events or organizations.

On social media, people also use “psyop” much more loosely to mean something they believe is deliberately designed to manipulate public opinion. That usage does not necessarily mean an actual military or government psychological operation has occurred.

structureNotes.summary: This structure note collects unresolved questions about Feldman, the Society, unidentified men, unused characters, and the tattoo on the figure connected to Feldman. Each question must be reviewed against the manuscript, character profiles, and confirmed story information before any answer is added.
structureNotes.outline:
Feldman

Resolve the tattoo on the figure with Feldman.
Determine Feldman’s connection to the Society.
Determine whether the man in the back of Feldman’s car is from the Society.

The Society

Determine the Society’s name.
Determine the Society’s goal.
Confirm its connection to Feldman.
Confirm whether the man in Feldman’s car belongs to it.

Characters

Identify which defined characters have not been used.
Determine whether those characters still have a role in the story.
Do not assign new roles or actions without support from the manuscript or character profiles.

Coney Island Avenue

Identify the men on Coney Island Avenue.
Determine whether they are connected to Feldman, the Society, or another established group.

Canon Review

Review the manuscript before answering each question.
Separate confirmed information from unresolved possibilities.
Do not invent information to fill gaps.
Update the appropriate character, organization, manuscript, or story record after an answer is confirmed.

Central Question

What does safety mean to me?

1. Safety — Personal Reflection

This is the central writing Zettel.

Use it to develop:
- What safety means personally
- How safety is experienced
- What creates safety
- What removes safety
- Whether safety comes from relationships, environment, internal stability, or a combination

2. Physical Safety vs. Perceived Safety

Primary question:
What is the difference between being safe and feeling safe?

Research:
- Physical or objective safety
- Subjective or perceived safety
- Actual danger versus perceived danger
- Conditions that contribute to feeling secure

Return to the central question:
Does my personal meaning of safety refer to actual protection, the feeling of security, or both?

3. Trust and the Sense of Safety

Primary question:
What role does trust play in feeling safe?

Research:
- Interpersonal trust
- Reliability
- Consistency
- Trust after betrayal
- Trust within relationships

Return to the central question:
Do I need to trust someone in order to feel safe with them?

4. Predictability and Psychological Safety

Primary question:
What role does predictability play in feeling safe?

Research:
- Predictability
- Stability
- Familiarity
- Routine
- Consistency
- Uncertainty

Return to the central question:
Does knowing what to expect contribute to my own sense of safety?

5. Control, Autonomy, and Safety

Primary question:
What role do control and autonomy play in safety?

Research:
- Choice
- Agency
- Personal control
- Autonomy
- Ability to refuse
- Ability to leave
- Dependence

Return to the central question:
Do I feel safer when I have control over what happens to me and the ability to make choices?

6. Boundaries and Personal Safety

Primary question:
How do boundaries affect a person's sense of safety?

Research:
- Personal boundaries
- Emotional boundaries
- Physical boundaries
- Consent
- Privacy
- Respect for limits
- Boundary violations

Return to the central question:
Does my sense of safety depend on knowing that my limits will be respected?

7. Family as a Source of Safety

Primary question:
Does family make you safe?

Use the earlier research to examine:
- Trust
- Predictability
- Autonomy
- Boundaries
- Reliability
- Protection
- Belonging

Do not assume that family automatically creates safety.

Ask:
What qualities would have to exist within a family relationship for that relationship to be safe?

8. Friendship, Trust, and Safety

Primary question:
Do friends represent safety?

Use the earlier research to examine:
- Trust
- Reliability
- Boundaries
- Vulnerability
- Mutuality
- Respect
- Belonging

Ask:
Is friendship itself a source of safety, or does safety come from particular qualities within the friendship?

Research and Writing Process

For each research Zettel:

1. State the question being examined.
2. Record my current understanding.
3. Identify what I need evidence or outside information to understand.
4. Research credible sources.
5. Link those sources to the research Zettel.
6. Record what each source contributes.
7. Compare the findings with my original understanding.
8. Record what the research supports.
9. Record what the research challenges.
10. Record what the research adds or complicates.
11. Develop an answer to the research question.
12. Return that understanding to the central Safety Zettel.

Final Development

The central Safety writing should draw from the research Zettels without becoming only a research report.

The research exists to help answer the central personal question:

What does safety mean to me?

writingDraft.title: Author Interview Questions and Answers
writingDraft.body:
Author Interview Questions and Answers

Darrell Barrow-Pender

Prepared as conversational answers for a poetry and writing interview. The responses are intended to sound natural when spoken while preserving the personal history, creative work, and research that inform them.

1. For those meeting you for the first time, who are you?

I'm Darrell Barrow-Pender. I was born in Barbados and came to the United States in 1975, so my Bajan heritage is part of who I am. I'm a poet and multidisciplinary writer, but I'm also a photographer, musician, chef, technologist, and creator. From the outside, they may look like separate pursuits. To me, they are different ways of understanding and expressing myself and the world around me.

I often explain it this way: if you want to see my worldview, look at my photography; if you want to know my mind, read my words; and if you want to understand how I feel, listen to my music.

My creative work stems from lived experience, introspection, faith, grief, identity, love, observation, and questioning.

2. What part of your life do you think made you become the person you are today?

I don't think a single experience made me who I am. I think it was a combination of experiences that taught me very early to observe, question, adapt, and spend a great deal of time examining things internally.

One experience I am researching now is my handedness. I am naturally left-handed, but as a child I was punished for using my left hand and forced to use my right. I eventually complied to stop the punishment, but I always knew internally that I was left-handed. At the time, I did not understand what was happening. I only understood that something natural to me was considered wrong and that I had to change it.

What I didn't understand until I began researching it was that forced switching isn't simply teaching the other hand to write. Studies of converted left-handers have found lasting changes in how the brain organizes and activates the motor systems involved in handwriting, as well as structural differences associated with forced use of the nondominant hand. In everyday language, the brain is rewired. More precisely, it reorganizes through neuroplasticity. The research helped me understand that my brain was not merely learning a new habit; it had to adapt because my natural handedness was being overridden. [1][2][3]

That discovery has made me look back on my childhood differently. I am not saying that being forced to become right-handed made me a writer. What I am exploring is whether that neurological adaptation, together with the emotional experience of being punished and told that something natural about me was wrong, influenced how I learned to observe, process information, express myself, and communicate.

That question becomes especially important when I consider my writing, photography, music, cooking, and technology. I am highly observant. I notice details. I think in layers. Much of my writing explores identity, silence, suppression, perception, belonging, and finding a voice.

So now I am researching something I lived through without understanding it at the time: what happens when a child is forced to override something as fundamental as natural handedness, and how much of that adaptation persists into adulthood?

3. Do you remember the first moment when you realized writing was more than something you enjoyed - that it was something you needed? When was that?

I think I needed writing before I understood I was a writer.

For a long time, writing was a place to put my feelings. I did not think of it as art, and I did not really consider myself a writer.

That began to change when I was working on my GED through Channel Thirteen. My tutor, Judy Fresco, called to say Channel Thirteen wanted to use my poem "Positive" in a writing curriculum. Later, she submitted it to Symphony Space, where professional actors would read selected work. That was one of the first times I paused and thought, Maybe there really is something in my writing.

But the deeper realization came from understanding why I write. I have described my poetry as coming "from the silence that wanted to speak." Writing gives thoughts and feelings that might otherwise remain inside me a place to go. Writings: The Inner Echoes really grew out of that.

4. What is something life has taught you the hard way, but you are grateful you learned as a writer?

One lesson has been not to let recognition determine the value of my writing.

There were times when publication, awards, or acknowledgment meant a great deal to me because someone finally said my words mattered. But I have also learned that the literary world has its complications. Some opportunities I once viewed as accomplishments became more complicated when I later learned more about the organizations behind them.

That taught me to research publishers, contests, and opportunities carefully and to understand what I am getting involved in.

It also taught me something more personal: recognition can encourage you, but it cannot be the sole reason you believe in your own voice. At some point, you have to recognize the value of your own work.

5. As a writer, you spend so much time observing people. What have people taught you about humanity?

People have taught me that humanity is complex.

We can be extraordinarily compassionate, and we can also be incredibly dismissive of one another. Sometimes a small act - a thank-you, someone listening, or someone acknowledging another person's dignity - can mean far more than we realize.

I have also seen how easily people look past someone because of their circumstances. That bothers me deeply.

One belief that has become increasingly important to me is that every person possesses dignity regardless of circumstances, status, income, health, housing, background, or the type of service they receive.

So much of what it means to be human seems to come back to basic needs: to be seen, to be heard, to belong, to be respected, to be loved, and to know that we matter.

6. Do you think your writing reveals things about you that you might struggle to say in an ordinary conversation?

Absolutely.

Sometimes I do not fully understand something until I write it.

Writing allows me to sit with an emotion or question without having to immediately explain or defend it. I can examine it, turn it over, question it, and sometimes discover that what I thought I was writing about is not what was really underneath it at all.

That is part of why I call much of my work Introspective Poetry. It reflects, listens inwardly, and names what it finds.

There are things in Writings: The Inner Echoes that probably reveal more about me than I would ever sit down and tell someone in conversation. Some of that work gives voice to experiences I had lived through in silence.

So when I say, "If you want to know my mind, read my words," I mean it quite literally.

7. What is the one thing you are still trying to understand about yourself?

I think I am still trying to understand my own sense of worth without measuring it against someone else's recognition of me.

That is something that appears repeatedly throughout my writing.

I have accomplished things and have had teachers, friends, colleagues, readers, and others recognize qualities in me that I sometimes had difficulty recognizing in myself. There were also times when acknowledgment from the person I most wanted it from did not come, and that affected how I measured accomplishment and even how I saw myself.

So I am still learning the difference between being seen by others and seeing myself.

I do not think I have fully answered that question yet. Maybe that is one reason I keep writing.

8. Have you ever had to choose between protecting your peace and following your dreams? What did that choice teach you?

Yes, and sometimes I didn't make the right choice.

One of the hardest examples for me involves music. There was a time when Juilliard was within reach, but I turned away from that opportunity. It was not because I did not love music. I felt inadequate because I had not received the consistent formal training I believed I needed, and I allowed anger, hurt, and the feeling of not measuring up to influence my decision.

Looking back, that taught me something important: protecting yourself and avoiding something because you are afraid of being hurt are not necessarily the same thing.

Sometimes fear can disguise itself as protection.

I have learned to ask myself now: Am I choosing peace, or am I letting fear, hurt, anger, or someone else's voice make the decision for me?

9. What is something you deeply believe about life, love, people, or art that you think you will still believe many years from now?

I deeply believe in human dignity.

I believe every person possesses dignity regardless of their circumstances, status, income, health, housing, background, profession, or ability to do something for someone else.

I think that belief touches everything I do.

It affects how I think about hospitality and food, how I photograph people and the world, and whether the systems we create actually serve people. And it certainly affects my writing.

I also believe art gives us a place to put what ordinary language sometimes cannot convey. A poem, photograph, piece of music, story, or even a meal can say, "I see you. You were here. This mattered."

I do not think I will ever stop believing it.

10. If someone read everything you have ever written, what part of you would you hope they understood that they might otherwise never see?

I would hope they understood how deeply I question things.

I am not simply writing about sadness, love, anger, faith, identity, family, grief, or whatever subject happens to appear on the page. I am usually trying to understand what lies beneath.

My master collection, Writings: The Inner Echoes, includes poems, essays, prayers, reflections, visual pieces, experimental forms, and other writings. The work traverses emotional and spiritual landscapes of memory, identity, faith, desire, love, and the search for meaning.

I have also been developing projects such as Phrases People Hide Behind, Tesseract, Introspective Poetry, the Sequential Alphabet Index, and other writing and poetic frameworks. I also have fiction and other works still in development.

But beneath all those titles and forms, I would want someone who read everything I have written to understand that I was trying to see clearly - myself, other people, the world around me, and the things we sometimes leave unsaid.

Maybe that is the connection among all of my creative work:

Photography is how I see.
Writing is how I think and question.
Music is how I feel.
Food is one way I care for people.
Technology is how I organize and build.

They are different expressions, yet they are all parts of me.

And if someone finished reading everything I had ever written and understood something about me that I could not simply explain in conversation, then the writing had done its job.

Research Notes for Question 2

The phrase "the brain was rewired" is everyday language for neuroplastic reorganization.

The studies below examined groups of people who were naturally left-handed and forced during childhood to write with their right hand.

The 2002 PET study found persistent differences in the functional neuroanatomy of handwriting even after decades of right-hand writing. Converted left-handers showed a more bilateral activation pattern than natural right-handers.

The 2007 fMRI study found that converted left-handers retained strong activation in right-hemisphere motor-association areas while also recruiting left-hemisphere areas related to right-hand use. The researchers concluded that educational attempts to switch handedness do not simply erase the original motor organization.

The 2010 structural MRI study found differences involving the central sulcus and putamen. Its authors described the findings as evidence that forced use of the nondominant hand can shape the structure of motor-related brain regions.

These studies support saying that forced switching can reorganize the brain. They do not, by themselves, prove which exact functional or structural changes occurred in one particular individual without that person's neurological imaging.

Sources

[1] Siebner, H. R., Limmer, C., Peinemann, A., Drzezga, A., Bloem, B. R., Schwaiger, M., and Conrad, B. (2002). Long-Term Consequences of Switching Handedness: A Positron Emission Tomography Study on Handwriting in Converted Left-Handers. Journal of Neuroscience, 22(7), 2816-2825.
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6758284/

[2] Kloeppel, S., Vongerichten, A., van Eimeren, T., Frackowiak, R. S. J., and Siebner, H. R. (2007). Can Left-Handedness Be Switched? Insights from an Early Switch of Handwriting. Journal of Neuroscience, 27(29), 7847-7853.
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6672868/

[3] Kloeppel, S., Mangin, J.-F., Vongerichten, A., Frackowiak, R. S. J., and Siebner, H. R. (2010). Nurture versus Nature: Long-Term Impact of Forced Right-Handedness on Structure of Pericentral Cortex and Basal Ganglia. Journal of Neuroscience, 30(9), 3271-3275.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20203186/

What is a promise worth?
structureNotes.purpose:
• The promise when it is spoken — hope, sincerity, belief.

  • The trust placed in it — what the other person risks by believing.

  • The cost of keeping it — sacrifice, inconvenience, loyalty, endurance.

  • The breaking of it — disappointment, betrayal, circumstance, failure.

  • The question of intention — was it a lie, or was it once genuinely meant?

  • The aftermath — what remains after the words are gone.

  • The final measure of worth — whether a promise is valued by its words, intent, fulfillment, or consequences.
structureNotes.outline:
Darrell Barrow
(c) 9/25/2026

What is a promise worth?
Is a promise worth the words used to make it?
Is it worth the sacrifice required to keep it?
Does its worth depend on who makes it, 
considering cultural or societal contexts that shape trust and obligation?

What is a promise worth?
Does a broken promise become worthless, 
even if it once had value because it was genuinely meant?
Is a promise measured when it is spoken, 
or only when keeping it becomes difficult?

What is a promise worth?


The promise when it is spoken — hope, sincerity, belief.
The trust it inspires — what the other person risks by believing.
The cost of keeping it — sacrifice, inconvenience, loyalty, endurance.
The breaking of it — disappointment, betrayal, circumstance, failure.
The question of intention — was it a lie, or was it once genuinely meant?
The aftermath — what remains after the words are gone.
The final measure of worth — whether a promise is valued by its words, intent, fulfillment, or consequences.
That gives the poem movement instead of treating the question as one fixed idea.
You could keep returning to:
What is a promise worth?
But each return would carry more weight because the reader has passed through another stage of the question.
So the poem does not have to answer:
A promise is worth this.
It can gradually reveal that a promise's worth changes depending on where you stand in its life cycle: when it is made, when it is trusted, when it is tested, when it is kept, and when it is broken-fostering a sense of moral reflection and understanding of complexity.

structureNotes.title: How would the project remain affordable and sustainable?
structureNotes.purpose: Organize research into how an urban agriculture project could cover its costs, keep produce affordable, and sustain operations over time.
structureNotes.summary: The research connects operating costs, funding, revenue, pricing, land access, labor, infrastructure, resource use, crop economics, waste, and financial resilience. It also examines how shared resources and organizational structure could affect affordability and sustainability. Funding programs are research leads; their availability, eligibility, and requirements still need verification.
structureNotes.outline:
1. Cost management

    • Identify startup and recurring costs.

    • Distinguish fixed costs from variable costs.

    • Include labor, water, electricity, equipment, maintenance, transportation, refrigeration, and insurance.

    • Examine hidden costs, postharvest handling, and distribution.

    • Compare hydroponics with raised beds.

  2. Federal grants and assistance

    • Investigate USDA urban agriculture grants, NIFA programs, NRCS assistance, local food promotion, and composting and food-waste programs.

    • Determine eligibility for nonprofits and community groups without nonprofit status.

    • Identify eligible expenses and matching-fund requirements.

    • Examine evaluation criteria and reporting requirements.

    • Plan for operations after grant funding ends.

  3. State, city, and foundation funding

    • Investigate New York State agriculture programs.

    • Investigate NYC urban agriculture programs.

    • Identify relevant local foundations.

    • Compare eligibility, funding restrictions, and funding periods.

  4. Revenue models

    • Examine produce sales, CSA shares, institutional sales, and restaurant sales.

    • Examine workshops, donations, and sponsorships.

    • Assess which revenues could cover recurring expenses.

  5. Pricing and affordability

    • Examine sliding-scale pricing, SNAP participation, subsidized produce, and cross-subsidization.

    • Compare production costs with prices customers can afford.

    • Identify how any gap between costs and affordable prices would be funded.

  6. Land economics

    • Compare leases, land trusts, donated space, and public land.

    • Examine land costs and long-term site security.

  7. Labor models

    • Compare volunteer labor and paid staffing.

    • Examine workforce development and apprenticeships.

    • Assess labor costs and staffing continuity.

  8. Infrastructure costs

    • Compare raised beds, greenhouses, and hydroponic systems.

    • Include refrigeration, vehicles, and kitchens.

    • Account for maintenance and replacement.

  9. Energy use

    • Examine lighting, pumps, refrigeration, and greenhouse systems.

    • Assess the effect of energy costs on indoor farming.

  10. Water management

    • Examine irrigation costs, conservation, rainwater use, and metering.

  11. Crop economics

    • Calculate cost per crop and per pound harvested.

    • Compare yield per square foot, labor per crop, and value per growing cycle.

  12. Waste reduction

    • Examine losses from spoilage, overproduction, poor storage, and weak distribution.

    • Identify how reducing losses could improve affordability.

  13. Financial resilience and grant dependence

    • Plan reserves for equipment replacement, crop failures, and funding gaps.

    • Examine what happens when grants end.

    • Identify which ongoing expenses require dependable revenue.

  14. Cooperative economics

    • Examine shared equipment, transportation, kitchens, and food hubs.

    • Compare potential savings with participation costs.

  15. Nonprofit versus commercial structure

    • Compare effects on funding access, revenue, taxes, and governance.

    • Assess how each structure supports the project's affordability and sustainability goals.

outputs.title: The Voice of the Park
outputs.purpose: A poem centered on the park as a speaking witness to memory, movement, solitude, and shared human presence.
outputs.body:
The Voices of the Park


Darrell Barrow
© 6/30/2026

Green spaces,
as they're called.
Parks.

Each carries a unique color;
timbre.

Its emotions vary
throughout the day.

The park is
the canvas.

Mornings,
cool and open.

A few exercise
in the fresh air.

Passersby stop with breakfast
before gathering for work—
sometimes.

Traffic flows in syncopation
with the stoplight.

Light high in the sky.
Humidity moderated
by the trees.

Voices rise.
Accents mix.
Children laugh.
Chess tables fill.

Some—
smoke weed.
Others converse and rest.

Wind carries:
Weed,
Food,
Barbecue.
Occasional stench.
Sewer.
Garbage.

Occasionally,
soccer practice takes the field.
Public events assemble.
"Shakespeare
in the park."
Music plays in the background
like Goldilocks,
not too loud,
not too soft,
just right.

Light lowers.
Backpacks pass through.
Others arrive with bicycles,
basketballs,
scooters.

Chess tables fill
with teenagers
talking about the day.

A group leaves,
another takes the seats.
A chorus of voices,
the choir of youth.

Light fades.
The air lighter.
Reprieve
echoes through the trees.

Paper pause,
book closed—
Time to go home.
outputs.description: How the park has many voices throughout the day.

outputs.title: Shotgun Squirrel
outputs.description:
New poem idea: Shotgun Squirrel.

The squirrel shoots the bird after the bird steal his food.
outputs.body:
Shotgun Squirrel

Darrell Barrow
© 7/30/2026

I watch a squirrel I named "Carl."
He keeps count of everything.
Every nut,
every French fry,
every seed collected from the pavement.

He would greet me
as I sat on my favorite bench
with a McChicken, fries, and vanilla iced coffee.

I would watch him scurry behind me,
occasionally looking at me as we ate.
He would pause beside the bench.
"Good afternoon," I said
as I took a bite of a French fry.

He stood, looking across the ground.
I asked,
"Would you like some fries with that?"
I chuckled to myself,
pulling out a fry and tossing it his way.
Carl looked at the fry,
picked it up, and ate it.
"Would you like some ketchup with your fries?"
I said.

Carl would visit almost every day.
We exchanged looks
as we went about our routine.
We ate,
and he would pause on either side of me.

I'd break off a piece of my McChicken
and toss it his way.
He would grab it.
"Sorry, I have no French fries today."

"Would you like some for later?
Winter is coming,
and I know you have to prepare."

I prepared each day,
expecting to see Carl.
French fries, vanilla coffee,
and a McChicken.
I wonder if Carl is sad
on the days I don't show.

On one particular day,
Carl was heading my way.
I tossed a French fry in his direction.
A bird swooped down
and grabbed it.

Carl stopped,
sat back on his hind legs,
looked at me,
then at the bird.
He pulled out a shotgun,
shot the bird,
put it away,
then continued toward his fry.

I will never look at Carl the same again.
My "Shotgun Squirrel."

outputs.title: The View From Here
outputs.description: A reflective poem inspired by an image of a weathered wooden path leading through beach grass and palm trees toward the ocean at sunset. The speaker studies the path with hesitation, questioning whether the peace it appears to offer can be trusted. As the landscape responds through sunlight, wind, leaves, animals, sand, and sea, the speaker gradually moves forward, accepts the invitation to rest, and gains a changed perspective on the life left behind.
outputs.body:
The View From Here


Darrell Barrow
© 7/23/2026

You offer a destination,
but will I walk the path?

From here, it looks like peace,
but images can be deceiving.

You show everything I want
But will it be what I need?

What lies beyond what I can see?
I fear what I may find:
peace,
terror.
My mind wanders.

Should I trust your apparent relief?
It's wrong to judge you from what I feel.
Trust does not come easy for me.

You answer with a sea-filled gentle breeze.
Are you tempting me?
What are you trying to offer me?

Am I too hurt to see
your offer of peace,
solitude, and relief?

You answer,
in a gentle wave of palm leaves.
Are you responding to me?
Do you know the real me?
The me reluctant to accept your invitation of peace?

Ocean of blue
Sand tan
The sun low,
like a northern star.
I see solitude and peace,
but these questions lie beneath.

You answer by parting a palm tree.
The sun reflects wholly on me.
A peaceful, serene stage.
Sun rays tightly spotted on me.

I take a step,
the sun's rays energizing me.
You answer with a gentle breeze.

Take a few more steps.
The sun's rays ripple through the leaves.
Silhouettes caress my face.

I turn to see I have walked further than I thought.
Halfway between here and where.
Here is different from where I was.
You answer with the smell of the sea.

Why did I ever doubt?
You seem to know me.
A hermit crab greets me,
turns, and leads the way.

It waits at the end to the side,
Waiting—
I pause before the sand
the sun full on my face.
I look at the crab and smile
as he turns and goes his way.

I turn to the left.
A table with an umbrella and a chair greets me.
It seems you are expecting me.
You answer, showering the table in palm leaves.

Birds fly in formation toward the setting set for me,
circling the table
as if saying, "Have a seat."

Okay, I get it. This is for me.
I remove my shoes;
my feet touch the sand.
Perfectly warmed to soothe my tired feet.
I whisper, "Thank you. You did all this for me."

I move toward the seat while
the sun bathes me in warmth.
I tip my hat in thanks.

At the table, before I sit,
what do I see?
A fresh coconut lying, waiting for me.
A rock perfectly placed.
I crack open the shell,
careful not to spill its water.
I take a sip as I sit in the chair.
I set the other half aside for you.
My personal thank you.

You reply with a brisk ocean breeze.
Raising my coconut,
I toast the wind.

I embrace the warmth of the sun.
I accept the scent of the sea.
I find relief in the coolness of the breeze.
I play with the sand beneath my feet.
I gently talk to the palm trees.
Thank you all for making this space for me.

The hours pass.
The sun lowers its head.
A gull passes overhead,
drops a fish,
leaves; there is nothing to be said.
Thank you, Mr. Gull.
Now I'm even fed.

The sun yawns as it readies for bed.
I get up, find a leaf, and wrap my fish.
I head back to the path.
It's different now.

Why did I question?
Why did I hesitate?
Why did I fear?

I look back from whence I came.
Life was there,
but now reframed.


Author’s Note

This poem began during a therapy session while I was discussing deeply buried emotional experiences. During a pause in the conversation, I looked at a calendar image behind my therapist. The path stood out to me first, and I said that the image was speaking to me and that I needed to write about it.

I did not plan the poem or decide beforehand what the image should mean. I looked at the scene and allowed it to lead me. As I entered the image in my mind, the landscape responded through sunlight, wind, palm leaves, animals, and the sea.

I have always been drawn to nature, solitude, and the things that can happen when we become quiet enough to listen. For me, this poem became an experience of finding peace and gaining a different perspective on the difficulties I have encountered over time.

outputs.title: Petrichor
outputs.body:
Petrichor


Darrell Barrow
© 8/7/2026

The dryness.
The dirt—
Agh!
Look at the grass.

The yard.
Cross slowly,
the grass thins down to dirt in places,
wherever the green has dried out.

Look up.
The sky.
The blue is gone.
Clouds moving in.

Then—
A drop.
Dark on the ground.
Then a few more, sparse.

From the dark spots,
something rises;
the air changes.

Fresh,
Cool,
Clean,
Invigorating.

Leaves brighten and lift.
Dust settles.
Stones darken.
Green slowly returns.

The rain is harder now.
Run for the house.
Stand in the doorway.
Watch the falling rain.

You smile.
One less chore for the day.
Water the yard—
Checked.
Mother Nature lent a hand.

Breathe in.
Stay in the doorway.
Just a little longer.
Nothing needs doing.
Neither do you.

The rain stops.
Breathe in.
Something remains.
Still there.

Petrichor: The Smell of Rain

outputs.title: Peer Mentorship and Paying It Forward
outputs.body:
Peer Mentorship and Paying It Forward

Darrell Pender

© 8/19/2026

Becoming a mentor to my peers felt awkward at first. It doesn't feel as awkward now, which I think many others can relate to, and it has become increasingly rewarding over time.

I am still getting used to people calling me "Chef." Escoffier has given me a strong foundation, along with the wisdom of those who work and have worked in the field.

Externship was the best experience I've had. Starting in a French restaurant owned by Daniel Boulud was amazing: prep work, working the line, and garde manger.

Wegmans allowed me to see how a large operation runs and how everyone plays a part in the flow of production. I gained experience with food waste management, sustainability, ordering, and more.

I love mentoring because it is my way of giving back. Someone mentored me when I injured my hip and had to complete a remote catering externship.

Sharing knowledge not only reinforces what I've learned but also prompts mentees' questions that challenge me to think, research, and deepen my understanding.

I have come to see that mentorship is a two-way street. While I help someone work through a problem or understand a process, I also learn and grow through the experience.

Working with peers who run home-based businesses shows me how different experiences and challenges shape the way each person approaches their work, making mentorship a dynamic learning exchange.

When we exchange ideas or work through a problem together, I have to think carefully about what I know, why something works, and how that knowledge might apply to someone else's circumstances. In that process, I often strengthen my own understanding as well.

I do not see mentorship as one person having all the answers. Professional knowledge can flow both ways. Someone may come to me for guidance in an area where I have more experience, while they may have knowledge or perspective that teaches me something in return. That exchange is part of what makes peer mentorship valuable to me.

Paying it forward holds personal significance for me. Knowing that others invested in my growth motivates me to support my peers in the same way.

Helping my peers is one way I can extend that same support to someone else. I may be helping another person move forward, but I am continuing to move forward too.

revisions.title: Bajan Green Seasoning Tare
revisions.content: A ramen seasoning base built from Bajan green seasoning and a Japanese tare structure, using soy, mirin, rice vinegar, sugar, and chicken stock to control the broth's salt, acidity, umami, and herbaceous identity.

snapshot.title: Bajan Green Seasoning Tare
snapshot.mainIdea: A ramen seasoning base built from Bajan green seasoning and a Japanese tare structure, using soy, mirin, rice vinegar, sugar, and chicken stock to control the broth's salt, acidity, umami, and herbaceous identity.
snapshot.body:
Recipe Information

Recipe Name: Bajan Green Seasoning Tare

Cuisine: Caribbean-Japanese Fusion — Barbadian Focus

Course: Condiment

Category: Ramen Base Seasoning

Dietary Considerations: Contains soy

Yield: 1 cup, 8 fluid ounces, or 240 milliliters

Serving Size: 2 tablespoons, 1 fluid ounce, or 30 milliliters

Prep Time: 10 minutes

Cook Time: 5 minutes

Chill Time: 0 minutes

Rest Time: 15 minutes

Total Time: 30 minutes

Flavor Profile

Taste: Deep umami, herbaceous, lightly salty, citrus-balanced

Aroma: Thyme, scallion, soy, garlic

Mouthfeel: Lightly viscous, smooth, coating

General Description

A refined ramen seasoning base built from Bajan green seasoning, enhanced with Japanese umami components to anchor broth flavor and define the dish’s identity.

Suggested Price

$0.80–$1.50 per portion

Menu Description

Bajan herb tare with soy, aromatics, and umami depth.

Origins

Combines Barbadian green seasoning with the Japanese tare system used to season ramen broth.

History

Tare is the backbone of ramen flavor in Japanese cuisine. This adaptation replaces traditional tare aromatics with Bajan green seasoning to create a unique identity.

Cultural Significance

This is where fusion becomes intentional—blending structure through Japanese tare with identity through Bajan seasoning.

Techniques

Reduction

Flavor concentration

Balancing salt, acid, and umami

Controlled infusion

Equipment

Small saucepan

Whisk

Fine strainer

Measuring spoons

HACCP

H1: Proper refrigeration after preparation

H2: Cross-contamination prevention

H3: Temperature control during cooking

Critical Control Points

CCP1: Sauce briefly heated to at least 74°C

CCP2: Refrigerated promptly and stored at or below 5°C

Ingredients

½ cup / 120 milliliters Bajan green seasoning, prepared

¼ cup / 60 milliliters soy sauce

2 tablespoons / 30 milliliters mirin

1 tablespoon / 15 milliliters rice vinegar

1 teaspoon / 5 grams sugar

½ cup / 120 milliliters chicken stock

Instructions
Combine the green seasoning, soy sauce, mirin, rice vinegar, sugar, and chicken stock in a small saucepan.
Bring to a gentle simmer, whisking to combine.
Reduce slightly for 3–5 minutes to concentrate the flavor. Do not over-reduce.
Taste and adjust the balance between salt, acid, and herbs.

revisions.content:
Recipe Name: House Bajan Green Seasoning (Japanese-Adapted)
Cuisine: Barbadian (Bajan)
Course: Condiment
Category: Foundational Sauce
Dietary Considerations: Gluten-Free, Vegan
Yield: 2 cups (16 fl oz | 475 ml)
Serving Size: 2 tbsp (1 fl oz | 30 ml)
Prep Time: 20 minutes
Cook Time: 0 minutes
Chill Time: 0 minutes
Rest Time 30 minutes
Total Time: 50 minutes
Flavor Profile:
Taste: Herbaceous, savory, lightly spicy, citrus-bright
Aroma: Fresh thyme, scallion, garlic, subtle pepper heat
Mouthfeel: Lightly coarse, slightly oily, fresh

🧠 General Description:
A vibrant Barbadian green seasoning designed as a foundational flavor base for marinades, broths, and finishing oils, adapted for precision cooking and fusion applications.

💵 Suggested Price:
$0.75–$1.25 per portion

📋 Menu Description:
Fresh Bajan herb seasoning with thyme, scallion, garlic, and citrus.

🌍 Origins
Traditional Barbadian kitchens use green seasoning as a daily base for meats and stews.

📜 History
Green seasoning evolved across the Caribbean as a fresh herb marinade system, with Barbados emphasizing thyme, scallion, and balanced aromatics rather than heavy heat.

Cultural Significance
This is the backbone of Bajan cooking—flavor starts here. Every household version is slightly different, making it deeply personal and identity-driven.

🔪 Techniques
• Fine chopping or blending
• Balance of acid and aromatics
• Controlled hydration for versatility
• Flavor resting

🛠️ Equipment
• Blender or food processor
• Knife
• Cutting board
• Measuring spoons
• Storage container

🧯 HACCP Table

HACCP Code #DescriptionH1Proper herb washing and sanitationH2Cross-contamination preventionH3Refrigerated storage below 5°C

CCP Table

CCP Code #MetricIngredientPreparationCCP1≤5°CFinished seasoningRefrigerate immediatelyCCP2CleanHerbsWashed thoroughlyCCP3pH <4.6CitrusAcid balance for safety

🧾 Ingredients

ImperialMetricIngredientPreparationTime1 cup40 gScallionsRough chopped—½ cup20 gFresh thymeLeaves picked—¼ cup10 gParsleyRough chopped—4 cloves4 clovesGarlicPeeled—1 tbsp15 mlFresh gingerChopped—11Scotch bonnetSeeded (optional heat)—2 tbsp30 mlLime juiceFresh—2 tbsp30 mlNeutral oil——1 tsp5 gSalt——2 tbsp30 mlWaterAdjust texture—

📖 Instructions

  1. Wash all herbs thoroughly (CCP2) and dry well.

  2. Rough chop scallions, thyme, parsley, garlic, ginger, and pepper.

  3. Add all ingredients to blender.

  4. Pulse to a coarse paste—do not over-blend (texture matters).

  5. Taste and adjust salt and lime for balance.

  6. Transfer to container and refrigerate immediately (CCP1).

  7. Let rest at least 30 minutes before use to allow flavors to develop.

🍽️ Plating:
Serve as marinade, broth base, or finishing drizzle—do not over-plate, this is a supporting component.

📝 Notes
Keep it fresh and green—over-blending or overheating kills flavor. This should taste alive, not cooked.

🧊 Storage:
Refrigerate up to 5 days. Freeze in portions for extended use.

🔬 Nutritional Information (table)

revisions.content:
Recipe Name: Bajan Seasoned Chicken Ramen
Cuisine: Caribbean-Japanese Fusion (Barbadian Focus)
Course: Main
Category: Signature Dish
Dietary Considerations: Contains gluten, soy, egg
Yield: 4 servings (4 servings | 4 servings)
Serving Size: 1 bowl (16 oz | 475 ml)
Prep Time: 35 minutes
Cook Time: 1 hour
Chill Time: 0 minutes
Rest Time 10 minutes
Total Time: 1 hour 45 minutes
Flavor Profile:
Taste: Herbaceous, savory, mildly spiced, umami-balanced
Aroma: Thyme, garlic, scallion, subtle spice
Mouthfeel: Clean broth, tender chicken, springy noodles

🧠 General Description:
A refined fusion ramen using traditional Bajan green seasoning as the primary flavor base, paired with a clean Japanese-style broth for balance and structure.

💵 Suggested Price:
$20–$26

📋 Menu Description:
Bajan seasoned chicken ramen, clear broth, soft egg, scallion.

🌍 Origins
Combines Barbadian green seasoning with Japanese ramen technique.

📜 History
Bajan cuisine relies heavily on green seasoning—a blend of herbs, aromatics, and peppers. Japanese ramen emphasizes broth clarity and balance.

Cultural Significance
This dish preserves Barbadian identity through seasoning while using Japanese technique to elevate structure and presentation.

🔪 Techniques
• Green seasoning marination
• Searing
• Broth clarification
• Soft boiling
• Noodle preparation

🛠️ Equipment
• Stockpot
• Sauté pan
• Mixing bowls
• Strainer
• Tongs
• Ladle

🧯 HACCP Table

HACCP Code #DescriptionH1Raw poultry storageH2Cross-contamination controlH3Temperature control

CCP Table

CCP Code #MetricIngredientPreparationCCP174°CChickenFully cookedCCP2≤5°CEggsSafe storageCCP3100°CBrothBoiled

🧾 Ingredients

ImperialMetricIngredientPreparationTime2 lb900 gChicken thighsBajan green seasoned4–12 hr4 cups950 mlChicken stock——2 tbsp30 mlSoy sauce——2 tbsp30 mlBajan green seasoningFresh blend—1 tbsp15 mlGarlicMinced—1 tbsp15 mlGingerSliced—4 portions—Ramen noodles——44EggsSoft boiled6 min22ScallionsSliced—

📖 Instructions

  1. Prepare mise en place: slice scallions, mince garlic, slice ginger, portion noodles.

  2. Coat chicken with Bajan green seasoning and marinate 4–12 hours.

  3. Sear chicken until internal temperature reaches 74°C (CCP1). Rest 10 minutes, slice.

  4. Bring stock to boil with garlic, ginger, and a small amount of green seasoning (CCP3). Reduce to simmer.

  5. Season broth lightly with soy sauce—do not overpower herbal profile.

  6. Cook noodles separately, drain well.

  7. Soft boil eggs for 6 minutes, chill immediately (CCP2), peel.

  8. Assemble: noodles → broth → sliced chicken → egg → scallions.

  9. Serve immediately.

🍽️ Plating:
Clean, minimal ramen bowl—focus on clarity and green herb tones.

📝 Notes
Green seasoning is the identity—keep it fresh, not cooked out or muted.

🧊 Storage:
Store components separately up to 3 days refrigerated.

🔬 Nutritional Information (table)

📖 Instructions

  8. Assemble: noodles → broth → sliced chicken → egg → scallions.

  9. Serve immediately.

Clean, minimal ramen bowl—focus on clarity and green herb tones.

Green seasoning is the identity—keep it fresh, not cooked out or muted.

Store components separately up to 3 days refrigerated.

Menu Description

Origins

Combines Barbadian green seasoning with Japanese ramen technique.

History

Bajan cuisine relies heavily on green seasoning—a blend of herbs, aromatics, and peppers. Japanese ramen emphasizes broth clarity and balance.

Cultural Significance

This dish preserves Barbadian identity through seasoning while using Japanese technique to elevate structure and presentation.

Techniques

HACCP

H2: Cross-contamination control

H3: Temperature control

Critical Control Points

CCP1: Chicken cooked to 74°C

CCP2: Eggs stored at or below 5°C

CCP3: Broth brought to 100°C

Ingredients

2 pounds / 900 grams chicken thighs, seasoned with Bajan green seasoning for 4–12 hours

4 cups / 950 milliliters chicken stock

2 tablespoons / 30 milliliters soy sauce

2 tablespoons / 30 milliliters Bajan green seasoning, fresh blend

1 tablespoon / 15 milliliters garlic, minced

1 tablespoon / 15 milliliters ginger, sliced

4 portions ramen noodles

4 eggs, soft-boiled for 6 minutes

2 scallions, sliced

Instructions

  1. Prepare the mise en place: slice the scallions, mince the garlic, slice the ginger, and portion the noodles.

  2. Coat the chicken with Bajan green seasoning and marinate for 4–12 hours.

  3. Sear the chicken until its internal temperature reaches 74°C. Rest for 10 minutes, then slice.

  4. Bring the chicken stock to a boil with the garlic, ginger, and a small amount of green seasoning. Reduce to a simmer.

  5. Season the broth lightly with soy sauce without overpowering the herbal profile.

  6. Cook the noodles separately and drain well.

  7. Soft-boil the eggs for 6 minutes, chill immediately, and peel.

  8. Assemble each bowl:

    Noodles

    Broth

    Sliced chicken

    Egg

    Scallions

  9. Serve immediately.

Plating

Clean, minimal ramen bowl with emphasis on broth clarity and green herb tones.

Notes

Green seasoning is the identity—keep it fresh, not cooked out or muted.

Storage

Store the components separately under refrigeration for up to 3 days.
