revisions.title: Five Foundations of Successful Cocktail Making
revisions.content: Successful cocktail making depends on attention to detail before, during, and after mixing: quality ingredients, preparation, proper glass temperature, accurate measurement, and thoughtful garnish.

snapshot.title: Five Foundations of Successful Cocktail Making
snapshot.mainIdea: Successful cocktail making depends on attention to detail before, during, and after mixing: quality ingredients, preparation, proper glass temperature, accurate measurement, and thoughtful garnish.
snapshot.body:
The Darlingtons identify five foundational practices for successful cocktail making.

  1. Use quality spirits
    The quality of the base spirit directly affects the quality of the finished drink. A cocktail cannot fully overcome poor-quality foundational ingredients.

  2. Prep before mixing
    Cocktail preparation benefits from mise en place just as cooking does. Bottles, tools, juices, and garnishes should be prepared and arranged before mixing begins.
    This reduces interruptions and allows the drink to be assembled efficiently and consistently.

  3. Prepare the glass
    Glass temperature is part of drink preparation.
    Cold drinks benefit from chilled glassware because it helps preserve the intended temperature and crispness of the cocktail. If freezer space is unavailable, the glass can be chilled with ice while the drink is prepared.
    Hot drinks benefit from warming the serving vessel beforehand.

  4. Measure ingredients
    Accurate measurement protects balance and proportion.
    A cocktail should allow its individual ingredients to remain perceptible without one component overwhelming the others. Using a jigger helps maintain consistency and balance.
    When measuring, beginning with the least expensive ingredient can reduce waste if a mistake occurs.
    The finished cocktail should also be tasted before serving to confirm that it is balanced.

  5. Remember the garnish
    Garnish is not merely decorative.
    Citrus twists, peels, wheels, herbs, and other garnishes can contribute aroma and flavor as well as visual appeal. Because aroma is experienced immediately when the drink approaches the nose, garnish can influence the drink before the first sip is taken.

Together, these five practices show that cocktail quality is created through a sequence of intentional details rather than through mixing ingredients alone.

revisions.title: Flavor development
revisions.content: Flavor development is the deliberate process of building, balancing, concentrating, layering, and connecting flavors throughout preparation and cooking.

snapshot.title: Flavor development
snapshot.mainIdea: Flavor development is the deliberate process of building, balancing, concentrating, layering, and connecting flavors throughout preparation and cooking.
snapshot.body:
Flavor development does not happen only when seasoning is added at the end of cooking. It begins with ingredient selection and continues through preparation, seasoning, cooking technique, temperature, timing, texture, and finishing.

Each stage can alter how an ingredient tastes. Browning can create depth, reduction can concentrate flavor, acid can add brightness, salt can improve clarity, fat can carry flavor, and heat can transform aroma, texture, and intensity.

Developing flavor requires understanding how individual elements interact rather than treating seasoning as a single final adjustment. The goal is not always to make flavor stronger. The goal may be balance, contrast, clarity, depth, restraint, or harmony.

revisions.title: Flavor pairing
revisions.content: Flavor pairing is the deliberate combination of ingredients whose tastes, aromas, textures, and culinary functions support, contrast with, or transform one another.

snapshot.title: Flavor pairing
snapshot.mainIdea: Flavor pairing is the deliberate combination of ingredients whose tastes, aromas, textures, and culinary functions support, contrast with, or transform one another.
snapshot.body:
Flavor pairing involves more than identifying ingredients that taste good together. A pairing may work because ingredients share aromatic characteristics, create contrast, balance one another, or perform complementary roles within a dish.

Some pairings reinforce similar flavors, while others create interest through differences such as sweet and bitter, rich and acidic, soft and crisp, or earthy and bright. Cultural traditions, ingredient seasonality, cooking techniques, and personal experience also influence whether a combination feels coherent.

Flavor-pairing references can provide useful starting points, but they do not replace tasting or culinary judgment. A pairing must still be evaluated within the complete dish, including proportion, preparation, texture, temperature, seasoning, and intended experience.

revisions.content: Food science helps explain how ingredients change during preparation and cooking, allowing culinary decisions to be made with greater understanding and control.

snapshot.title: Food science in cooking
snapshot.mainIdea: Food science helps explain how ingredients change during preparation and cooking, allowing culinary decisions to be made with greater understanding and control.
snapshot.body:
Food science examines the physical and chemical changes that occur in ingredients. These changes include browning, protein coagulation, starch gelatinization, emulsification, fermentation, moisture movement, fat crystallization, and the release or loss of aromatic compounds.

Understanding these processes can help explain why a technique succeeds or fails. It can support decisions about temperature, timing, ingredient ratios, equipment, texture, and preservation.

Scientific knowledge should support culinary judgment rather than replace it. A technically correct process must still produce food that tastes good, has the intended texture, reflects its cultural context, and serves the purpose of the dish.

The purchased weight or volume of an ingredient is not always the quantity available for serving or recipe production. Peeling, trimming, deboning, cleaning, cooking, draining, and portioning can reduce the usable amount.

Emperor’s Earth is a speculative-fiction manuscript centered on Kido Thompson after a Mirrian attack destroys much of Earth’s population. The manuscript follows Kido’s relationships with Ricky Chapman, Kenji Nakamura, Mira Devereaux, Xavier, Ja-Jorel, and others as he struggles with trauma, responsibility, power, identity, manipulation, and rebuilding. Doctor Henry Feldman attempts to study, control, program, and use Kido through genetic research, behavioral manipulation, and ancient technology.

The story also involves The Order, the Russian Federation, Colonel Reed Hawkes, the Mirrians, political and military power, covert experimentation, alien contact, survival, reconciliation, and the ethical consequences of power. The manuscript includes twelve chapters, character profiles, organization profiles, Mirrian terminology, a working Mirrinese lexicon, and Kido’s notes concerning what Earth must build going forward.

revisions.title: Mount Gay Rum
revisions.content:
Mount Gay presents Barbados and its rum-making tradition as inseparable, shaped by the island’s geology, culture, landscape, and centuries of craftsmanship.

Water
Mount Gay uses water from a deep artesian well located on its original property in Saint Lucy, Barbados. The well was first dug in 1703 and remains in use. The water rises from coral caverns hundreds of feet underground and is naturally filtered through the island’s coral geology.

Yeast and Fermentation
Yeast converts the sugars in molasses into alcohol during fermentation. Mount Gay uses two fermentation methods.

Closed fermentation is used for column distillation and uses a proprietary heirloom yeast strain developed by Mount Gay’s rum makers.

Open-air fermentation is used for pot-still distillation. The molasses-and-water mixture is exposed to the Barbadian environment, allowing native airborne yeasts to enter the fermentation and contribute to the rum’s aromatic character.

Molasses
Mount Gay uses molasses produced from selected Barbadian and Caribbean sugarcane. The molasses has a malty character with notes of caramel and toffee, along with acidity and slight bitterness in the finish.

snapshot.author: Mount Gay Distilleries Ltd.
snapshot.copiedText:
Mount Gay presents Barbados and its rum-making tradition as inseparable, shaped by the island’s geology, culture, landscape, and centuries of craftsmanship.

Water
Mount Gay uses water from a deep artesian well located on its original property in Saint Lucy, Barbados. The well was first dug in 1703 and remains in use. The water rises from coral caverns hundreds of feet underground and is naturally filtered through the island’s coral geology.

Yeast and Fermentation
Yeast converts the sugars in molasses into alcohol during fermentation. Mount Gay uses two fermentation methods.

Closed fermentation is used for column distillation and uses a proprietary heirloom yeast strain developed by Mount Gay’s rum makers.

Open-air fermentation is used for pot-still distillation. The molasses-and-water mixture is exposed to the Barbadian environment, allowing native airborne yeasts to enter the fermentation and contribute to the rum’s aromatic character.

Molasses
Mount Gay uses molasses produced from selected Barbadian and Caribbean sugarcane. The molasses has a malty character with notes of caramel and toffee, along with acidity and slight bitterness in the finish.

Key Significance
The character of Mount Gay rum is connected to Barbados through its water, native yeasts, sugarcane, climate, geology, and traditional production methods.

revisions.title: The Voice of the Park
revisions.content:
The Voices of the Park


Darrell Barrow
© 6/30/2026

Green spaces,
as they're called.
Parks.

Each carries a unique color;
timbre.

Its emotions vary
throughout the day.

The park is
the canvas.

Mornings,
cool and open.

A few exercise
in the fresh air.

Passersby stop with breakfast
before gathering for work—
sometimes.

Traffic flows in syncopation
with the stoplight.

Light high in the sky.
Humidity moderated
by the trees.

Voices rise.
Accents mix.
Children laugh.
Chess tables fill.

Some—
smoke weed.
Others converse and rest.

Wind carries:
Weed,
Food,
Barbecue.
Occasional stench.
Sewer.
Garbage.

Occasionally,
soccer practice takes the field.
Public events assemble.
"Shakespeare
in the park."
Music plays in the background
like Goldilocks,
not too loud,
not too soft,
just right.

Light lowers.
Backpacks pass through.
Others arrive with bicycles,
basketballs,
scooters.

Chess tables fill
with teenagers
talking about the day.

A group leaves,
another takes the seats.
A chorus of voices,
the choir of youth.

Light fades.
The air lighter.
Reprieve
echoes through the trees.

Paper pause,
book closed—
Time to go home.

snapshot.purpose: A poem centered on the park as a speaking witness to memory, movement, solitude, and shared human presence.

revisions.title: Prepare for Death and Follow Me — Traditional Memento Mori Epitaph
revisions.content:
Remember me as you pass by.

As you are now, so once was I.

As I am now, so you must be.

Prepare for death and follow me.

snapshot.title: Prepare for Death and Follow Me — Traditional Memento Mori Epitaph

subtypeId.name: Recipe

snapshot.author: raditional / Unknown
snapshot.copiedText:
Remember me as you pass by.

As you are now, so once was I.

As I am now, so you must be.

Prepare for death and follow me.
snapshot.summary: raditional funerary epitaph appearing in numerous variations on gravestones in Britain, Ireland, and the United States. The verse addresses the living from the perspective of the dead: the deceased was once as the reader is now, and the reader will eventually share the deceased's condition. It functions as a memento mori—a reminder of mortality and the inevitability of death. Versions of the epitaph appear extensively in historic American cemeteries, including colonial and nineteenth-century New England, while related forms also occur in British and Irish churchyards. Its underlying idea is substantially older than any single surviving gravestone and belongs to a broader tradition of the dead warning or addressing the living.

revisions.content: Escoffier reorganized kitchen production by dividing work into specialized departments or stations based on the foods being produced.

snapshot.title: The Classical Brigade as a Division of Labor
snapshot.mainIdea: Escoffier reorganized kitchen production by dividing work into specialized departments or stations based on the foods being produced.
snapshot.body: The classical brigade divides a kitchen into stations, with each station responsible for a particular category of production. A chef de partie manages each station, while larger stations may include assistants. This creates defined responsibility, specialization, and an organized production structure. The system remains influential even though modern kitchens often modify it

revisions.title: Information Access Without Visible File Structures
revisions.content: A computer interface does not necessarily need to expose folders, files, and storage locations if information can be retrieved according to meaning, context, or user intent.

revisions.title: Mirrinese Lexicon
revisions.content:
Core Roots

ja-jorel — peace; state of harmonious stillness; also used as a personal name.

lin — light; illumination; associated with First Rise.

len — sustain; foundational root for nourishment and vitality.

hal — food; sustenance; tied to offerings and daily provision.

ra — give; provide; offer.

sha — expression of gratitude; used in formal thanks.

va — our; collective belonging.

no — my; individual affirmation.

sa — nourish; restore; used in blessings.

vash — until; up to a future meeting or moment; temporal marker of continuation.

 

Compound Forms (Derived from Roots)

Ha’lin — to greet the light; morning acknowledgment.

Shalen — we thank; communal gratitude.

Ven-hal — for the food; gratitude for sustenance.

No’reth — that which you provide; offering or gift.

Sa’len — nourish; restore our being.

Va-lin — our being; shared essence.

Prayer (Mirrinese + English)

Ha’lin ja-jorel.

We greet the light in peace.

Mirria, shalen ven-hal no’reth to-ra.

Mirria, we thank you for the food you provide.

Sa’len va-lin.

Nourish our being.

KIDO’S TABLET NOTES — WHAT EARTH MUST BUILD GOING FORWARD

(This is the REAL list you were asking for — the actionable future work.)

1. A global transparency framework

– no secret programs

– no hidden labs

– no unilateral decisions

– mandatory disclosure rules

 2. A planetary ethics board independent of government

– can veto experiments

– can halt research instantly

– protects biological life (human + non-human)

3. Reconstruction of leadership structures

– remove military-first decision models

– civilian oversight

– remove anyone tied to old abuses

– establish clear chains of accountability

4. A unified education initiative

– teach the real history (genocide, misuse of tech)

– teach Mirrian principles of balance/respect

– dismantle the aggressive worldview that caused Na Ja-Jorel

 5. A technology-governance charter

– rules for developing, testing, and storing any advanced tech

– mandatory fail-safes

– restrictions on energy-based weapons or manipulation systems

6. A planetary council of nations

– replaces secret coalitions

– open decision-making

– one global body to prevent individual nations from going rogue

7. A new conflict-resolution system

– early-warning mechanisms

– mediation teams

– no escalation without planetary approval

 8. A scientific oversight alliance

– independent review of any genetic or technological research

– cross-examination from multiple fields

– no single scientist or agency can steer humanity

9. Survivor support and stabilization

– mental health framework

– rebuilding housing

– restoring lost communities

– foundations for long-term cultural stability

 

10. A planetary value statement

– respect for life

– no subjugation, no domination

– no exploitation of other species

– stewardship of power

 

11. A long-term evolution plan

– benchmarks for maturity

– social, technological, and ethical milestones

– periodic self-audit to track growth

 

12. A blueprint for interspecies relationships

– guidelines for respecting other civilizations

– rules for exchange, communication, and shared technology

– protocols for accountability if Earth slips again

 

13. Kido’s internal responsibilities

– maintain balance between power and restraint

– create a successor structure not dependent on him

– train others to act as guardians of the new system

revisions.content: Continuity in Emperor’s Earth requires established characters, organizations, locations, technology, relationships, events, and chronology to remain consistent across the manuscript.

snapshot.title: Emperor’s Earth continuity
snapshot.mainIdea: Continuity in Emperor’s Earth requires established characters, organizations, locations, technology, relationships, events, and chronology to remain consistent across the manuscript.
snapshot.body:
The continuity of Emperor’s Earth depends on tracking confirmed story information rather than filling unresolved areas through assumption.

Important continuity areas include:

Character continuity

Characters must retain their established histories, motivations, relationships, knowledge, abilities, and emotional development.

Doctor Feldman’s actions must remain consistent with his obsession with control, genetic experimentation, behavioral manipulation, relationship with The Order, and attempts to control Kido.

Organization continuity

The organization connected to Feldman is established in the manuscript as The Order. Earlier references to the Society must be reviewed to determine whether they refer to The Order, represent an earlier working name, or identify a separate organization.

Event continuity

Events must remain consistent with when characters learn information, when organizations become visible, when alliances form, and when technologies or abilities are revealed.

Location continuity

Locations such as Feldman’s laboratory, the command center, the safehouse, Warehouse 9B, Coney Island, the Russian Federation command center, and The Order’s command center must remain consistent in purpose and sequence.

Technology continuity

The ancient device, genetic experimentation, behavioral programming, transit-disruption systems, Mirrian technology, and Kido’s abilities must follow their established limits and development.

Canon standard

Unresolved information must remain marked as unresolved until the manuscript or an established profile confirms it. New information should not be added merely to close a gap.

revisions.title: Emperor’s Earth organizations
revisions.content: The organizations in Emperor’s Earth represent different forms of political, scientific, military, social, and extraterrestrial power, and their goals and relationships must remain clearly distinguished.

snapshot.title: Emperor’s Earth organizations
snapshot.mainIdea: The organizations in Emperor’s Earth represent different forms of political, scientific, military, social, and extraterrestrial power, and their goals and relationships must remain clearly distinguished.
snapshot.body:
Emperor’s Earth contains several organizations and organized power structures that influence the plot.

The Order

A covert organization that provides Feldman with protection and resources. Its members pursue profit, political dominance, technological development, genetic enhancement, obedience, and social control.

Russian Federation

A political and military power with its own interest in Kido, Feldman’s research, genetic enhancement, strategic infiltration, and global dominance.

Its relationship with Feldman overlaps with The Order but also follows its own national agenda.

Kido’s Command Center

A survivor-led organization that develops from Kido’s former home. It coordinates communication, medical care, food, protection, scouting, research, and rebuilding after the attack.

The Mirrian High Council

The governing body involved in Mirrian political decisions, diplomacy, judgment, and the response to humanity’s actions.

The Mirrian Monarchy

Ka-Jorel and Ja-Jorel represent another form of Mirrian leadership that intersects with the High Council, Kido, and the relationship between Earth and Mirria.

Medical and scientific teams

Feldman’s medical team and associated researchers participate in testing, observation, manipulation, and reprogramming. Their individual knowledge, loyalty, and responsibility must be distinguished.

Military and security structures

Colonel Reed Hawkes and related personnel represent organized military or covert operations connected to capturing and controlling Kido.

Continuity concern

The manuscript uses both Society and The Order. This must be resolved so that readers can determine whether they are the same organization or separate organizations. Based on the developed chapters and profiles, The Order is the established name.

revisions.content: Emperor’s Earth is primarily present-day speculative science fiction, with strong elements of alien-contact apocalyptic fiction, post-apocalyptic survival science fiction, and philosophical and psychological science fiction.

snapshot.title: Genre labels for Emperor’s Earth
snapshot.mainIdea: Emperor’s Earth is primarily present-day speculative science fiction, with strong elements of alien-contact apocalyptic fiction, post-apocalyptic survival science fiction, and philosophical and psychological science fiction.
snapshot.body:
Primary Genre: Present-Day Speculative Science Fiction

Emperor’s Earth is set within recognizable present-day geography and history, but the ordinary world is altered through alien contact, extraordinary powers, survival systems, advanced technology, and consequences that extend beyond Earth.

The story uses real locations such as Caton Avenue, Ocean Avenue, Prospect Park, Rikers Island, the Pulaski Skyway, Route 22, and Plainfield. These familiar settings ground the story in a recognizable world while the Mirrian attack and Kido’s transformation break that reality open. The manuscript follows Kido and Ricky from Rikers Island toward Plainfield through these identifiable locations.

Strong Secondary Genre: Alien-Contact Apocalyptic Fiction

The Mirrians and humanity initially exist within a peaceful relationship, but that relationship collapses after the Mirrians discover concealed acts committed by humanity. The resulting attack devastates Earth and leaves only part of its population alive.

The story is therefore not only about aliens existing or arriving. It examines the destruction that follows failed contact and the question of why peace became “Na-Ja-Jorel”—no peace. The manuscript connects the attack to the Mirrians’ discovery of humanity’s hidden violence and exploitation of another alien species.

Another Accurate Label: Post-Apocalyptic Survival Science Fiction

After the Mirrian attack, survival and rebuilding become central to the story.

Kido searches for people he loves, frees Ricky from Rikers Island, finds shelter, helps survivors, and becomes involved in building systems for food, medical care, communication, protection, and recovery.

The story moves beyond surviving the initial attack. It also examines how people organize, rebuild community, and determine what kind of society will follow the collapse.

Deeper Thematic Label: Philosophical and Psychological Science Fiction

The story is not only about aliens, powers, or destruction. It examines peace and control, trauma, responsibility, manipulation, moral collapse, abuse of power, identity, and the consequences of using power without restraint.

The conflict between Kido and Doctor Feldman establishes this structure. Kido struggles with responsibility, trauma, leadership, and the possibility of becoming either a protector or a destroyer. Feldman pursues control through manipulation, experimentation, and programming.

Kido’s conflict is also internal. The manuscript presents a struggle between the person he understands himself to be and the entity or power developing within him.

These labels are not competing classifications. They describe different levels of the same work:

  • Present-day speculative science fiction identifies the broad primary genre.

  • Alien-contact apocalyptic fiction identifies the event that breaks the ordinary world.

  • Post-apocalyptic survival science fiction identifies the survival and rebuilding structure.

  • Philosophical and psychological science fiction identifies the deeper moral and internal concerns

snapshot.title: Edible-Portion Quantity
snapshot.mainIdea: Edible-portion quantity is the usable amount of an ingredient available after preparation losses have been remove
snapshot.body:
Edible-portion quantity represents the amount that can enter a recipe, be cooked, or be served after unusable material has been removed. It may be measured by weight, volume, or count.

The difference between as-purchased quantity and edible-portion quantity may result from peeling, trimming, deboning, cleaning, draining, or discarding damaged material. Cooking losses may also be included when the required quantity is based on the finished cooked product.

snapshot.title: Some edible greens still need moderation
snapshot.mainIdea: Greens like beet greens and purslane can be edible but may need moderation because of oxalate content.
snapshot.body: Edible does not always mean unlimited or suitable for every person. Some greens contain higher oxalates and may need moderation, especially for people who already need to watch oxalate intake. This kind of safety note should not mark the plant as forbidden by default. It should mark the plant as edible with a caution or moderation note.

snapshot.title: Leaf edibility depends on correct identification
snapshot.mainIdea: A leaf should not be used in food unless the plant is confidently identified and separated from unsafe look-alikes.
snapshot.body: The edible status of a leaf depends on knowing the exact plant, not only matching a general appearance. A reference image can suggest possible ingredients, but it cannot replace identification. Before using a leaf, confirm the plant, edible variety, growing source, and whether the leaf has been exposed to unsafe sprays, mold, pollution, or other contamination.

revisions.title: Dipping Sauce for Curry Goat Gyoza
revisions.content: Develop a dipping sauce that complements curry goat gyoza without overpowering the curry filling.

snapshot.title: Dipping Sauce for Curry Goat Gyoza
snapshot.mainIdea: Develop a dipping sauce that complements curry goat gyoza without overpowering the curry filling.
snapshot.body:
The dipping sauce should support the curry goat filling and the gyoza preparation.

It should provide enough acidity, salt, or brightness to balance the richness of the goat while allowing the curry flavor to remain central.

The sauce may use Japanese seasoning elements while keeping the Caribbean identity of the dish clear.

revisions.title: Jerk Chicken Ramen
revisions.content: A Caribbean–Japanese fusion ramen where jerk-marinated chicken provides bold Caribbean flavor, supported by a clean and balanced Japanese-style broth.

snapshot.title: Jerk Chicken Ramen
snapshot.mainIdea: A Caribbean–Japanese fusion ramen where jerk-marinated chicken provides bold Caribbean flavor, supported by a clean and balanced Japanese-style broth.
snapshot.body:
Recipe Information

Recipe Name: Jerk Chicken Ramen

Cuisine: Caribbean–Japanese Fusion

Course: Main

Category: Signature Dish

Dietary Considerations: Contains gluten, soy, and egg

Yield: 4 servings

Serving Size: 1 bowl, 16 ounces or 475 milliliters

Prep Time: 30 minutes

Cook Time: 1 hour

Chill Time: 0 minutes

Rest Time: 10 minutes

Total Time: 1 hour 40 minutes

Flavor Profile

Taste: Smoky, savory, umami with balanced heat

Aroma: Jerk spice, garlic, ginger

Mouthfeel: Clean broth, tender chicken, firm noodles

General Description

A structured ramen dish where jerk-marinated chicken provides bold Caribbean flavor, supported by a clean, balanced Japanese-style broth.

Suggested Price

$20–$26

Menu Description

Jerk chicken ramen with clear broth, soft egg, and scallions.

Origins

Fusion of Jamaican jerk cooking and Japanese ramen technique.

History

Jerk seasoning originates from Jamaica’s preservation methods. Ramen is a Japanese adaptation of Chinese noodle soups focused on broth clarity.

Cultural Significance

A disciplined fusion where Caribbean identity leads and Japanese technique refines execution.

Techniques

Marination

Searing

Broth simmering

Soft boiling

Noodle cooking

Equipment

Stockpot

Sauté pan

Mixing bowls

Strainer

Tongs

Ladle

HACCP

H1: Raw poultry storage

H2: Cross-contamination control

H3: Temperature control

Critical Control Points

CCP1: Chicken cooked to 74°C

CCP2: Eggs stored and handled at or below 5°C

CCP3: Broth brought to 100°C

Ingredients

2 pounds / 900 grams chicken thighs, jerk-marinated for 4–12 hours

4 cups / 950 milliliters chicken stock

2 tablespoons / 30 milliliters soy sauce

1 tablespoon / 15 milliliters garlic, minced

1 tablespoon / 15 milliliters ginger, sliced

4 portions ramen noodles

4 eggs, soft-boiled for 6 minutes

2 scallions, sliced

Instructions

  1. Prepare all ingredients: slice the scallions, mince the garlic, and slice the ginger.

  2. Marinate the chicken with jerk seasoning for 4–12 hours.

  3. Sear the chicken until its internal temperature reaches 74°C. Rest for 10 minutes, then slice.

  4. Bring the chicken stock to a boil with the garlic and ginger, then reduce to a simmer. Add the soy sauce.

  5. Cook the noodles separately, then drain.

  6. Soft-boil the eggs for 6 minutes, cool immediately, and peel.

  7. Assemble each bowl:

    Noodles

    Broth

    Sliced chicken

    Egg

    Scallions

  8. Serve immediately.

Plating

Clean bowl with centered noodles, neatly layered sliced chicken, a halved egg, and minimal garnish.

Notes

Do not overpower the broth. The jerk should be present but controlled.

Storage

Store components separately under refrigeration for up to 3 days.

revisions.title: Standard Lines
revisions.content: Standard lines provide east-west correction lines within the PLSS survey framework.

snapshot.title: Standard Lines
snapshot.mainIdea: Standard lines provide east-west correction lines within the PLSS survey framework.
snapshot.body: Standard parallels or correction lines are introduced periodically to control the effects of meridian convergence and maintain manageable township dimensions across large survey regions.

revisions.title: Modeling the Shape of the Earth
revisions.content: Geospatial coordinate systems require mathematical approximations of the Earth's irregular physical shape.

snapshot.title: Modeling the Shape of the Earth
snapshot.mainIdea: Geospatial coordinate systems require mathematical approximations of the Earth's irregular physical shape.
snapshot.body: The physical Earth is too irregular to serve directly as a mathematical reference surface. Geodesy therefore uses simplified models such as spheres and ellipsoids for coordinate calculations while other surfaces such as the geoid describe gravity-related characteristics.
questions: Why is an ellipsoid preferred over a sphere for precise geographic positioning?

revisions.title: Reference Ellipsoids
revisions.content: A reference ellipsoid is a mathematically defined surface used to approximate the size and shape of the Earth.

snapshot.title: Reference Ellipsoids
snapshot.mainIdea: A reference ellipsoid is a mathematically defined surface used to approximate the size and shape of the Earth.
snapshot.body: Reference ellipsoids provide a regular mathematical surface upon which geodetic coordinates can be defined. Their dimensions and flattening determine the geometry used for calculations involving latitude, longitude, distance, and position.
questions: How do different reference ellipsoids affect calculated positions?

revisions.title: GRS 80
revisions.content: GRS 80 defines an ellipsoid and related parameters used in modern geodetic reference systems.

snapshot.title: GRS 80
snapshot.mainIdea: GRS 80 defines an ellipsoid and related parameters used in modern geodetic reference systems.
snapshot.body: The Geodetic Reference System 1980 provides geometric and physical constants used in geodesy. Its ellipsoid forms the geometric basis of NAD 83 and other modern positioning work.

revisions.title: Semi-Major and Semi-Minor Axes
revisions.content: The semi-major and semi-minor axes define the primary dimensions of an ellipsoid.

snapshot.title: Semi-Major and Semi-Minor Axes
snapshot.mainIdea: The semi-major and semi-minor axes define the primary dimensions of an ellipsoid.
snapshot.body: The semi-major axis represents the equatorial radius of an ellipsoid while the semi-minor axis represents the polar radius. Their difference reflects the flattening of the ellipsoid.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: Ellipsoid Flattening
revisions.content: Flattening measures how much an ellipsoid differs from a sphere because its polar radius is shorter than its equatorial radius.

snapshot.title: Ellipsoid Flattening
snapshot.mainIdea: Flattening measures how much an ellipsoid differs from a sphere because its polar radius is shorter than its equatorial radius.
snapshot.body: Earth-reference ellipsoids are slightly compressed at the poles. Flattening provides a numerical description of that difference and is one of the defining parameters of a reference ellipsoid.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: Latitude and Longitude
revisions.content: Latitude and longitude provide angular measurements used to describe positions relative to an Earth reference surface.

snapshot.title: Latitude and Longitude
snapshot.mainIdea: Latitude and longitude provide angular measurements used to describe positions relative to an Earth reference surface.
snapshot.body: Latitude expresses angular position north or south of the equator while longitude expresses angular position east or west of a reference meridian. Their precise spatial meaning depends on the datum or reference frame in which they are expressed.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: How does geodetic latitude differ from geocentric latitude?

revisions.title: Geodetic Latitude
revisions.content: Geodetic latitude is defined by the angle between the equatorial plane and the normal to the reference ellipsoid.

snapshot.title: Geodetic Latitude
snapshot.mainIdea: Geodetic latitude is defined by the angle between the equatorial plane and the normal to the reference ellipsoid.
snapshot.body: Geodetic latitude is the form of latitude commonly used in GIS and surveying. Because the Earth is modeled as an ellipsoid rather than a perfect sphere, geodetic latitude is not identical to geocentric latitude.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: Where is the difference between geodetic and geocentric latitude greatest?

revisions.title: Meridians of Longitude
revisions.content: Meridians are lines of constant longitude extending between the Earth's poles.

snapshot.title: Meridians of Longitude
snapshot.mainIdea: Meridians are lines of constant longitude extending between the Earth's poles.
snapshot.body: Longitude is measured relative to meridians. All meridians converge at the poles, and a designated prime meridian provides the zero-longitude reference from which east and west longitude are measured.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: Parallels of Latitude
revisions.content: Parallels are lines connecting locations with the same latitude.

snapshot.title: Parallels of Latitude
snapshot.mainIdea: Parallels are lines connecting locations with the same latitude.
snapshot.body: Parallels circle the Earth east to west and remain parallel to the equator. Unlike meridians, their circumferences decrease toward the poles.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: The Equator as a Reference
revisions.content: The equator provides the zero-latitude reference for geographic coordinate systems.

snapshot.title: The Equator as a Reference
snapshot.mainIdea: The equator provides the zero-latitude reference for geographic coordinate systems.
snapshot.body: The equator is the intersection of the Earth's reference surface with the plane perpendicular to its rotational axis through the center. Latitude is measured north or south from this reference.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: Prime Meridian
revisions.content: The prime meridian establishes the zero-longitude reference used to measure longitude east and west.

snapshot.title: Prime Meridian
snapshot.mainIdea: The prime meridian establishes the zero-longitude reference used to measure longitude east and west.
snapshot.body: A geographic coordinate system requires a reference meridian from which longitudes are measured. Modern global systems use a meridian associated with the international terrestrial reference system.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: How does the modern reference meridian relate to the historical Greenwich meridian?

revisions.title: Geographic Coordinates
revisions.content: Geographic coordinates describe positions on the Earth using angular measurements within a defined geodetic reference system.

snapshot.title: Geographic Coordinates
snapshot.mainIdea: Geographic coordinates describe positions on the Earth using angular measurements within a defined geodetic reference system.
snapshot.body: Geographic coordinates normally use latitude and longitude to describe location on an ellipsoid. The numeric values alone are insufficient unless the associated datum or reference frame is also known.
questions: When should geographic coordinates be transformed before combining GIS datasets?

revisions.title: Cartesian Coordinate Systems
revisions.content: Cartesian coordinates describe position along mutually perpendicular axes measured from an origin.

snapshot.title: Cartesian Coordinate Systems
snapshot.mainIdea: Cartesian coordinates describe position along mutually perpendicular axes measured from an origin.
snapshot.body: Cartesian coordinates use x and y in two dimensions and add z in three dimensions. The system provides the mathematical basis for many projected and Earth-centered geospatial coordinate systems.
questions: How are Cartesian coordinates used in Earth-centered Earth-fixed systems?

revisions.title: Polar Coordinates
revisions.content: Polar coordinates describe position using distance and direction relative to an origin.

snapshot.title: Polar Coordinates
snapshot.mainIdea: Polar coordinates describe position using distance and direction relative to an origin.
snapshot.body: Instead of perpendicular x and y values, a polar system locates a point using a radial distance from an origin and an angular direction. This form is useful in surveying and other measurements based on distance and azimuth.

revisions.title: Terrestrial Reference Frames
revisions.content: A terrestrial reference frame realizes a coordinate reference system through measured coordinates assigned to physical or continuously observed points.

snapshot.title: Terrestrial Reference Frames
snapshot.mainIdea: A terrestrial reference frame realizes a coordinate reference system through measured coordinates assigned to physical or continuously observed points.
snapshot.body: A reference system defines the theoretical rules for coordinates while a reference frame provides a practical realization of that system. Modern terrestrial reference frames account for Earth motion and changes through time.
questions: Why must epochs be considered when using modern terrestrial reference frames?

revisions.title: International Terrestrial Reference Frame
revisions.content: The ITRF provides a global terrestrial reference frame derived from high-precision geodetic observations.

snapshot.title: International Terrestrial Reference Frame
snapshot.mainIdea: The ITRF provides a global terrestrial reference frame derived from high-precision geodetic observations.
snapshot.body: The International Terrestrial Reference Frame provides coordinates and velocities for globally distributed stations. It supports precise positioning and provides an important foundation for global satellite-based reference systems.
questions: How are individual ITRF realizations distinguished by epoch and observation period?

revisions.title: Geodetic Datums
revisions.content: A geodetic datum provides the reference framework that gives coordinate values their spatial meaning.

snapshot.title: Geodetic Datums
snapshot.mainIdea: A geodetic datum provides the reference framework that gives coordinate values their spatial meaning.
snapshot.body: Latitude and longitude do not independently define an absolute location. Their meaning depends on a datum or reference frame that establishes how a reference surface relates to the physical Earth.
questions: What is the practical difference between a datum and a reference frame?

revisions.title: North American Datum 1983
revisions.content: NAD 83 is a modern geodetic datum used extensively for positioning and mapping in North America.

snapshot.title: North American Datum 1983
snapshot.mainIdea: NAD 83 is a modern geodetic datum used extensively for positioning and mapping in North America.
snapshot.body: NAD 83 replaced NAD 27 and is based on an Earth-centered approach associated with the GRS 80 ellipsoid. It has undergone multiple realizations as positioning technology and geodetic measurements improved.
questions: How do different NAD83 realizations affect high-accuracy coordinates?

revisions.title: Datum Transformations
revisions.content: Datum transformations convert coordinates between different geodetic reference systems.

snapshot.title: Datum Transformations
snapshot.mainIdea: Datum transformations convert coordinates between different geodetic reference systems.
snapshot.body: Coordinates representing the same physical location may have different numeric values in different datums. A datum transformation applies mathematical parameters or models to convert coordinates while preserving the intended physical location.
questions: When is a simple transformation insufficient for high-accuracy GIS work?

revisions.title: Dynamic Reference Frames
revisions.content: Dynamic reference frames account for the fact that positions on the Earth's surface change through time.

snapshot.title: Dynamic Reference Frames
snapshot.mainIdea: Dynamic reference frames account for the fact that positions on the Earth's surface change through time.
snapshot.body: Tectonic motion and other geophysical processes cause coordinates to change. Dynamic reference frames incorporate time, velocity, or an epoch so that coordinates can describe both location and when that location applies.
questions: How should GIS systems store coordinate epoch information?

revisions.title: Building a Coordinate System
revisions.content: A usable coordinate system requires a defined origin, orientation, scale, reference surface, and method for realizing those definitions physically.

snapshot.title: Building a Coordinate System
snapshot.mainIdea: A usable coordinate system requires a defined origin, orientation, scale, reference surface, and method for realizing those definitions physically.
snapshot.body: Constructing a coordinate system involves more than selecting coordinate units. The system must define how positions relate mathematically and physically to the Earth so that independent measurements can reproduce consistent coordinates.

snapshot.title: GRS 80
snapshot.mainIdea: GRS 80 defines an ellipsoid and related parameters used in modern geodetic reference systems.
snapshot.body: The Geodetic Reference System 1980 provides geometric and physical constants used in geodesy. Its ellipsoid forms the geometric basis of NAD 83 and other modern positioning work.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: How does GRS 80 differ from WGS 84 in practical GIS use?

revisions.title: Modeling the Shape of the Earth
revisions.content: Geospatial coordinate systems require mathematical approximations of the Earth's irregular physical shape.

snapshot.title: Modeling the Shape of the Earth
snapshot.mainIdea: Geospatial coordinate systems require mathematical approximations of the Earth's irregular physical shape.
snapshot.body: The physical Earth is too irregular to serve directly as a mathematical reference surface. Geodesy therefore uses simplified models such as spheres and ellipsoids for coordinate calculations while other surfaces such as the geoid describe gravity-related characteristics.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: Why is an ellipsoid preferred over a sphere for precise geographic positioning?

revisions.title: Standard Lines
revisions.content: Standard lines provide east-west correction lines within the PLSS survey framework.

snapshot.title: Standard Lines
snapshot.mainIdea: Standard lines provide east-west correction lines within the PLSS survey framework.
snapshot.body: Standard parallels or correction lines are introduced periodically to control the effects of meridian convergence and maintain manageable township dimensions across large survey regions.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: Coordinate System Origins
revisions.content: A coordinate-system origin establishes the point or reference from which coordinate values are measured.

snapshot.title: Coordinate System Origins
snapshot.mainIdea: A coordinate-system origin establishes the point or reference from which coordinate values are measured.
snapshot.body: Every coordinate system requires an origin, whether explicitly represented as a physical point, Earth center, intersection of axes, or mathematically defined reference. Changing the origin changes coordinate values even when physical positions remain unchanged.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: Coordinate Axes
revisions.content: Coordinate axes establish the directions along which coordinate values are measured.

snapshot.title: Coordinate Axes
snapshot.mainIdea: Coordinate axes establish the directions along which coordinate values are measured.
snapshot.body: Axes define the orientation and dimensional structure of a coordinate system. Their ordering and positive directions must be known because different systems and software may use different axis conventions.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: Why can axis-order differences cause GIS data to appear in the wrong location?

revisions.title: Scale in Coordinate Systems
revisions.content: Scale defines the relationship between coordinate measurements and corresponding physical distances.

snapshot.title: Scale in Coordinate Systems
snapshot.mainIdea: Scale defines the relationship between coordinate measurements and corresponding physical distances.
snapshot.body: A coordinate system must maintain a defined relationship between its numerical units and the physical space represented. Projection, measurement, and reference-frame effects can introduce differences between coordinate-system scale and ground distance.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: The Rectangular System
revisions.content: The rectangular land-survey system organizes land descriptions using a hierarchy of meridians, baselines, townships, ranges, sections, and subdivisions.

snapshot.title: The Rectangular System
snapshot.mainIdea: The rectangular land-survey system organizes land descriptions using a hierarchy of meridians, baselines, townships, ranges, sections, and subdivisions.
snapshot.body: The Public Land Survey System provides a systematic method for describing and subdividing land in much of the United States. Its structure is based on principal meridians and baselines rather than latitude-longitude coordinates alone.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: How is the rectangular survey system represented in modern GIS parcel data?

revisions.title: Public Land Survey System
revisions.content: The Public Land Survey System is a standardized framework for surveying and describing public lands in much of the United States.

snapshot.title: Public Land Survey System
snapshot.mainIdea: The Public Land Survey System is a standardized framework for surveying and describing public lands in much of the United States.
snapshot.body: PLSS divides land into progressively smaller units using principal meridians, baselines, townships, ranges, sections, and aliquot subdivisions. It is both a surveying framework and a legal land-description system.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: Where in the United States is PLSS not the dominant land-description system?

revisions.title: Subdivision of Public Lands
revisions.content: PLSS land descriptions move from large survey regions to progressively smaller standardized subdivisions.

snapshot.title: Subdivision of Public Lands
snapshot.mainIdea: PLSS land descriptions move from large survey regions to progressively smaller standardized subdivisions.
snapshot.body: The rectangular survey hierarchy proceeds from principal meridians and baselines to townships and ranges, then sections, quarter sections, quarter-quarter sections, aliquot parts, and irregular lots where necessary.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: How can PLSS legal descriptions be converted reliably into GIS geometry?

revisions.title: Vertical Datum Modernization
revisions.content: Modern vertical reference systems increasingly rely on gravity models and GNSS rather than extensive physical leveling networks.

snapshot.title: Vertical Datum Modernization
snapshot.mainIdea: Modern vertical reference systems increasingly rely on gravity models and GNSS rather than extensive physical leveling networks.
snapshot.body: Advances in satellite positioning and gravity measurement allow vertical coordinates to be derived from geodetic observations and geoid models. This reduces dependence on aging physical benchmarks and long leveling traverses.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: How will modernized vertical reference systems change surveying practice?

revisions.title: Standard Parallels
revisions.content: Standard parallels are selected latitudes at which certain projections are designed to maintain true scale.

snapshot.title: Standard Parallels
snapshot.mainIdea: Standard parallels are selected latitudes at which certain projections are designed to maintain true scale.
snapshot.body: Conic projections commonly use one or two standard parallels to control distortion. Scale distortion generally increases as distance from these reference parallels increases.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: Ellipsoidal Height
revisions.content: Ellipsoidal height is the vertical distance from a reference ellipsoid to a point measured along the ellipsoid normal.

snapshot.title: Ellipsoidal Height
snapshot.mainIdea: Ellipsoidal height is the vertical distance from a reference ellipsoid to a point measured along the ellipsoid normal.
snapshot.body: GNSS positioning naturally produces ellipsoidal height. Because the ellipsoid is a mathematical surface rather than a gravity-based approximation of sea level, ellipsoidal height is not equivalent to conventional elevation.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: How can ellipsoidal height be converted into orthometric height?

revisions.title: Map Projection Distortion
revisions.content: Flattening the curved Earth onto a plane necessarily introduces distortion.

snapshot.title: Map Projection Distortion
snapshot.mainIdea: Flattening the curved Earth onto a plane necessarily introduces distortion.
snapshot.body: A projection may distort distance, area, direction, shape, or combinations of these properties. Distortion varies across the projection and can be minimized for selected regions or properties but cannot be eliminated globally.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: How can distortion be evaluated before selecting a projection?

revisions.title: Grid Factor
revisions.content: Grid factor is used to relate ground or ellipsoidal distances to distances represented on a projected coordinate grid.

snapshot.title: Grid Factor
snapshot.mainIdea: Grid factor is used to relate ground or ellipsoidal distances to distances represented on a projected coordinate grid.
snapshot.body: Surveying workflows may combine projection scale with elevation effects to convert between measured ground distances and grid distances. This relationship is essential when high positional accuracy is required.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: How is a combined scale factor derived from elevation and projection scale?

revisions.title: Aliquot Parts
revisions.content: Aliquot parts describe land by repeatedly dividing PLSS sections into equal fractional portions.

snapshot.title: Aliquot Parts
snapshot.mainIdea: Aliquot parts describe land by repeatedly dividing PLSS sections into equal fractional portions.
snapshot.body: Aliquot descriptions use halves and quarters of sections and their subdivisions to specify land parcels. The method creates a hierarchical legal description tied directly to the PLSS framework.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: PLSS Base Lines
revisions.content: A baseline is a primary east-west reference line used with a principal meridian to organize PLSS surveys.

snapshot.title: PLSS Base Lines
snapshot.mainIdea: A baseline is a primary east-west reference line used with a principal meridian to organize PLSS surveys.
snapshot.body: Townships are numbered north or south relative to a baseline while ranges are numbered east or west relative to a principal meridian.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: Lambert Conformal Conic Projection
revisions.content: Lambert Conformal Conic is a conformal projection well suited to regions with greater east-west extent.

snapshot.title: Lambert Conformal Conic Projection
snapshot.mainIdea: Lambert Conformal Conic is a conformal projection well suited to regions with greater east-west extent.
snapshot.body: The projection commonly uses one or two standard parallels and preserves local angles and shapes. It is widely used in State Plane Coordinate System zones whose geographic extent is predominantly east-west.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: Why is Lambert Conformal Conic preferred for many east-west State Plane zones?

revisions.title: Geoid Height
revisions.content: Geoid height expresses the separation between the geoid and the reference ellipsoid.

snapshot.title: Geoid Height
snapshot.mainIdea: Geoid height expresses the separation between the geoid and the reference ellipsoid.
snapshot.body: Because the geoid and ellipsoid are different surfaces, their vertical separation varies geographically. Geoid height is used with ellipsoidal height to derive orthometric height.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: Principal Meridians
revisions.content: A principal meridian is a primary north-south reference line used to organize PLSS surveys.

snapshot.title: Principal Meridians
snapshot.mainIdea: A principal meridian is a primary north-south reference line used to organize PLSS surveys.
snapshot.body: Principal meridians originate at designated initial points and provide the reference from which ranges are numbered east or west within their associated survey regions.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: Geodetic North
revisions.content: Geodetic north follows the direction of a meridian toward the geographic pole on the reference ellipsoid.

snapshot.title: Geodetic North
snapshot.mainIdea: Geodetic north follows the direction of a meridian toward the geographic pole on the reference ellipsoid.
snapshot.body: Geodetic north provides the directional reference for geodetic azimuth. It may differ from grid north because projected coordinate grids do not generally align perfectly with meridians everywhere.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: PLSS Sections
revisions.content: Sections subdivide PLSS townships into nominal one-mile-square units.

snapshot.title: PLSS Sections
snapshot.mainIdea: Sections subdivide PLSS townships into nominal one-mile-square units.
snapshot.body: A standard township is divided into 36 numbered sections. Each section nominally contains 640 acres but actual acreage can vary because of convergence, measurement error, corrections, and irregular boundaries.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: Why do some PLSS sections contain more or less than 640 acres?

revisions.title: Quarter Sections
revisions.content: A quarter section is a nominal 160-acre subdivision of a PLSS section.

snapshot.title: Quarter Sections
snapshot.mainIdea: A quarter section is a nominal 160-acre subdivision of a PLSS section.
snapshot.body: Sections can be divided into northeast, northwest, southeast, and southwest quarters. These aliquot divisions create standardized legal land descriptions without requiring unique coordinate descriptions for every parcel.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: Section Lines
revisions.content: Section lines form the surveyed boundaries separating sections within a PLSS township.

snapshot.title: Section Lines
snapshot.mainIdea: Section lines form the surveyed boundaries separating sections within a PLSS township.
snapshot.body: Section boundaries were established through field surveying and monumentation. Their actual positions may depart from idealized rectangular geometry because original survey evidence governs legal boundaries.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: Why should GIS parcel lines not automatically replace original survey evidence?

revisions.title: Coordinate Transformations
revisions.content: Coordinate transformations mathematically convert positions from one coordinate system or reference frame to another.

snapshot.title: Coordinate Transformations
snapshot.mainIdea: Coordinate transformations mathematically convert positions from one coordinate system or reference frame to another.
snapshot.body: A transformation may account for differences in origin, orientation, scale, datum, projection, or reference-frame realization. Selecting the correct transformation is essential for maintaining positional accuracy.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: How should an appropriate coordinate transformation be selected?

revisions.title: Transverse Mercator Projection
revisions.content: The Transverse Mercator projection is a conformal cylindrical projection oriented to minimize distortion along a selected central meridian.

snapshot.title: Transverse Mercator Projection
snapshot.mainIdea: The Transverse Mercator projection is a conformal cylindrical projection oriented to minimize distortion along a selected central meridian.
snapshot.body: Transverse Mercator is well suited to regions with greater north-south extent. It forms the basis of the UTM system and many State Plane zones.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: How does distortion change with distance from the central meridian?

revisions.title: Geoid Models
revisions.content: Geoid models provide calculated estimates of geoid-ellipsoid separation for converting GNSS heights into gravity-referenced elevations.

snapshot.title: Geoid Models
snapshot.mainIdea: Geoid models provide calculated estimates of geoid-ellipsoid separation for converting GNSS heights into gravity-referenced elevations.
snapshot.body: A geoid model represents the shape of the geoid numerically. GIS and surveying workflows can use these models to convert ellipsoidal heights from GNSS into orthometric heights.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: How does geoid-model accuracy affect derived elevations?

revisions.title: PLSS Initial Points
revisions.content: An initial point establishes the intersection from which a principal meridian and baseline originate within a PLSS survey region.

snapshot.title: PLSS Initial Points
snapshot.mainIdea: An initial point establishes the intersection from which a principal meridian and baseline originate within a PLSS survey region.
snapshot.body: A PLSS survey begins from an initial point that anchors its principal north-south and east-west reference lines. Township and range numbering is related to these foundational lines.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: PLSS Townships
revisions.content: A PLSS township is a nominal six-mile-square survey unit identified by its position north or south of a baseline and east or west of a principal meridian.

snapshot.title: PLSS Townships
snapshot.mainIdea: A PLSS township is a nominal six-mile-square survey unit identified by its position north or south of a baseline and east or west of a principal meridian.
snapshot.body: Townships form a major organizational unit of the rectangular survey system. Each standard township is intended to contain 36 sections, although convergence and surveying adjustments can produce irregularities.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: Quarter-Quarter Sections
revisions.content: Quarter-quarter sections further subdivide quarter sections into nominal 40-acre units.

snapshot.title: Quarter-Quarter Sections
snapshot.mainIdea: Quarter-quarter sections further subdivide quarter sections into nominal 40-acre units.
snapshot.body: A quarter section can itself be divided into four quarters. This repeated subdivision produces common legal descriptions such as the southwest quarter of the northeast quarter of a section.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: The Geoid
revisions.content: The geoid is an equipotential gravity surface used as a reference for physically meaningful heights.

snapshot.title: The Geoid
snapshot.mainIdea: The geoid is an equipotential gravity surface used as a reference for physically meaningful heights.
snapshot.body: The geoid approximates global mean sea level extended beneath the continents. Unlike a smooth ellipsoid, it is irregular because it reflects variations in the Earth's gravity field.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: Why does the geoid depart from the reference ellipsoid?

revisions.title: Gravity and Height
revisions.content: Physically meaningful elevation is connected to the Earth's gravity field rather than geometry alone.

snapshot.title: Gravity and Height
snapshot.mainIdea: Physically meaningful elevation is connected to the Earth's gravity field rather than geometry alone.
snapshot.body: Water flow and the concept of level are governed by gravity. Vertical datums therefore rely on gravity-related surfaces when defining elevations used for engineering, surveying, and physical terrain analysis.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: Grid Azimuth
revisions.content: Grid azimuth expresses direction relative to grid north within a projected coordinate system.

snapshot.title: Grid Azimuth
snapshot.mainIdea: Grid azimuth expresses direction relative to grid north within a projected coordinate system.
snapshot.body: Grid azimuth differs from geodetic azimuth when grid north does not coincide with true or geodetic north. Meridian convergence provides the angular relationship between these directions.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: How is grid azimuth converted to geodetic azimuth?

revisions.title: State Plane Coordinate Systems
revisions.content: State Plane Coordinate Systems provide high-accuracy projected coordinates for defined zones within U.S. states.

snapshot.title: State Plane Coordinate Systems
snapshot.mainIdea: State Plane Coordinate Systems provide high-accuracy projected coordinates for defined zones within U.S. states.
snapshot.body: The State Plane system divides states into zones and selects projections suited to each zone's shape. Lambert Conformal Conic and Transverse Mercator are commonly used to limit distortion over relatively small areas.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: How are State Plane zones selected and assigned projection parameters?

revisions.title: Equipotential Surfaces
revisions.content: An equipotential surface is a surface of constant gravitational potential.

snapshot.title: Equipotential Surfaces
snapshot.mainIdea: An equipotential surface is a surface of constant gravitational potential.
snapshot.body: No work is required to move an object along an ideal equipotential surface against gravity. The geoid is one important equipotential surface used in geodesy to define a physically meaningful vertical reference.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: GNSS-Based Geodetic Control
revisions.content: Continuously operating GNSS stations provide active geodetic control without requiring users to occupy traditional monuments.

snapshot.title: GNSS-Based Geodetic Control
snapshot.mainIdea: Continuously operating GNSS stations provide active geodetic control without requiring users to occupy traditional monuments.
snapshot.body: Modern control networks increasingly rely on continuously observed satellite-positioning stations. Their observations support high-accuracy positioning and provide coordinates tied to current reference frames.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: What advantages does active control provide over passive monument networks?

revisions.title: Plane Coordinate Systems
revisions.content: Plane coordinate systems represent locations using linear x and y measurements on a projected surface.

snapshot.title: Plane Coordinate Systems
snapshot.mainIdea: Plane coordinate systems represent locations using linear x and y measurements on a projected surface.
snapshot.body: Projected coordinate systems transform positions from a curved reference surface onto a plane so that locations can be expressed using linear units such as meters or feet.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: Coordinate-System Errors
revisions.content: Incorrect coordinate-system definitions or transformations can produce substantial positional errors even when the underlying measurements are accurate.

snapshot.title: Coordinate-System Errors
snapshot.mainIdea: Incorrect coordinate-system definitions or transformations can produce substantial positional errors even when the underlying measurements are accurate.
snapshot.body: Common GIS positioning errors occur when data are assigned the wrong coordinate reference system, transformed incorrectly, interpreted with the wrong units, or combined without accounting for different datums.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: What symptoms indicate that a GIS layer has been assigned the wrong coordinate system?

revisions.title: PLSS Ranges
revisions.content: A range identifies the east-west position of a PLSS township relative to a principal meridian.

snapshot.title: PLSS Ranges
snapshot.mainIdea: A range identifies the east-west position of a PLSS township relative to a principal meridian.
snapshot.body: Ranges are numbered east or west of a principal meridian. Combined township and range designations locate a particular six-mile-square survey township within a PLSS region.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: Vertical Datums
revisions.content: A vertical datum establishes the reference from which heights or depths are measured.

snapshot.title: Vertical Datums
snapshot.mainIdea: A vertical datum establishes the reference from which heights or depths are measured.
snapshot.body: Vertical coordinates require a defined reference just as horizontal coordinates do. Vertical datums may be based on leveling networks, tidal observations, gravity models, or modern geodetic reference systems.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: What problems occur when elevation datasets use different vertical datums?

revisions.title: Universal Transverse Mercator
revisions.content: UTM is a global projected coordinate system that divides most of the Earth into narrow longitudinal zones.

snapshot.title: Universal Transverse Mercator
snapshot.mainIdea: UTM is a global projected coordinate system that divides most of the Earth into narrow longitudinal zones.
snapshot.body: Each UTM zone uses a Transverse Mercator projection centered on its own central meridian. The zone structure limits projection distortion while providing coordinates in meters.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: When is UTM preferable to geographic latitude and longitude for analysis?

revisions.title: Heights in GIS
revisions.content: Height values depend on the reference surface from which vertical position is measured.

snapshot.title: Heights in GIS
snapshot.mainIdea: Height values depend on the reference surface from which vertical position is measured.
snapshot.body: GIS can use several forms of height, including ellipsoidal and orthometric heights. These values are not interchangeable because each is measured from a different reference surface.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: Which vertical reference should be used for different GIS applications?

revisions.title: Ground Distance vs Grid Distance
revisions.content: Ground distance and grid distance differ because projected coordinates and physical measurements exist on different reference surfaces.

snapshot.title: Ground Distance vs Grid Distance
snapshot.mainIdea: Ground distance and grid distance differ because projected coordinates and physical measurements exist on different reference surfaces.
snapshot.body: A measured ground distance may need correction for elevation and projection scale before it corresponds to a distance calculated from grid coordinates. High-accuracy surveying therefore distinguishes between the two.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: How are ground distances reduced to grid distances?

revisions.title: Geodetic Distance
revisions.content: Geodetic distance represents distance measured or calculated with respect to the Earth's reference surface.

snapshot.title: Geodetic Distance
snapshot.mainIdea: Geodetic distance represents distance measured or calculated with respect to the Earth's reference surface.
snapshot.body: Distances over the Earth cannot always be treated as simple planar measurements. Geodetic distance calculations account for the geometry of the ellipsoid and differ from projected grid distances or physical ground distances.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: When is planar distance sufficiently accurate for GIS analysis?

revisions.title: Guide Meridians
revisions.content: Guide meridians are correction lines used in the PLSS to compensate for convergence and accumulated survey error.

snapshot.title: Guide Meridians
snapshot.mainIdea: Guide meridians are correction lines used in the PLSS to compensate for convergence and accumulated survey error.
snapshot.body: Because meridians converge toward the poles, a perfectly rectangular grid cannot continue indefinitely across the curved Earth. Guide meridians help reset and control township dimensions within the survey framework.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: Projection Scale Factor
revisions.content: Projection scale factor expresses the relationship between a distance on a projected grid and the corresponding distance on the reference surface.

snapshot.title: Projection Scale Factor
snapshot.mainIdea: Projection scale factor expresses the relationship between a distance on a projected grid and the corresponding distance on the reference surface.
snapshot.body: Scale factor varies with position in most projections. A value of one indicates no local scale distortion while values above or below one indicate enlargement or reduction.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: Survey Corner Monuments
revisions.content: Survey corner monuments physically mark key locations established during land surveys.

snapshot.title: Survey Corner Monuments
snapshot.mainIdea: Survey corner monuments physically mark key locations established during land surveys.
snapshot.body: PLSS boundaries depend on monuments placed or referenced during original surveys. In boundary law and retracement surveying, the location of controlling monuments can carry greater authority than mathematically reconstructed coordinates.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: How are lost or obliterated PLSS corners restored?

revisions.title: Fractional Lots
revisions.content: Fractional lots are irregular PLSS subdivisions used where standard aliquot divisions cannot accommodate survey corrections or geographic boundaries.

snapshot.title: Fractional Lots
snapshot.mainIdea: Fractional lots are irregular PLSS subdivisions used where standard aliquot divisions cannot accommodate survey corrections or geographic boundaries.
snapshot.body: Convergence of meridians, shorelines, prior claims, and other irregularities can prevent complete rectangular subdivisions. Numbered government lots are used to identify these nonstandard areas.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: North American Vertical Datum 1988
revisions.content: NAVD 88 is a major vertical datum used for orthometric heights in the United States.

snapshot.title: North American Vertical Datum 1988
snapshot.mainIdea: NAVD 88 is a major vertical datum used for orthometric heights in the United States.
snapshot.body: NAVD 88 was established through a continent-scale adjustment of leveling observations. It provides a common elevation reference but is being superseded by newer gravity-based approaches.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: Why is NAVD88 being replaced by a geopotential-based vertical reference system?

revisions.title: UTM Zones
revisions.content: UTM divides the Earth into longitudinal zones so each area can use a locally centered Transverse Mercator projection.

snapshot.title: UTM Zones
snapshot.mainIdea: UTM divides the Earth into longitudinal zones so each area can use a locally centered Transverse Mercator projection.
snapshot.body: The standard UTM system uses numbered zones spanning six degrees of longitude. A location's zone determines the central meridian and projected coordinate framework used for its easting and northing.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: What problems arise when a project crosses multiple UTM zones?

revisions.title: Dynamic Height
revisions.content: Dynamic height is a gravity-related vertical coordinate designed to preserve relationships between equipotential surfaces.

snapshot.title: Dynamic Height
snapshot.mainIdea: Dynamic height is a gravity-related vertical coordinate designed to preserve relationships between equipotential surfaces.
snapshot.body: Dynamic heights are useful where physical water-flow relationships matter because they account for variations in gravity rather than treating height solely as geometric distance.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: Foundation of a Coordinate System
revisions.content: A coordinate system provides the mathematical framework needed to describe the position of a point.

snapshot.title: Foundation of a Coordinate System
snapshot.mainIdea: A coordinate system provides the mathematical framework needed to describe the position of a point.
snapshot.body: Coordinates acquire meaning from the reference system in which they are expressed. A coordinate system establishes the reference surface, origin, axes, orientation, units, and conventions required to describe positions consistently.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

questions: What elements must be defined before coordinate values can be interpreted correctly?

revisions.title: Coordinate System Rotation
revisions.content: Rotation describes an angular difference in orientation between coordinate systems.

snapshot.title: Coordinate System Rotation
snapshot.mainIdea: Rotation describes an angular difference in orientation between coordinate systems.
snapshot.body: When two coordinate frames have differently oriented axes, rotation parameters can be used as part of a transformation between them. Rotation is commonly combined with translation and scale differences.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: Grid Distance
revisions.content: Grid distance is the distance between projected coordinate positions measured on a planar coordinate grid.

snapshot.title: Grid Distance
snapshot.mainIdea: Grid distance is the distance between projected coordinate positions measured on a planar coordinate grid.
snapshot.body: Grid distance is calculated from projected coordinates and can differ from ground or ellipsoidal distance because of projection scale and elevation effects.

sourceIds.title: Basic GIS Coordinates

revisions.title: Grid North
revisions.content: Grid north is the direction of increasing northing along the vertical grid lines of a projected coordinate system.

snapshot.title: Grid North
snapshot.mainIdea: Grid north is the direction of increasing northing along the vertical grid lines of a projected coordinate system.
snapshot.body: Grid north is a property of the projection and is not necessarily identical to geodetic north except along particular lines such as a central meridian in some projections.
