questionAnswers.question: How do current FDA Food Code temperature danger-zone limits differ from older culinary textbook standards?
questionAnswers.answer:
Under the current FDA Food Code, Time/Temperature Control for Safety (TCS) food should normally be held at 41°F (5°C) or below for cold holding and at 135°F (57°C) or above for hot holding. Consequently, FDA describes the temperature “Danger Zone” for TCS food as 41°F to 135°F (5°C to 57°C). The 2022 Food Code is still the FDA's most recent complete edition, and the 2024 Supplement did not change these holding-temperature limits.

This differs from the traditional 40°F–140°F (4°C–60°C) danger zone commonly found in older culinary training materials and consumer food-safety guidance. Importantly, 40°F–140°F is not simply an erroneous or obsolete range. USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service continues to use 40°F–140°F as its consumer “Danger Zone,” recommending cold foods at 40°F or below and hot foods at 140°F or above.

StandardCold limitDanger zoneHot limitCurrent FDA Food Code — retail/foodservice≤ 41°F / 5°C41°F–135°F / 5°C–57°C≥ 135°F / 57°CTraditional culinary / current USDA consumer guidance≤ 40°F / 4.4°C40°F–140°F / 4.4°C–60°C≥ 140°F / 60°C

The change on the hot-holding side is well documented historically. FDA reports that the 1997 Food Code required hot holding at 140°F, but the temperature was lowered to 135°F in the 2003 Supplement to the 2001 Food Code. FDA based the change on scientific assessment of organisms such as Clostridium perfringens and Bacillus cereus. FDA concluded that holding food at 135°F or higher provides sufficient control against pathogen growth.

The cold-holding history is different. FDA's 1976 Food Service Sanitation Manual recommended 45°F for cold holding. The 1993 Food Code lowered that temperature to 41°F, although FDA allowed a phase-in period because existing commercial refrigeration equipment often could not reliably maintain 41°F. Eventually, the option to use 45°F was deleted from the Food Code, and 41°F became the standard cold-holding limit. One reason was greater concern about the survival and growth of Listeria monocytogenes in refrigerated ready-to-eat foods.

FDA provides quantitative evidence for the importance of refrigeration temperature in its Food Code annex. Its cited Listeria monocytogenes risk assessment estimated substantially fewer listeriosis cases under a modeled 41°F maximum refrigeration temperature than under a 45°F maximum. FDA therefore continues to recommend 41°F as the maximum cold-holding temperature for TCS foods.

There is also a related change in how commercial kitchens are expected to think about the danger zone. The current Food Code does not merely say “avoid 41°F–135°F”; it provides specific time-temperature controls. Cooked TCS food must cool:

135°F → 70°F within 2 hours, and
135°F → 41°F or below within a total of 6 hours.

Connection to culinary textbooks

Wayne Gisslen's Professional Cooking, 8th edition, already reflects the newer foodservice standard. It describes 41°F–135°F as the Food Danger Zone and notes that the 40°F–140°F range had previously been used in the United States.

That distinction is useful for your answer because it shows why different numbers can appear in culinary sources:

40°F–140°F is still a valid USDA consumer-safety guideline, whereas 41°F–135°F is the current FDA Food Code model standard used for retail and professional foodservice.

So I would not write that “40–140 is wrong.” A more accurate conclusion is:

The standards serve different regulatory and educational contexts. For professional U.S. foodservice, the FDA Food Code uses 41°F–135°F. The traditional 40°F–140°F range remains in USDA consumer guidance, which helps explain why it continues to appear in culinary literature and general food-safety education.

References you can cite

U.S. Food and Drug Administration. (2023). Food Code 2022. Section 3-501.16, Time/Temperature Control for Safety Food, Hot and Cold Holding. U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.

U.S. Food and Drug Administration. (2024). Cooling Cooked Time/Temperature Control for Safety Foods and the FDA Food Code: For Food Employees. FDA identifies the danger zone as 41°F–135°F and specifies the two-stage cooling process.

U.S. Food and Drug Administration. (2009). Report on the Occurrence of Foodborne Illness Risk Factors in Selected Institutional Foodservice, Restaurant, and Retail Food Store Facility Types. FDA documents the change in hot holding from 140°F to 135°F in the Supplement to the 2001 Food Code.

U.S. Department of Agriculture, Food Safety and Inspection Service. (2024). What is the Danger Zone? USDA identifies 40°F–140°F as the danger zone for consumer food safety.

Gisslen, W. (2014). Professional Cooking (8th ed.). Wiley. Chapter 2, Sanitation and Safety. The text identifies 41°F–135°F as the U.S. food danger zone while discussing the older 40°F–140°F standard.

For your Zettelkasten/research answer, I would preserve that FDA-versus-USDA distinction rather than entering simply “old = 40–140; new = 41–135.” The historical evidence shows that the actual regulatory development was more nuanced.

revisions.title: Slavery and Capitalism: A New Marxist History
revisions.content:
The first systematic Marxist account of the capitalist character of Atlantic slavery.

Karl Marx’s writings on enslavement and labor have fallen out of favor among historians, but David McNally injects new life into them. Slavery and Capitalism gives the first systematic Marxist account of the capitalist character of Atlantic slavery—using colonial travel literature, planter records and diaries, and slave narratives—to support the provocative claim for enslaved labor in the plantation system as capitalist commodity production.

Weaving together history, political economy, and radical abolitionism, McNally demonstrates that plantation slaves formed a modern working class. Unlike those scholars who insist that enslaved people were too sensible to set their sights on liberty, he highlights the self-activity of enslaved people fighting for their freedom and reframes their resistance as labor struggles over production and reproduction, with significant implications for US and Atlantic history and for understanding the roots of racial capitalism.

revisions.content: Hypercritical describes a person, judgment, or attitude that is excessively or severely critical.

snapshot.body:
Hypercritical is an adjective describing criticism that goes beyond ordinary evaluation and becomes excessive, severe, or overly fault-finding.

Dictionary Source:
The Free Dictionary

American Heritage definition:
"Excessively critical; captious."

The page also includes definitions describing hypercritical as excessively or severely critical and as being inclined to judge too severely.

This definition is useful for distinguishing ordinary criticism from a pattern of criticism that is excessive or disproportionately severe.

snapshot.body:
Source:
The Psychological Safety Playbook

Author:
Karolin Helbig

Page:
8

Exact Quote:
“It takes courage to not have all the answers, to ask for help, to invite dissent, and to laugh at yourself.”

Research Note:
This passage expands what courage means within psychological safety. Courage can involve giving up the expectation that I must always know the answer or appear completely certain.

Asking for help requires admitting that I need something from another person.

Inviting dissent requires being willing to hear disagreement rather than surrounding myself only with agreement.

Laughing at myself requires letting go of some of the pressure to appear perfect or always be right.

These behaviors can support psychological safety because they make room for vulnerability, participation, disagreement, learning, and imperfection.

Connection to Courageous Communication:
Courageous communication is not only about speaking difficult truths. It also involves creating room for other people to contribute, challenge ideas, offer help, and participate honestly.

researchedQuestions: How does asking for help contribute to psychological safety?

questionAnswers.question: How does asking for help contribute to psychological safety?
questionAnswers.answer:
Asking for help contributes to psychological safety because it requires a person to admit that they do not know something, cannot do something alone, or need support from another person. That creates interpersonal vulnerability. When a person can ask for help without being mocked, embarrassed, punished, or treated as incompetent, the response communicates that uncertainty and dependence are acceptable within that environment.

In The Psychological Safety Playbook, Karolin Helbig connects courage with asking for help, writing on page 8: “It takes courage to not have all the answers, to ask for help, to invite dissent, and to laugh at yourself.” This suggests that asking for help is not simply obtaining assistance; it involves being willing to reveal that I do not have every answer.

Amy Edmondson similarly describes asking for help as a learning behavior that involves interpersonal risk. Harvard Business School reports her explanation that saying “I need help. I’m not sure what to do here” is a learning behavior because it can feel embarrassing or risky. When people are able to take that risk, teams are better able to learn, identify mistakes, share knowledge, and solve problems.

The response to the request for help is also important. Edmondson explains that when someone asks for help and receives a kind and constructive response, psychological safety is preserved. When the response is ridicule, harsh criticism, exasperation, or another negative reaction, the person may become less willing to speak up or ask for help again.

Research also shows a relationship between respectful workplace interactions and help-seeking. Friedman, Carmeli, and Dutton found that respectful engagement with supervisors encouraged help-seeking behavior, and that help-seeking was associated with improved job performance.

This means asking for help and psychological safety can reinforce one another. Psychological safety makes it easier for a person to risk asking for help, while a supportive response to that request provides evidence that vulnerability is acceptable. Repeated experiences of asking for help and being treated respectfully can strengthen the expectation that it is safe to admit uncertainty, seek assistance, learn, and participate honestly.

References

Helbig, Karolin. The Psychological Safety Playbook: Lead More Powerfully by Being More Human. Page 8.

Harvard Business School Working Knowledge. Four Steps to Building the Psychological Safety That High-Performing Teams Need.
Harvard Business School source

Harvard Business School Working Knowledge. New Hires Lose Psychological Safety After Year One. How to Fix It.
Harvard Business School source

Friedman, Anat, Abraham Carmeli, and Jane E. Dutton. “When does respectful engagement with one's supervisor foster help-seeking behaviors and performance?” Journal of Vocational Behavior, Vol. 104, 2018, pp. 184–198.
Journal article

questionAnswers.question: Why is inviting dissent important for psychological safety?
questionAnswers.answer:
Inviting dissent is important for psychological safety because disagreement is one of the interpersonal risks people often avoid when they fear embarrassment, rejection, punishment, or being viewed as difficult. When people are explicitly invited to disagree, question a decision, identify a problem, or offer another point of view, they receive a signal that speaking honestly is acceptable rather than dangerous.

Karolin Helbig connects dissent with courageous communication in The Psychological Safety Playbook. On page 8 she writes, “It takes courage to not have all the answers, to ask for help, to invite dissent, and to laugh at yourself.” Inviting dissent therefore involves more than allowing disagreement after it happens. It means deliberately creating space for another person to challenge an idea or decision.

Amy Edmondson explains that people commonly hold back because they fear the interpersonal consequences of disagreeing, particularly with someone who has more authority. She notes that people may avoid criticizing the status quo because they do not want to be seen as negative. When important concerns are withheld, teams lose opportunities for learning and improvement. Psychological safety helps reduce this interpersonal fear so that concerns, questions, mistakes, and opposing views can be discussed.

Inviting dissent also communicates that another person's perspective has value. Edmondson recommends that leaders actively ask for input rather than simply claiming that people are free to speak. Questions such as “What are we missing?” encourage people to contribute information that a leader or group may not already have. She specifically warns against reacting angrily when someone brings a dissenting view or bad news because a negative response can teach people that speaking honestly is unsafe.

Research on psychological safety supports this connection between safety and voice. Edmondson and Lei's review of the research describes psychological safety as people's perception of the consequences of interpersonal risk and identifies it as an important factor in voice, teamwork, team learning, and organizational learning. This matters because dissent is a form of voice: a person is choosing to reveal a concern or different perspective even though doing so may carry social risk.

Inviting dissent does not mean that every disagreement must be accepted as correct or that the final decision must change. Its importance for psychological safety is that disagreement can be expressed, considered, and responded to respectfully. When people learn that they can disagree without humiliation or retaliation, they are more likely to reveal concerns, challenge assumptions, identify errors, and contribute information that might otherwise remain unspoken. In this way, inviting dissent both depends on psychological safety and helps reinforce it.

References

Helbig, Karolin. The Psychological Safety Playbook: Lead More Powerfully by Being More Human. Page 8.

Edmondson, Amy C., and Zhike Lei. “Psychological Safety: The History, Renaissance, and Future of an Interpersonal Construct.” Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior, Vol. 1, 2014, pp. 23–43. Annual Reviews article

revisions.title: A Hurtful Comment About My Weight and Its Effect on My Self-Esteem
revisions.content: A comment a Taxi driver made about being able to feel my weight while he was driving made me feel insecure, mocked, insulted, and hurt, and it further lowered my self-esteem. The memory remains significant because the comment affected not only how I felt about my body but also how I felt about myself as a person.

revisions.title: Being Asked to Step Down From Praise Ministry and Losing a Place of Safety and Belonging
revisions.content: Being asked by my pastor to step down from leading the praise ministry because I was in a homosexual relationship with Gus affected more than my ministry role. At that time, the praise ministry was one of the only things I had left that gave me a sense of safety, belonging, connection, purpose, and stability. Being asked to step down therefore felt like losing both a role and one of the places where I felt that I belonged.

snapshot.title: Being Asked to Step Down From Praise Ministry and Losing a Place of Safety and Belonging
snapshot.mainIdea: Being asked by my pastor to step down from leading the praise ministry because I was in a homosexual relationship with Gus affected more than my ministry role. At that time, the praise ministry was one of the only things I had left that gave me a sense of safety, belonging, connection, purpose, and stability. Being asked to step down therefore felt like losing both a role and one of the places where I felt that I belonged.
snapshot.body:
I remember being asked by my pastor to step down from leading the praise ministry because I was in a homosexual relationship with Gus.

At that time, leading the praise ministry felt like the only thing I had left to hold on to. The ministry had become a place where I felt safe, connected, useful, and that I belonged.

Being asked to step down therefore meant more to me than losing a leadership position. I experienced it as losing something that had become connected to my sense of safety, belonging, purpose, connection, and stability.

An important part of this memory is the reason I was asked to step down. I was in a homosexual relationship with Gus. The same church and ministry environment where I had experienced safety and belonging became the environment where I experienced rejection because of that relationship.

This creates a tension in the memory between belonging and rejection. I had experienced the ministry as a place where I belonged, yet I was then told that I could no longer continue leading because of a relationship that was part of my life.

The experience raises questions for me about what belonging actually means. If belonging depends on meeting particular expectations or conditions, then that belonging may feel secure only while those conditions are being met.

It also connects to my larger exploration of safety. A place, community, relationship, or role can become psychologically important because it represents stability, acceptance, identity, and connection. When that place of belonging is lost, the loss can affect a person's sense of safety as well.

There is also a connection to human dignity. Regardless of whether people agree about sexuality, doctrine, or church leadership requirements, the way a person is treated during disagreement, correction, exclusion, or removal can affect that person's sense of dignity, worth, safety, and belonging.

Romans 1:26–27 is a Scripture passage I want to research separately in the King James Version with Apocrypha because of its relevance to biblical discussions of same-sex sexual relations. I do not want to assume that this specific passage was the pastor's stated biblical basis unless I can establish that. The historical memory remains that I was asked to step down because I was in a homosexual relationship with Gus.

questionAnswers.question: What is the relationship between belonging and psychological safety?
questionAnswers.answer:
Belonging and psychological safety are closely related because both involve whether a person feels accepted and able to participate without fear of rejection, embarrassment, humiliation, or punishment. Belonging concerns whether a person feels that they are accepted, connected, and that they have a legitimate place within a group or relationship. Psychological safety concerns whether that person believes it is safe to take interpersonal risks, such as speaking honestly, asking questions, admitting mistakes, requesting help, disagreeing, or showing vulnerability.

Amy Edmondson explains psychological safety as an environment in which candor and vulnerability are welcome and people do not expect to be punished or humiliated for speaking up. She also connects psychological safety with inclusion, explaining that a genuinely inclusive environment must be psychologically safe for everyone, including people from historically marginalized or underrepresented groups.

Data from the American Psychological Association show a strong relationship between psychological safety and belonging. In the APA's 2024 Work in America survey, 95% of workers experiencing higher psychological safety said they felt that they belonged at work, compared with 69% of workers experiencing lower psychological safety. Workers with higher psychological safety were also more likely to report that they could be themselves at work: 95% compared with 75% among those experiencing lower psychological safety. These results show an association between psychological safety, belonging, and the ability to be authentic, although the survey does not by itself establish that one directly causes the other.

Belonging may also contribute to psychological safety. A 2025 study involving 377 participants found that belongingness significantly predicted psychological safety (B = 0.26, p < .01). The researchers also found a significant pathway in which ethical leadership was associated with belongingness, belongingness was associated with psychological safety, and psychological safety was then associated with creativity. This provides evidence that feeling connected and accepted within a group may help create conditions in which people feel safer taking interpersonal risks.

The relationship can therefore work in both directions. When I feel that I belong, I may be less concerned that a mistake, disagreement, request for help, or expression of vulnerability will cause me to lose acceptance or connection. That can make interpersonal risk feel safer. At the same time, when an environment repeatedly shows me that I can speak honestly, ask questions, make mistakes, disagree, and still be treated with respect, those experiences can strengthen my sense that I am accepted and that I belong.

The opposite can also occur. If belonging feels conditional—if acceptance depends on remaining silent, hiding parts of myself, agreeing with others, or avoiding mistakes—I may technically be part of a group while still not feeling psychologically safe. Psychological safety therefore adds an important dimension to belonging: it is not only whether I am included, but whether I can participate as myself without constantly fearing that honesty, vulnerability, disagreement, or mistakes will threaten my place in the group.

For my Safety research, this distinction is important because belonging can provide connection and acceptance, while psychological safety concerns whether that connection remains secure when I become vulnerable. A place can give me a strong sense of belonging, but if I believe that revealing something about myself, disagreeing, making a mistake, or failing to meet certain expectations could result in rejection, then my sense of psychological safety may still be fragile.

References

American Psychological Association. “A Sense of Belonging Is Crucial for Employees. How Employers Can Foster Connection and Social Support.” Updated June 26, 2024. APA article on belonging and psychological safety

American Psychological Association. “2024 Work in America Survey: Psychological Safety in the Changing Workplace.” 2024. APA 2024 Work in America report

Harvard Business School. “Leading in Tough Times: HBS Faculty Member Amy C. Edmondson on Psychological Safety.” November 22, 2022. Harvard Business School source

Harvard Business School. “Fostering Candor in Teams and Organizations.” Harvard Business School source on psychological safety and inclusion

Frontiers in Psychology. “Belonging through values: ethical leadership, creativity, and psychological safety with ethical climate as a moderator.” 2025. Peer-reviewed Frontiers article

revisions.content: Research how personal and interpersonal boundaries may contribute to a person's sense of security within relationships and environments.

snapshot.title: Boundaries and Personal Safety
snapshot.mainIdea: Research how personal and interpersonal boundaries may contribute to a person's sense of security within relationships and environments.
snapshot.body:
Research Focus

This Zettel examines boundaries as they relate to personal safety.

Areas to research:
- Personal boundaries
- Emotional boundaries
- Physical boundaries
- Interpersonal boundaries
- Privacy
- Consent
- Respect for limits
- Boundary violations
- Communication of boundaries

The research should examine whether boundaries themselves create safety or whether safety depends on other people respecting those boundaries.

Personal Connection

Consider what boundaries mean within my own understanding of safety.

What happens to my sense of safety when I can establish a limit?

What happens when that limit is ignored?

This research can later be compared with research on trust, autonomy, family, and friendship.

revisions.content: Safety is not only the absence of danger; it can also be understood personally through the people, relationships, environments, and conditions that create or fail to create a sense of security.

snapshot.title: Safety
snapshot.mainIdea: Safety is not only the absence of danger; it can also be understood personally through the people, relationships, environments, and conditions that create or fail to create a sense of security.
snapshot.body:
This writing begins with a set of personal questions about safety:

  • What does safety mean to me?

  • How do I view safety?

  • What is safety for others?

  • Does family make you safe?

  • Do friends represent safety?

    The questions came from psychology work in therapy, but the purpose here is personal writing rather than clinical analysis.

    The central focus is what safety means personally and how that meaning may differ from common assumptions about safety. Family and friendship are part of that examination because those relationships are often associated with protection, trust, belonging, and security, but they do not automatically create safety for everyone.

    The writing can explore the difference between being physically safe and feeling safe, as well as the role of trust, familiarity, control, vulnerability, boundaries, and relationships in shaping a personal sense of safety.

    It can also examine whether safety comes from other people, from environment, from internal stability, from predictability, or from some combination of these.

    Research Directions

    1. Physical Safety vs. Perceived Safety

    Research the distinction between being objectively protected from danger and subjectively feeling secure.

    Questions to explore:
    - What is the difference between being safe and feeling safe?
    - Can a person be physically safe while not feeling safe?
    - Can a person feel safe while actually being in an unsafe situation?
    - What creates a subjective sense of safety?

    Possible research Zettel:
    Physical Safety vs. Perceived Safety

    2. Trust and Safety

    Research how trust affects a person's ability to experience security in relationships and environments.

    Questions to explore:
    - What role does trust play in feeling safe?
    - Can safety exist without trust?
    - How is trust established?
    - What happens to a sense of safety when trust is damaged?

    Possible research Zettel:
    Trust and the Sense of Safety

    3. Predictability and Safety

    Research whether knowing what to expect contributes to feeling secure.

    Questions to explore:
    - What role does predictability play in feeling safe?
    - Does uncertainty reduce a person's sense of safety?
    - Can familiar routines create security?
    - Is familiarity the same thing as safety?

    Possible research Zettel:
    Predictability and Psychological Safety

    4. Control, Choice, and Autonomy

    Research the relationship between having control over one's circumstances and feeling safe.

    Questions to explore:
    - What role does control play in safety?
    - Does having choices increase a sense of security?
    - How does autonomy affect safety?
    - Can a person feel safe when they have little control over their environment?

    Possible research Zettel:
    Control, Autonomy, and Safety

    5. Boundaries and Safety

    Research how personal, emotional, and interpersonal boundaries contribute to security.

    Questions to explore:
    - How do boundaries affect a person's sense of safety?
    - Can boundaries create emotional security?
    - What happens when boundaries are ignored or violated?
    - How are trust and boundaries connected?

    Possible research Zettel:
    Boundaries and Personal Safety

    6. Vulnerability and Safety

    Research the relationship between vulnerability, trust, exposure, and security.

    Questions to explore:
    - How does vulnerability relate to safety?
    - What conditions make vulnerability feel safe?
    - Can a person be vulnerable without trusting another person?
    - Does feeling safe make vulnerability possible?

    Possible research Zettel:
    Vulnerability and Safety

    7. Family and Safety

    Examine the assumption that family naturally represents protection, belonging, trust, and security.

    Questions to explore:
    - Does family make you safe?
    - Does family inherently provide safety?
    - Why is family commonly associated with safety?
    - Can family provide familiarity without providing safety?
    - What makes a family relationship feel safe?
    - What causes a family relationship to feel unsafe?

    Possible research Zettel:
    Family as a Source of Safety

    8. Friendship and Safety

    Examine friendship as a possible source of trust, belonging, emotional security, and protection.

    Questions to explore:
    - Do friends represent safety?
    - Do friendships inherently provide safety?
    - What makes a friendship feel safe?
    - What role does trust play in safe friendships?
    - What role do boundaries play in friendship?
    - Can someone be a friend without being a source of safety?

    Possible research Zettel:
    Friendship, Trust, and Safety

    9. Environment and Safety

    Research how physical surroundings and social environments influence a person's sense of security.

    Questions to explore:
    - How does environment influence perceived safety?
    - What characteristics make an environment feel safe?
    - Does familiarity with a place create safety?
    - How do privacy, stability, predictability, and control affect environmental safety?

    Possible research Zettel:
    Environment and the Sense of Safety

    10. Internal and External Safety

    Examine whether safety comes primarily from external circumstances, internal stability, relationships, or a combination of these.

    Questions to explore:
    - Can safety come from within a person?
    - Does safety depend on external conditions?
    - What is internal safety?
    - Can someone develop a sense of internal stability when the external environment is uncertain?
    - How do internal and external sources of safety interact?

    Possible research Zettel:
    Internal and External Sources of Safety

    Research Process

    Begin with personal reflection before researching outside material.

    For each research direction:

    1. Write what I currently think or believe.
    2. Identify the specific question I want to investigate.
    3. Find credible sources addressing that question.
    4. Create a separate research Zettel for the concept or finding.
    5. Link the research back to this Safety Zettel.
    6. Compare the research with my original understanding.
    7. Record where the research supports, challenges, complicates, or changes my thinking.
    8. Return to the personal writing and consider what the research means to me.

    The purpose of the research is not to replace the personal reflection with psychological or academic explanations. The research should provide language, concepts, evidence, and contrasting perspectives that help deepen the original question: What does safety mean to me?

    Planned Research Zettels

    - Physical Safety vs. Perceived Safety
    - Trust and the Sense of Safety
    - Predictability and Psychological Safety
    - Control, Autonomy, and Safety
    - Boundaries and Personal Safety
    - Vulnerability and Safety
    - Family as a Source of Safety
    - Friendship, Trust, and Safety
    - Environment and the Sense of Safety
    - Internal and External Sources of Safety

questionAnswers.question: How do boundaries affect a person's sense of safety?
questionAnswers.answer:
Boundaries can affect a person’s sense of safety because they help establish what is acceptable, what is not acceptable, and what a person can expect from other people. Boundaries may involve physical space, privacy, communication, emotional demands, time, personal information, touch, sexual contact, responsibilities, and other areas in which a person needs some control over what happens to them.

Clear boundaries can contribute to safety by creating predictability. When people know what the limits of a relationship or environment are, they have more information about what to expect and how others are likely to behave. Research examining autonomy and safety in mental health care found that clear agreements, rules, and limitations could provide structure and predictability and foster a sense of safety. The study also found an important qualification: boundaries were more likely to feel safe when they were communicated warmly and established collaboratively. Rigidly imposed limits could instead be experienced as a loss of autonomy. (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13219197/)

Boundaries are also connected to autonomy—the ability to have some control over oneself, one’s body, choices, privacy, and participation in relationships. Respecting another person’s boundaries communicates that their preferences and limits matter. When those boundaries are repeatedly ignored, crossed, or controlled by someone else, the person may experience uncertainty about whether their wishes will be respected. Research on close relationships describes intrusive behavior as a potential threat to autonomy and notes that people may respond by distancing themselves in an effort to restore personal boundaries and autonomy. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0191886909004991)

The American Psychological Association discusses boundaries in psychotherapy as a way of protecting both the therapeutic relationship and the people involved in it. Clear boundaries can help people understand what kind of relationship they are in, what support is available, what its limits are, and what they can reasonably expect. APA also notes that appropriate boundaries can help people develop healthier relationships and greater independence. (https://www.apa.org/topics/psychotherapy/better-boundaries-clinical-practice)

Research involving people’s experiences in psychotherapy has similarly found that unclear boundaries can create uncertainty and threaten a person’s sense of safety. Participants in one qualitative study described unclear or poorly explained boundaries as contributing to feelings of being ignored, manipulated, invalidated, or disrespected. The researchers emphasized that how a boundary is communicated matters, not simply the existence of the boundary itself. (https://doi.org/10.25215/1101.028)

Boundary violations can also be relevant to safety in personal relationships. A qualitative study of young people exposed to family violence found that participants sometimes allowed others to overstep their personal boundaries, which was associated in their accounts with stress and negative feelings about themselves. Participants also described mistrust, controlling behavior, and difficulty balancing closeness with autonomy. (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11199443/)

There is also evidence connecting the ability to establish boundaries with harmful relationship experiences. Research examining adolescents’ knowledge of their rights, beliefs about relationships, boundary-setting, and dating violence found that the ability to set personal boundaries was an important part of the relationship between these factors and dating-violence victimization. This does not mean that failure to set a boundary makes someone responsible for another person’s harmful behavior. Rather, the research treats boundaries as one aspect of understanding rights, autonomy, and relationship functioning. (https://doi.org/10.19090/pp.v19i1.2654)

For my Safety research, boundaries therefore seem important because they help answer questions such as: Do I have control over what happens to me? Can I say no? Will my no be respected? Can I decide what I disclose and when? Can I ask for space without losing the relationship? Do I know what another person expects from me? Can I express discomfort without being punished, mocked, pressured, or rejected?

A boundary can contribute to safety when it creates clarity, predictability, autonomy, and respect. The response to the boundary may be just as important as setting it. If I communicate a limit and another person respects it, that experience can provide evidence that my autonomy matters and that the relationship can tolerate my needs. If my boundaries are repeatedly ignored, challenged, mocked, or punished, I may instead learn that expressing my needs carries interpersonal risk. In that way, boundaries can influence not only physical safety but also emotional and psychological safety.

References

https://www.apa.org/topics/psychotherapy/better-boundaries-clinical-practice

“Balancing autonomy and safety in care for youth with severe and enduring mental health problems.” PMC.

snapshot.title: Water Activity Measures Water Available to Microorganisms
snapshot.mainIdea: Microbial growth depends on available water rather than simply the total amount of water present in food.
snapshot.body:
Bacteria require water in a usable form to absorb nutrients and grow. Water availability is measured as water activity, abbreviated aw, on a scale from 0 to 1.0.

The chapter states that most pathogens grow best between 0.85 and 1.0 aw.

Dry foods generally do not support bacterial growth well. High concentrations of salt or sugar can also inhibit bacterial growth because they reduce bacteria's ability to use the moisture present in food.

Water activity therefore provides a more useful microbial-safety concept than simply describing a food as containing moisture.

questionAnswers.question: How do salt and sugar concentrations alter water activity?
questionAnswers.answer:
Salt and sugar concentrations alter water activity by reducing the amount of water that is freely available for microorganisms to use. Water activity (aw) is different from total moisture content: a food can contain water, but some of that water may be bound to dissolved substances and therefore less available to support microbial growth.

When salt or sugar is dissolved in water, the dissolved particles interact with water molecules and lower the vapor pressure of the water. As the concentration of salt or sugar increases, the water activity generally decreases. The FDA explains that the greater the concentration of dissolved substances, or solutes, in a given amount of water, the lower the water activity. Salt and sugar are therefore commonly used as preservation agents because they reduce the water available to bacteria, yeasts, and molds.

This means:

Increasing salt concentration → decreases water activity.

Increasing sugar concentration → decreases water activity.

Decreasing water activity → reduces the ability of many microorganisms to grow and reproduce.

The effect occurs partly because high concentrations of salt or sugar create osmotic stress. Water tends to move out of microbial cells when the surrounding food contains a high concentration of dissolved substances. This makes it more difficult for the microorganism to maintain normal cellular functions. Research reviews describe increasing sodium chloride or sucrose concentrations as both lowering water activity and increasing osmotic pressure, producing conditions less favorable for bacterial growth.

The USDA defines water activity as the water that is not tightly bound to the food matrix and is available to support microbial growth. Most potentially hazardous foods have water activity values between approximately 0.85 and 0.99. USDA also notes that water activity is affected by all dissolved substances in the food, not simply sodium chloride, so the actual water activity of a finished food should be measured rather than assumed from salt concentration alone.

The preservation effect can be seen in foods containing large quantities of salt or sugar. Jams and jellies, for example, typically have a water activity around 0.80, while fresh meat and fish are around 0.99. The difference helps explain why high-sugar foods generally support less bacterial growth than highly moist fresh foods, although some yeasts and molds can still grow at substantially lower water activities.

Therefore, salt and sugar do not necessarily remove all of the water from food. Instead, increasing their concentration reduces the availability of that water. The higher the concentration of these dissolved substances, the lower the water activity generally becomes, which can slow or prevent the growth of microorganisms.

References

U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Science and Our Food Supply: Food Safety A to Z Reference Guide. Water Activity (aw).
https://www.fda.gov/media/90663/download

U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Water Activity (aw) in Foods.
https://www.fda.gov/inspections-compliance-enforcement-and-criminal-investigations/inspection-technical-guides/water-activity-aw-foods

USDA Agricultural Research Service. PMP FAQs — Water Activity.
https://www.ars.usda.gov/northeast-area/wyndmoor-pa/eastern-regional-research-center/microbial-and-chemical-food-safety/docs/pathogen-modeling-program/pmp-faqs-water-activity/

USDA Agricultural Research Service. Overview of Predictive Microbiology — Water Activity.
https://apps.ars.usda.gov/node/6166

USDA Agricultural Research Service. Water Activity in Food.
https://pmp.ars.usda.gov/WaterActivity.aspx

Grant, W. D. “Life at Low Water Activity.” Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 2004.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15306380/

questionAnswers.question: What water activity thresholds apply to different pathogens?
questionAnswers.answer:
Water activity thresholds differ among foodborne pathogens because each organism has a different minimum amount of available water required for growth. In general, the lower the water activity (aw), the fewer bacterial pathogens are able to grow. These values are approximate minimum growth limits under otherwise favorable conditions; temperature, pH, salt type, food composition, preservatives, and other factors can change the actual limit. FDA specifically cautions that water activity should not be considered by itself when predicting microbial growth.

Approximate minimum water activity values for important foodborne pathogens are:

Campylobacter spp.: approximately 0.98 aw.

Clostridium botulinum type E: approximately 0.97 aw.

Shigella spp.: approximately 0.97 aw.

Yersinia enterocolitica: approximately 0.97 aw.

Vibrio vulnificus: approximately 0.96 aw.

Pathogenic/enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli: approximately 0.95 aw.

Salmonella spp.: approximately 0.94 aw.

Vibrio parahaemolyticus: approximately 0.94 aw.

Clostridium perfringens: approximately 0.943 aw.

Bacillus cereus: approximately 0.93 aw.

Clostridium botulinum types A and B: approximately 0.93 aw.

Listeria monocytogenes: approximately 0.92 aw.

Staphylococcus aureus: growth can occur at approximately 0.83 aw under favorable conditions. Staphylococcal enterotoxin production requires somewhat more available water; an FDA technical report gives an approximate minimum of 0.88 aw for toxin production.

Staphylococcus aureus is therefore especially important in reduced-water-activity foods because it can grow at lower aw values than most other pathogenic bacteria. The FDA Bad Bug Book reports that S. aureus growth has been demonstrated at aw as low as 0.83 under ideal conditions, although its optimum is much higher, around 0.99.

Listeria monocytogenes is another important example. FDA states that L. monocytogenes does not grow when the water activity of a food is 0.92 or lower. This is why controlling aw can be one of several barriers used to prevent Listeria growth in foods.

Clostridium botulinum requires greater water availability than S. aureus. FDA describes approximately 0.93 aw as the minimum for C. botulinum growth, although the exact value depends on the organism type and characteristics of the food. The 2022 FDA Food Code also states that C. botulinum will not produce toxin below approximately 0.91 aw in the reduced-oxygen-packaging context discussed there.

Salmonella generally requires approximately 0.94 aw for growth. However, preventing growth does not necessarily mean that Salmonella has been killed. FDA notes that bacteria can remain alive or dormant at water activities below their growth minimum. Low-water-activity foods can therefore still contain surviving pathogens even though those organisms cannot multiply in the product.

A commonly used practical dividing point is 0.85 aw. FDA uses 0.85 in several regulatory and food-safety contexts because controlling a finished food to approximately 0.85 aw or below prevents the growth of most bacterial foodborne pathogens. This does not make the food sterile, and some yeasts and molds can grow at water activities below 0.85.

Therefore, water activity thresholds can be understood as microbial growth barriers rather than absolute kill points. For example, a food at 0.94 aw may permit Salmonella growth, while lowering it below approximately 0.94 prevents favorable growth conditions for Salmonella. A food would have to be lowered farther to control Listeria monocytogenes, and farther still to prevent Staphylococcus aureus growth. Because several factors interact, the actual safety of a food should be evaluated using water activity together with pH, temperature, processing conditions, packaging, and other controls.

References

revisions.title: Flowers and Thorns
revisions.content:
Flowers and Thorns is a collection of recent prose and poetry that explores the beauty and the pain that live side by side in the human experience. Through tender reflections and unflinching truths, Praise Mk Nkhoma writes about love and heartbreak, hope and silence, joy and sorrow.

These pieces are drawn from real life, (its thorns and its flowers), and speak to anyone who has ever been wounded, healed, lost, found, or still becoming.

Praise Mk Nkhoma is a Malawian poet whose work is concerned with the ordinary burdens and consolations of being alive. He writes about love, memory, poverty, faith, loss, and the difficult business of becoming oneself, believing that the most enduring subjects are often those encountered in everyday life.

revisions.title: Interview Request From Praise Mk Nkhoma About My Upcoming Book
revisions.content:
Praise Mk Nkhoma asked:

“Can I have an interview with you on your upcoming book, Sir? Okay ... Be yourself for this is to the people out there who have not met your work yet ...”

Interview Questions

  1. For those meeting you for the first time, who are you?

  2. What part of your life do you think made you become the person you are today?

  3. Do you remember the first moment when you realised that writing was more than just something you enjoyed...that it was something you needed? When was that?

  4. What is something life has taught you the hard way, but you’re grateful you learned (as a writer)?

  5. As a writer, you spend so much time observing people. What have people taught you about humanity?

  6. Do you think your writing reveals things about you that you might struggle to say in an ordinary conversation?

  7. What is the one thing you’re still trying to understand about yourself?

  8. Have you ever had to choose between protecting your peace and following your dreams? What did that choice teach you?

  9. What is something you deeply believe about life, love, people, or art that you think you’ll still believe many years from now?

  10. If someone read everything you have ever written, what part of you would you hope they understood that they might otherwise never see?

Additional Note From Praise Mk Nkhoma

“You can tell us about your books and even the ones you're working on (that is if you don't mind) and even share the links and stuff. I'll post on my blog, on my page and my groups too.”

writingDraft.title: Author Interview Questions and Answers
writingDraft.body:
Author Interview Questions and Answers

Darrell Barrow-Pender

Prepared as conversational answers for a poetry and writing interview. The responses are intended to sound natural when spoken while preserving the personal history, creative work, and research that inform them.

1. For those meeting you for the first time, who are you?

I'm Darrell Barrow-Pender. I was born in Barbados and came to the United States in 1975, so my Bajan heritage is part of who I am. I'm a poet and multidisciplinary writer, but I'm also a photographer, musician, chef, technologist, and creator. From the outside, they may look like separate pursuits. To me, they are different ways of understanding and expressing myself and the world around me.

I often explain it this way: if you want to see my worldview, look at my photography; if you want to know my mind, read my words; and if you want to understand how I feel, listen to my music.

My creative work stems from lived experience, introspection, faith, grief, identity, love, observation, and questioning.

2. What part of your life do you think made you become the person you are today?

I don't think a single experience made me who I am. I think it was a combination of experiences that taught me very early to observe, question, adapt, and spend a great deal of time examining things internally.

One experience I am researching now is my handedness. I am naturally left-handed, but as a child I was punished for using my left hand and forced to use my right. I eventually complied to stop the punishment, but I always knew internally that I was left-handed. At the time, I did not understand what was happening. I only understood that something natural to me was considered wrong and that I had to change it.

What I didn't understand until I began researching it was that forced switching isn't simply teaching the other hand to write. Studies of converted left-handers have found lasting changes in how the brain organizes and activates the motor systems involved in handwriting, as well as structural differences associated with forced use of the nondominant hand. In everyday language, the brain is rewired. More precisely, it reorganizes through neuroplasticity. The research helped me understand that my brain was not merely learning a new habit; it had to adapt because my natural handedness was being overridden. [1][2][3]

That discovery has made me look back on my childhood differently. I am not saying that being forced to become right-handed made me a writer. What I am exploring is whether that neurological adaptation, together with the emotional experience of being punished and told that something natural about me was wrong, influenced how I learned to observe, process information, express myself, and communicate.

That question becomes especially important when I consider my writing, photography, music, cooking, and technology. I am highly observant. I notice details. I think in layers. Much of my writing explores identity, silence, suppression, perception, belonging, and finding a voice.

So now I am researching something I lived through without understanding it at the time: what happens when a child is forced to override something as fundamental as natural handedness, and how much of that adaptation persists into adulthood?

3. Do you remember the first moment when you realized writing was more than something you enjoyed - that it was something you needed? When was that?

I think I needed writing before I understood I was a writer.

For a long time, writing was a place to put my feelings. I did not think of it as art, and I did not really consider myself a writer.

That began to change when I was working on my GED through Channel Thirteen. My tutor, Judy Fresco, called to say Channel Thirteen wanted to use my poem "Positive" in a writing curriculum. Later, she submitted it to Symphony Space, where professional actors would read selected work. That was one of the first times I paused and thought, Maybe there really is something in my writing.

But the deeper realization came from understanding why I write. I have described my poetry as coming "from the silence that wanted to speak." Writing gives thoughts and feelings that might otherwise remain inside me a place to go. Writings: The Inner Echoes really grew out of that.

4. What is something life has taught you the hard way, but you are grateful you learned as a writer?

One lesson has been not to let recognition determine the value of my writing.

There were times when publication, awards, or acknowledgment meant a great deal to me because someone finally said my words mattered. But I have also learned that the literary world has its complications. Some opportunities I once viewed as accomplishments became more complicated when I later learned more about the organizations behind them.

That taught me to research publishers, contests, and opportunities carefully and to understand what I am getting involved in.

It also taught me something more personal: recognition can encourage you, but it cannot be the sole reason you believe in your own voice. At some point, you have to recognize the value of your own work.

5. As a writer, you spend so much time observing people. What have people taught you about humanity?

People have taught me that humanity is complex.

We can be extraordinarily compassionate, and we can also be incredibly dismissive of one another. Sometimes a small act - a thank-you, someone listening, or someone acknowledging another person's dignity - can mean far more than we realize.

I have also seen how easily people look past someone because of their circumstances. That bothers me deeply.

One belief that has become increasingly important to me is that every person possesses dignity regardless of circumstances, status, income, health, housing, background, or the type of service they receive.

So much of what it means to be human seems to come back to basic needs: to be seen, to be heard, to belong, to be respected, to be loved, and to know that we matter.

6. Do you think your writing reveals things about you that you might struggle to say in an ordinary conversation?

Absolutely.

Sometimes I do not fully understand something until I write it.

Writing allows me to sit with an emotion or question without having to immediately explain or defend it. I can examine it, turn it over, question it, and sometimes discover that what I thought I was writing about is not what was really underneath it at all.

That is part of why I call much of my work Introspective Poetry. It reflects, listens inwardly, and names what it finds.

There are things in Writings: The Inner Echoes that probably reveal more about me than I would ever sit down and tell someone in conversation. Some of that work gives voice to experiences I had lived through in silence.

So when I say, "If you want to know my mind, read my words," I mean it quite literally.

7. What is the one thing you are still trying to understand about yourself?

I think I am still trying to understand my own sense of worth without measuring it against someone else's recognition of me.

That is something that appears repeatedly throughout my writing.

I have accomplished things and have had teachers, friends, colleagues, readers, and others recognize qualities in me that I sometimes had difficulty recognizing in myself. There were also times when acknowledgment from the person I most wanted it from did not come, and that affected how I measured accomplishment and even how I saw myself.

So I am still learning the difference between being seen by others and seeing myself.

I do not think I have fully answered that question yet. Maybe that is one reason I keep writing.

8. Have you ever had to choose between protecting your peace and following your dreams? What did that choice teach you?

Yes, and sometimes I didn't make the right choice.

One of the hardest examples for me involves music. There was a time when Juilliard was within reach, but I turned away from that opportunity. It was not because I did not love music. I felt inadequate because I had not received the consistent formal training I believed I needed, and I allowed anger, hurt, and the feeling of not measuring up to influence my decision.

Looking back, that taught me something important: protecting yourself and avoiding something because you are afraid of being hurt are not necessarily the same thing.

Sometimes fear can disguise itself as protection.

I have learned to ask myself now: Am I choosing peace, or am I letting fear, hurt, anger, or someone else's voice make the decision for me?

9. What is something you deeply believe about life, love, people, or art that you think you will still believe many years from now?

I deeply believe in human dignity.

I believe every person possesses dignity regardless of their circumstances, status, income, health, housing, background, profession, or ability to do something for someone else.

I think that belief touches everything I do.

It affects how I think about hospitality and food, how I photograph people and the world, and whether the systems we create actually serve people. And it certainly affects my writing.

I also believe art gives us a place to put what ordinary language sometimes cannot convey. A poem, photograph, piece of music, story, or even a meal can say, "I see you. You were here. This mattered."

I do not think I will ever stop believing it.

10. If someone read everything you have ever written, what part of you would you hope they understood that they might otherwise never see?

I would hope they understood how deeply I question things.

I am not simply writing about sadness, love, anger, faith, identity, family, grief, or whatever subject happens to appear on the page. I am usually trying to understand what lies beneath.

My master collection, Writings: The Inner Echoes, includes poems, essays, prayers, reflections, visual pieces, experimental forms, and other writings. The work traverses emotional and spiritual landscapes of memory, identity, faith, desire, love, and the search for meaning.

I have also been developing projects such as Phrases People Hide Behind, Tesseract, Introspective Poetry, the Sequential Alphabet Index, and other writing and poetic frameworks. I also have fiction and other works still in development.

But beneath all those titles and forms, I would want someone who read everything I have written to understand that I was trying to see clearly - myself, other people, the world around me, and the things we sometimes leave unsaid.

Maybe that is the connection among all of my creative work:

Photography is how I see.
Writing is how I think and question.
Music is how I feel.
Food is one way I care for people.
Technology is how I organize and build.

They are different expressions, yet they are all parts of me.

And if someone finished reading everything I had ever written and understood something about me that I could not simply explain in conversation, then the writing had done its job.

Research Notes for Question 2

The phrase "the brain was rewired" is everyday language for neuroplastic reorganization.

The studies below examined groups of people who were naturally left-handed and forced during childhood to write with their right hand.

The 2002 PET study found persistent differences in the functional neuroanatomy of handwriting even after decades of right-hand writing. Converted left-handers showed a more bilateral activation pattern than natural right-handers.

The 2007 fMRI study found that converted left-handers retained strong activation in right-hemisphere motor-association areas while also recruiting left-hemisphere areas related to right-hand use. The researchers concluded that educational attempts to switch handedness do not simply erase the original motor organization.

The 2010 structural MRI study found differences involving the central sulcus and putamen. Its authors described the findings as evidence that forced use of the nondominant hand can shape the structure of motor-related brain regions.

These studies support saying that forced switching can reorganize the brain. They do not, by themselves, prove which exact functional or structural changes occurred in one particular individual without that person's neurological imaging.

Sources

[1] Siebner, H. R., Limmer, C., Peinemann, A., Drzezga, A., Bloem, B. R., Schwaiger, M., and Conrad, B. (2002). Long-Term Consequences of Switching Handedness: A Positron Emission Tomography Study on Handwriting in Converted Left-Handers. Journal of Neuroscience, 22(7), 2816-2825.
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6758284/

[2] Kloeppel, S., Vongerichten, A., van Eimeren, T., Frackowiak, R. S. J., and Siebner, H. R. (2007). Can Left-Handedness Be Switched? Insights from an Early Switch of Handwriting. Journal of Neuroscience, 27(29), 7847-7853.
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6672868/

[3] Kloeppel, S., Mangin, J.-F., Vongerichten, A., Frackowiak, R. S. J., and Siebner, H. R. (2010). Nurture versus Nature: Long-Term Impact of Forced Right-Handedness on Structure of Pericentral Cortex and Basal Ganglia. Journal of Neuroscience, 30(9), 3271-3275.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20203186/

I have also been developing projects such as Phrases People Hide Behind, Tesseract, Introspective Poetry, the Sequential Alphabet Index, and other writing and poetic frameworks. I also have fiction and other works still in development.

But beneath all those titles and forms, I would want someone who read everything I have written to understand that I was trying to see clearly - myself, other people, the world around me, and the things we sometimes leave unsaid.

Maybe that is the connection among all of my creative work:

Photography is how I see.
Writing is how I think and question.
Music is how I feel.
Food is one way I care for people.
Technology is how I organize and build.

They are different expressions, yet they are all parts of me.

And if someone finished reading everything I had ever written and understood something about me that I could not simply explain in conversation, then the writing had done its job.

Research Notes for Question 2

The phrase "the brain was rewired" is everyday language for neuroplastic reorganization.

The studies below examined groups of people who were naturally left-handed and forced during childhood to write with their right hand.

The 2002 PET study found persistent differences in the functional neuroanatomy of handwriting even after decades of right-hand writing. Converted left-handers showed a more bilateral activation pattern than natural right-handers.

The 2007 fMRI study found that converted left-handers retained strong activation in right-hemisphere motor-association areas while also recruiting left-hemisphere areas related to right-hand use. The researchers concluded that educational attempts to switch handedness do not simply erase the original motor organization.

The 2010 structural MRI study found differences involving the central sulcus and putamen. Its authors described the findings as evidence that forced use of the nondominant hand can shape the structure of motor-related brain regions.

These studies support saying that forced switching can reorganize the brain. They do not, by themselves, prove which exact functional or structural changes occurred in one particular individual without that person's neurological imaging.

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6758284/

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6672868/

[3] Kloeppel, S., Mangin, J.-F., Vongerichten, A., Frackowiak, R. S. J., and Siebner, H. R. (2010). Nurture versus Nature: Long-Term Impact of Forced Right-Handedness on Structure of Pericentral Cortex and Basal Ganglia. Journal of Neuroscience, 30(9), 3271-3275.

revisions.title: Flowers and Thorns
revisions.content: Flowers and Thorns is a collection of recent prose and poetry that explores the beauty and the pain that live side by side in the human experience. Through tender reflections and unflinching truths, Praise Mk Nkhoma writes about love and heartbreak, hope and silence, joy and sorrow. These pieces are drawn from real life, (its thorns and its flowers), and speak to anyone who has ever been wounded, healed, lost, found, or still becoming. Praise Mk Nkhoma is a Malawian poet whose work is concerned with the ordinary burdens and consolations of being alive. He writes about love, memory, poverty, faith, loss, and the difficult business of becoming oneself, believing that the most enduring subjects are often those encountered in everyday life.

revisions.content: My understanding of safety includes having stable, adequate, and affordable housing and confidence that I will be able to remain housed.

snapshot.body:
Housing is another separate form of safety I want to examine.

HUD's Worst Case Housing Needs: 2025 Report to Congress defines worst case housing needs as affecting very-low-income renters who do not receive housing assistance and who either spend more than half of their income on rent, live in severely inadequate housing, or both.

HUD reported 8.46 million renter households with worst case housing needs in 2023.

Reference

Worst Case Housing Needs: 2025 Report to Congress
U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development

Executive Summary:
Printed pages vii-viii
PDF viewer pages 8-9

The Federal Reserve's Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025 also reported that 23 percent of renters had been behind on rent at some point during 2025.

Federal Reserve Reference:
Housing section
Printed page 73
PDF viewer page 77

For my Safety research, housing safety concerns not simply having a physical structure around me but having stability and confidence that my housing can be maintained.

revisions.title: A Culinary Garden Can Be Designed for Sensory Interaction
revisions.content: A culinary garden can be designed around the sensory experience of moving through and interacting with plants, not only around growing and harvesting ingredients.

snapshot.title: A Culinary Garden Can Be Designed for Sensory Interaction
snapshot.mainIdea: A culinary garden can be designed around the sensory experience of moving through and interacting with plants, not only around growing and harvesting ingredients.
snapshot.body:
A culinary garden has practical requirements: sunlight, water, drainage, plant size, accessibility, compatibility, and yield. Those factors determine whether plants can grow successfully, but they do not have to be the only considerations when deciding where plants belong.

Aroma introduces another possibility.

If rosemary or thyme is planted beside a path, normal movement through the garden can brush the foliage and release fragrance. Mint or lemon balm can provide a similar aromatic experience from containers without allowing their spreading growth to dominate a bed.

Placement can therefore ask two different questions:

Where will this plant grow well?

What will I experience when I encounter this plant here?

That distinction changes the garden from a purely productive space into a sensory environment.

The idea is particularly relevant to culinary gardening because sensory interaction with a plant can continue into cooking. A cook may first see the plant growing, touch its leaves, smell its aroma, learn how it grows, harvest it, transform it through cooking, and finally taste it.

The garden becomes part of ingredient education rather than simply the place where an ingredient originates.

Explore whether a broken promise becomes worthless even when it was genuinely meant when spoken.

revisions.content: The fixed value. Its worth may be understood differently when it is spoken, trusted, tested, kept, broken, and remembered afterward.

snapshot.title: What is a promise worth?
snapshot.mainIdea: The fixed value. Its worth may be understood differently when it is spoken, trusted, tested, kept, broken, and remembered afterward.
snapshot.body:
Poem development structure:

  1. The promise when it is spoken
    Hope, sincerity, belief.

  2. The trust it inspires
    What the other person risks by believing.

  3. The cost of keeping it
    Sacrifice, inconvenience, loyalty, endurance.

  4. The breaking of it
    Disappointment, betrayal, circumstance, failure.

  5. The question of intention
    Was it a lie, or was it once genuinely meant?

  6. The aftermath
    What remains after the words are gone.

  7. The final measure of worth
    Whether a promise is valued by its words, intent, fulfillment, or consequences.

Structural movement:

Return throughout the poem to the question:

"What is a promise worth?"

Each return can carry more weight because the reader has passed through another stage of the promise.

The poem does not have to answer:

"A promise is worth this."

Instead, it can gradually reveal that a promise's worth changes depending on where one stands in its life cycle:

  • when it is made

  • when it is trusted

  • when it is tested

  • when it is kept

  • when it is broken

This allows the poem to move toward moral reflection and an understanding of complexity rather than reducing the promise to a single fixed value.

revisions.title: Bacteria, Bacterial Growth, and TCS Foods
revisions.content: Food safety depends on understanding the types of bacteria associated with food, the conditions that allow pathogenic bacteria to grow, and the foods that require time and temperature control to prevent foodborne illness.

snapshot.title: Bacteria, Bacterial Growth, and TCS Foods
snapshot.mainIdea: Food safety depends on understanding the types of bacteria associated with food, the conditions that allow pathogenic bacteria to grow, and the foods that require time and temperature control to prevent foodborne illness.
snapshot.body:
Bacteria are present throughout the environment, including air, water, soil, food, human skin, and the human body. In food sanitation, bacteria can be grouped according to their practical effect on food and human health.

Harmless Bacteria

Most bacteria are neither beneficial nor harmful. These bacteria generally are not a concern in food sanitation.

Beneficial Bacteria

Beneficial bacteria perform useful functions. Some live in the intestinal tract, where they help control harmful bacteria, assist digestion, and contribute to nutrient production.

Beneficial bacteria are also important in food production and are used to produce foods such as:

Cheese
Yogurt
Sauerkraut

Undesirable Bacteria

Undesirable bacteria cause food spoilage, including:

Souring
Putrefaction
Decomposition
Slimy or sticky surfaces
Discoloration
Unpleasant odors

Spoilage organisms may or may not cause disease.

Food spoilage is important because:

It causes financial loss.
It can indicate improper food handling or storage.
Conditions that allow spoilage organisms to grow may also allow pathogens to grow.

Disease-Causing Bacteria

Disease-causing bacteria are called pathogens.

Pathogenic bacteria are responsible for many foodborne illnesses.

Food contaminated with pathogens may show no visible, aromatic, or flavor-related signs of contamination. Food therefore cannot be judged safe simply by smelling, tasting, or visually inspecting it.

Protection against pathogenic bacteria requires:

Proper personal hygiene
Sanitary food handling
Correct storage
Proper temperature control

Foodborne bacterial illness can occur in three general ways.

Intoxication

Intoxication occurs when bacteria grow in food and produce toxins before the food is eaten.

The illness is caused primarily by the toxins already present in the food rather than by bacterial growth inside the body.

Infection

Infection occurs when living bacteria or other microorganisms enter the intestinal system and multiply or attack the body.

The organisms themselves cause the illness.

Toxin-Mediated Infection

Toxin-mediated infection occurs when bacteria enter the body, grow or multiply, and then produce toxins within the body.

The toxins produced during bacterial growth cause illness.

Bacterial Growth

Bacteria reproduce primarily by binary fission, in which one bacterial cell divides into two.

Under favorable conditions, some bacteria can double approximately every 15 to 30 minutes.

Rapid multiplication means that a small initial population can become very large within only a few hours.

Conditions Required for Bacterial Growth

Food

Bacteria require nutrients.

Foods containing substantial amounts of protein are particularly favorable environments for many bacteria.

Examples include:

Meat
Poultry
Fish
Dairy products
Eggs
Some grains
Some vegetables

Moisture

Bacteria require available water to grow and absorb nutrients.

Dry foods generally support less bacterial growth.

High concentrations of salt or sugar can also reduce the amount of water available to microorganisms.

Water Activity

The amount of water available for microbial growth is measured as water activity, abbreviated aw.

The scale ranges from:

0 = essentially no available water
1.0 = maximum water availability

Many foodborne pathogens require relatively high water activity.

pH

pH measures the acidity or alkalinity of a substance.

The scale ranges from:

0 = strongly acidic
7 = neutral
14 = strongly alkaline

Many foodborne pathogens prefer environments that are near neutral or only moderately acidic.

In general, increasing acidity inhibits the growth of many pathogenic bacteria.

Different bacterial species have different pH tolerances.

Salmonella, for example, can tolerate a wider pH range than some other foodborne bacteria.

Temperature

Temperature strongly affects bacterial growth.

Many foodborne pathogens grow rapidly at moderate or warm temperatures.

The temperature range traditionally called the Food Danger Zone is approximately:

40°F–140°F
4°C–60°C

Food safety standards may use slightly different temperature boundaries depending on the regulatory authority or edition of the food-safety standard being followed.

Oxygen

Bacteria differ in their oxygen requirements.

Aerobic Bacteria

Aerobic bacteria require oxygen for growth.

Anaerobic Bacteria

Anaerobic bacteria grow in environments where oxygen is absent or very limited.

Clostridium botulinum, the organism associated with botulism, is an important anaerobic food-safety hazard.

Facultative Bacteria

Facultative bacteria can grow either in the presence or absence of oxygen.

Many bacteria associated with foodborne disease are facultative.

Time

Bacteria require sufficient time under favorable conditions to multiply.

When bacteria enter a new environment, they may initially undergo a lag phase while adapting to their surroundings.

During this period, bacterial reproduction occurs slowly or may temporarily stop.

Once adaptation is complete and environmental conditions are favorable, rapid growth can begin.

Temperature Classifications of Bacteria

Psychrophiles

Psychrophiles grow well at cold temperatures.

Thermophiles

Thermophiles grow well at high temperatures.

Some extreme thermophiles can survive or grow at exceptionally high temperatures.

Mesophiles

Mesophiles grow best at moderate temperatures.

Many foodborne pathogens are mesophilic organisms.

Potentially Hazardous Foods and TCS Foods

Foods capable of supporting rapid growth of pathogenic microorganisms were traditionally called potentially hazardous foods.

The modern term TCS food means:

Time/Temperature Control for Safety.

TCS foods require careful control of time and temperature to limit pathogen growth or toxin production.

Foods most likely to support bacterial growth commonly have:

Available moisture
Suitable nutrients
A relatively favorable pH
Appropriate growth temperatures

Major Categories of TCS Foods

Animal Foods

Foods derived from animals are generally TCS foods.

Examples include:

Meat
Poultry
Fish
Shellfish
Eggs
Milk
Dairy products

Heat-Treated Plant Foods

Plant foods that have been cooked or otherwise heat-treated may become TCS foods.

Examples include:

Cooked vegetables
Cooked pasta
Cooked rice
Tofu

Other Important TCS Foods

Raw seed sprouts

Cut melons

Cut tomatoes

Garlic-and-oil mixtures that have not been specially treated to prevent pathogen growth

Produce and Foodborne Illness

Foodborne illness is not limited to meat, poultry, seafood, eggs, or dairy products.

Fresh fruits and vegetables can become contaminated through:

Soil
Animal waste
Irrigation water
Harvesting
Packing
Transportation
Storage
Food preparation

Cutting produce can transfer microorganisms from the exterior surface into edible portions.

Produce should therefore be washed and handled according to safe food-handling procedures.

Foods Generally Less Supportive of Pathogen Growth

Foods that generally present lower bacterial-growth risk include:

Dried foods
Dehydrated foods
Strongly acidic foods
Commercially processed foods remaining in unopened, intact containers

Whether a particular food requires time and temperature control depends on factors including:

pH
Water activity
Ingredients
Processing method
Packaging
Storage conditions
